Book / Chapter 2 / Section 4
Section 4 of 5 · Summary

Framing ML Problems

"Customer support is slow" is a problem, not an ML problem. An ML problem is defined by its inputs, its outputs and the objective function that guides learning. The output decides the task type; how you frame it can make a problem easy or painful; the objective (loss) function is what the model actually optimises; and when goals compete, decouple them.

4.1Problem → ML problem4.2Task types4.3Multiclass & multilabel4.4Framing choices4.5Objective functions4.6Decoupling objectives
4.1

From a business problem to an ML problem

Watch · Framing "support is slow"

Our version of the book's example, for an Indian online retailer.

Say your boss hears a rival handles support requests twice as fast with ML, and wants the same. Slow support isn't an ML problem yet. Investigating, you find the bottleneck is routing: getting each request to the right one of four departments (accounting, inventory, HR, IT).

  • Input: the customer's request text.
  • Output: one of four departments. That makes it classification.
  • Objective: minimise the difference between predicted and actual department.

Turning raw inputs into features is Chapter 5. This section focuses on outputs and objectives.

Code lab · Python

A ticket router in 10 lines

Setup for this section is the same as before. Step 7 trains a TF-IDF + logistic regression classifier on 24 hand-written tickets, six per department, and routes four new ones.

Python · step 7 · frame it: inputs, outputs, objective
tickets = [
    ("refund not received for order", "accounting"), ("invoice shows wrong GST amount", "accounting"),
    ("charged twice on my card", "accounting"), ("need a copy of last month's bill", "accounting"),
    ("payment failed but money deducted", "accounting"), ("EMI amount looks incorrect", "accounting"),
    ("item out of stock when will it return", "inventory"), ("wrong size delivered need exchange", "inventory"),
    ("product arrived damaged", "inventory"), ("is the blue variant available", "inventory"),
    ("order shows shipped but not delivered", "inventory"), ("received fewer items than ordered", "inventory"),
    ("my salary slip is missing", "hr"), ("how many leaves do I have left", "hr"),
    ("update my bank details for payroll", "hr"), ("joining letter not received", "hr"),
    ("need experience certificate", "hr"), ("question about health insurance policy", "hr"),
    ("cannot log in to the app", "it"), ("password reset link not working", "it"),
    ("app crashes when I open orders", "it"), ("OTP not coming on my phone", "it"),
    ("website very slow today", "it"), ("two factor authentication error", "it"),
]
texts, depts = zip(*tickets)

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
router = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)), LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=1000))
router.fit(texts, depts)            # input: ticket text | output: department | objective: cross-entropy

new = ["money deducted twice", "parcel damaged in transit", "forgot my password", "payslip for March missing"]
for t, d, p in zip(new, router.predict(new), router.predict_proba(new).max(axis=1)):
    print(f"{t:<28} -> {d:<10} ({p:.0%} sure)")
Output
money deducted twice         -> accounting (67% sure)
parcel damaged in transit    -> inventory  (37% sure)
forgot my password           -> it         (39% sure)
payslip for March missing    -> hr         (44% sure)
How to read it

All four go to the right department. The confidence numbers are modest (37–67%) because 24 examples is tiny; in production you'd train on thousands of real tickets, and send low-confidence ones to a person instead of guessing.

4.2

Classification vs regression

Play · A score becomes a class

Same eight emails as the code lab. Pink dots are real spam.

Classification puts inputs into categories (spam or not). Regression outputs a number (a flat's rent). They convert easily:

  • Regression → classification: put prices into buckets and predict the bucket.
  • Classification → regression: output a score from 0 to 1, then pick a threshold (e.g. above 0.5 = spam).

Within classification, fewer classes are easier. Binary (toxic or not, cancer or not, fraud or not) is the simplest; F1 scores and confusion matrices are far more intuitive with two classes.

Code lab · Python

Thresholds and buckets

Step 8 turns eight spam scores into decisions at three thresholds, and five rents into price bands.

Python · step 8 · regression and classification are cousins
spam_scores = np.array([0.04, 0.12, 0.35, 0.48, 0.52, 0.61, 0.77, 0.93])
is_spam     = np.array([0,    0,    0,    1,    0,    1,    1,    1])
for t in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
    pred = (spam_scores >= t).astype(int)
    print(f"threshold {t}: flagged {pred.sum()}  precision {precision_score(is_spam, pred):.2f}  "
          f"recall {recall_score(is_spam, pred):.2f}")

rents = pd.Series([14_000, 28_500, 41_000, 66_000, 1_25_000])
buckets = pd.cut(rents, [0, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000, np.inf],
                 labels=["under 20k", "20–40k", "40–80k", "80k+"])
print("\nrent as a class:", list(zip(rents, buckets)))
Output
threshold 0.3: flagged 6  precision 0.67  recall 1.00
threshold 0.5: flagged 4  precision 0.75  recall 0.75
threshold 0.7: flagged 2  precision 1.00  recall 0.50

rent as a class: [(14000, 'under 20k'), (28500, '20–40k'), (41000, '40–80k'), (66000, '40–80k'), (125000, '80k+')]
How to read it

Precision: of the emails flagged, how many were spam. Recall: of the real spam, how much was flagged. A low threshold catches all spam but flags good mail too; a high one flags only sure cases but lets spam through. The threshold is a business choice, not a model property. The rents show the reverse trick: a number turned into a class.

4.3

Multiclass, high cardinality and multilabel

Play · How much data for many classes?
At about 100 examples per class, you need at least

The book's rule of thumb from the author's experience.

With more than two classes, it's multiclass. With thousands (diseases, product categories), it has high cardinality, which makes data collection hard, especially for rare classes. Hierarchical classification helps: first pick a big group (electronics, fashion, home, pets), then a subgroup within it (shoes, shirts, jeans).

If an example can belong to several classes at once (an article about cricket and business), it's multilabel. Two approaches: one model whose label is a vector with several 1s, or one binary model per class.

Why multilabel hurtsAnnotators disagree on how many labels apply. And since the number of labels varies, turning probabilities into an answer is ambiguous: top one? top two? everything above a threshold?
Code lab · Python

One label or many?

Step 9 takes one article's four topic scores and reads them as multiclass, then with three multilabel rules. Then it turns labelled articles into multilabel vectors.

Python · step 9 · one label or many?
topics = ["cricket", "business", "tech", "politics"]
probs = np.array([0.08, 0.41, 0.36, 0.15])      # model's scores for one article

print("multiclass pick (one topic):", topics[probs.argmax()])
for rule, chosen in [("top-2", np.argsort(probs)[::-1][:2]),
                     ("score >= 0.3", np.where(probs >= 0.3)[0]),
                     ("score >= 0.1", np.where(probs >= 0.1)[0])]:
    print(f"multilabel, {rule:<13} ->", [topics[i] for i in chosen])

# One binary model per topic: each answers "is this article about X?"
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import MultiLabelBinarizer
articles = ["Sensex jumps as IT stocks rally", "India wins the T20 series", "Startup raises funds for AI chips",
            "Parliament debates data protection bill", "BCCI signs new broadcast deal worth crores",
            "New smartphone launch in Bengaluru", "Budget boosts semiconductor funding", "Ministry bans cricket betting apps"]
labels = [["business", "tech"], ["cricket"], ["business", "tech"], ["politics", "tech"],
          ["cricket", "business"], ["tech"], ["business", "politics", "tech"], ["cricket", "politics", "tech"]]
mlb = MultiLabelBinarizer(classes=topics)
Y = mlb.fit_transform(labels)
print("\nlabel vectors [cricket, business, tech, politics]:")
for a, row in zip(articles[:3], Y[:3]):
    print(f"  {row}  {a}")
Output
multiclass pick (one topic): business
multilabel, top-2         -> ['business', 'tech']
multilabel, score >= 0.3  -> ['business', 'tech']
multilabel, score >= 0.1  -> ['business', 'tech', 'politics']

label vectors [cricket, business, tech, politics]:
  [0 1 1 0]  Sensex jumps as IT stocks rally
  [1 0 0 0]  India wins the T20 series
  [0 1 1 0]  Startup raises funds for AI chips
How to read it

Multiclass forces one answer: business. Multilabel rules disagree: top-2 and "≥ 0.3" give business and tech; "≥ 0.1" adds politics. Same scores, different answers, which is why multilabel needs agreed rules. In the label vectors, each position is a topic, and more than one can be 1.

4.4

Many ways to frame a problem

Play · Predict the next app a user opens

Framing can change difficulty enormously. To predict which app someone opens next:

As multiclassInput: user and context features. Output: one probability per app on the phone. Each new app changes the output size, so you retrain (at least part of) the model.
As one score per appInput: user, context and the app's features. Output: one number, how likely this app is opened now. Score every app and rank. A new app is just a new row to score.
Code lab · Python

Add an app without retraining

Step 10 trains one scorer on (moment, app) pairs from 3,000 past moments: food apps at lunch and video apps at night are opened more. Then a new food app, Swiggy, is installed.

Python · step 10 · framing decides how painful change is
apps = pd.DataFrame({"app": ["WhatsApp", "PhonePe", "YouTube", "Zomato", "Gmail"],
                     "is_food": [0, 0, 0, 1, 0], "is_video": [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]})

# Score each (context, app) pair with ONE model. Output: a single number per pair.
def pair_rows(hour, apps):
    lunch, evening = int(12 <= hour <= 14), int(hour >= 19)
    return pd.DataFrame({"lunch": lunch, "evening": evening,
                         "is_food": apps["is_food"], "is_video": apps["is_video"],
                         "lunch_x_food": lunch * apps["is_food"], "evening_x_video": evening * apps["is_video"]})

hist = []
for _ in range(3000):                       # 3,000 past moments, each with every app
    hour = int(rng.integers(6, 24))
    rows = pair_rows(hour, apps)
    p = 0.15 + 0.55 * rows["lunch_x_food"] + 0.5 * rows["evening_x_video"]
    hist.append(rows.assign(opened=rng.random(len(rows)) < p))
hist = pd.concat(hist)
scorer = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(hist.drop(columns="opened"), hist["opened"])

def rank_apps(hour, apps):
    s = scorer.predict_proba(pair_rows(hour, apps))[:, 1]
    return apps.assign(score=s.round(2)).sort_values("score", ascending=False)[["app", "score"]]

print("1 pm:", rank_apps(13, apps).head(2).to_dict("records"))
print("9 pm:", rank_apps(21, apps).head(2).to_dict("records"))

# A new app is installed. No retraining: describe it with the same features and score it.
apps2 = pd.concat([apps, pd.DataFrame({"app": ["Swiggy"], "is_food": [1], "is_video": [0]})], ignore_index=True)
print("1 pm after installing Swiggy:", rank_apps(13, apps2).head(3).to_dict("records"))
Output
1 pm: [{'app': 'Zomato', 'score': 0.71}, {'app': 'WhatsApp', 'score': 0.15}]
9 pm: [{'app': 'YouTube', 'score': 0.63}, {'app': 'WhatsApp', 'score': 0.16}]
1 pm after installing Swiggy: [{'app': 'Zomato', 'score': 0.71}, {'app': 'Swiggy', 'score': 0.71}, {'app': 'WhatsApp', 'score': 0.15}]
How to read it

At 1 pm the food app leads; at 9 pm the video app does. The new app was never in the training data, yet it gets a sensible score immediately, because the model scores apps by their features (food, video), not by their identity. In the multiclass framing, Swiggy would have needed a new output and retraining.

4.5

Objective functions

Play · The price of being confidently wrong

Cross-entropy for one example: −log(probability of the true class).

To learn, a model needs an objective function, also called a loss function, since learning minimises the loss from wrong predictions. In supervised learning it compares outputs with true labels.

  • Regression: RMSE or MAE.
  • Binary classification: logistic loss (log loss).
  • Multiclass classification: cross-entropy.

Choosing one is usually easy, not because losses are easy, but because most engineers use these standard ones. (Objective functions are maths, distinct from the business and ML objectives of Section 1.)

Code lab · Python

Cross-entropy, MAE and RMSE by hand

Step 11 computes cross-entropy for three predictions on an article whose true topic is business, then MAE and RMSE for four rent predictions, and checks against scikit-learn.

Python · step 11 · objective functions by hand
def cross_entropy(true_onehot, probs):
    probs = np.clip(probs, 1e-12, 1)
    return -np.sum(true_onehot * np.log(probs))

truth = np.array([0, 1, 0, 0])                 # the article really is "business"
for name, p in [("confident and right", [0.05, 0.85, 0.05, 0.05]),
                ("unsure", [0.25, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15]),
                ("confident and wrong", [0.85, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05])]:
    print(f"{name:<22} cross-entropy {cross_entropy(truth, np.array(p)):.3f}")

y_true = np.array([42_000, 35_500, 61_000, 28_000])
y_pred = np.array([40_000, 36_000, 52_000, 29_000])
err = y_pred - y_true
print(f"\nrent model  MAE ₹{np.abs(err).mean():,.0f}   RMSE ₹{np.sqrt((err ** 2).mean()):,.0f}")
print("same as sklearn's log_loss for a binary case:",
      round(log_loss([1, 0, 1], [0.9, 0.2, 0.6]), 4))
Output
confident and right    cross-entropy 0.163
unsure                 cross-entropy 1.050
confident and wrong    cross-entropy 2.996

rent model  MAE ₹3,125   RMSE ₹4,644
same as sklearn's log_loss for a binary case: 0.2798
How to read it

Confident and right costs little (0.16); unsure costs more (1.05); confident and wrong costs a lot (3.0). That is what pushes a model to be calibrated as well as correct. For rents, RMSE (₹4,644) is higher than MAE (₹3,125) because squaring punishes the one big miss (₹9,000 on the ₹61,000 flat) more.

4.6

Decoupling objectives

Play · Rank a news feed

Same six posts as the code lab.

A news feed that maximises engagement learns that extreme posts get clicks. To keep it wholesome you add goals: filter spam, NSFW content and misinformation, and rank by quality as well as engagement. But quality and engagement conflict.

One model, combined lossloss = α·quality_loss + β·engagement_loss. Each time you change α or β, you retrain.
Two models, combined scoresA quality model and an engagement model, each with its own loss; rank by α·quality + β·engagement. Change the weights any time, no retraining.
Decouple firstSeparate models are easier to tune and to maintain: spam tactics change far faster than ideas of quality, so the spam filter can be updated weekly while the quality model stays put. Pareto optimisation is the systematic way to explore the trade-off.
Code lab · Python

Change the feed without retraining

Step 12 takes predicted quality and engagement for six posts (as if from two models) and ranks them with three weights.

Python · step 12 · decouple objectives
posts = pd.DataFrame({
    "post": ["Monsoon travel tips", "SHOCKING claim about vaccines", "Local school wins award",
             "Outrage over celebrity tweet", "How UPI works, explained", "Miracle cure for diabetes!!"],
    "pred_quality": [0.82, 0.10, 0.75, 0.30, 0.90, 0.05],          # from quality_model
    "pred_engagement": [0.40, 0.95, 0.35, 0.88, 0.45, 0.80],       # from engagement_model
})

def feed(alpha):
    s = alpha * posts["pred_quality"] + (1 - alpha) * posts["pred_engagement"]
    return posts.assign(score=s.round(2)).sort_values("score", ascending=False)["post"].head(3).tolist()

for alpha in [0.0, 0.5, 0.8]:
    print(f"alpha {alpha} (weight on quality): {feed(alpha)}")
Output
alpha 0.0 (weight on quality): ['SHOCKING claim about vaccines', 'Outrage over celebrity tweet', 'Miracle cure for diabetes!!']
alpha 0.5 (weight on quality): ['How UPI works, explained', 'Monsoon travel tips', 'Outrage over celebrity tweet']
alpha 0.8 (weight on quality): ['How UPI works, explained', 'Monsoon travel tips', 'Local school wins award']
How to read it

All engagement gives a feed of shock and outrage. At 0.5 the explainer and travel tips rise but outrage still makes the cut. At 0.8 the feed is all good posts. Three feeds, zero retraining: you just changed one number.

Book / Chapter 2 / Section 5
Section 5 of 5 · Summary

Mind vs Data

A decade of progress suggests ML success depends largely on the data, and most companies now focus on their data more than their algorithms. Yet a lively debate continues: mind (clever architectures, built-in assumptions) or data (with the compute that comes with it)? The real question isn't whether data is necessary, but whether finite data is sufficient.

5.1The debate5.2More data or a smarter model?5.3When more data hurts
5.1

The debate

Play · Which camp?

In theory you can pursue both clever design and big data, but time spent on one is often taken from the other. Every recent ML conference has had some version of this debate.

Monica Rogati's "AI hierarchy of needs" puts data at the base of data science: collect it, move and store it, explore and clean it, before any learning. Without data there's no data science.

The word finite matters: with infinite data you could just look the answer up. A lot of data is not infinite data.

5.2

More data or a smarter model?

Compare · Language-model training data

Tokens of training text, log scale. One Billion Word Benchmark (Chelba et al., 2013); GPT-2 and GPT-3 as reported by OpenAI.

Whoever wins the argument, data is essential for now. Models keep growing and eating more data: from under a billion tokens in a 2013 benchmark, to about 10 billion for GPT-2 in 2019, to about 500 billion for GPT-3 a year later. The success of AlexNet, BERT and GPT rested on access to large data.

Code lab · Python

A simple model with more data vs a strong model with less

Step 13 learns a tangled pattern two ways: a simple decision tree that gets all the data, and a gradient-boosted model that never sees more than 1,000 examples.

Python · step 13 · more data or a smarter model?
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

def make(n, seed):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = r.normal(size=(n, 6))
    y = (np.sin(X[:, 0] * 2) + X[:, 1] * X[:, 2] + 0.5 * X[:, 3] + r.normal(0, .4, n)) > 0
    return X, y

X_test2, y_test2 = make(5000, 123)
sizes = [100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000]
simple, fancy = [], []
for n_ in sizes:
    Xs, ys = make(n_, n_)
    simple.append(accuracy_score(y_test2, DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=0).fit(Xs, ys).predict(X_test2)))
    fancy.append(accuracy_score(y_test2, HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xs[:min(n_, 1000)], ys[:min(n_, 1000)]).predict(X_test2)))
print(pd.DataFrame({"examples": sizes, "simple model, all data": np.round(simple, 3),
                    "boosted model, max 1,000": np.round(fancy, 3)}).to_string(index=False))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.plot(sizes, simple, "o-", label="simple tree, all the data")
ax.plot(sizes, fancy, "s--", label="boosted model, capped at 1,000 examples")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="training examples available", ylabel="test accuracy")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
Output
 examples  simple model, all data  boosted model, max 1,000
      100                   0.612                     0.722
      300                   0.696                     0.802
     1000                   0.778                     0.858
     3000                   0.799                     0.854
    10000                   0.830                     0.846
    30000                   0.852                     0.856
How to read it

With little data, the smarter model wins easily (0.86 vs 0.78 at 1,000 examples). Give the simple model 30× more data and it catches up (0.852 vs 0.856). Both camps have a point: good design gets more out of little data; enough data can make up for a simpler design.

5.3

When more data hurts

Watch · Clean data plus noisy data

Our illustration. Pink squares are wrongly labelled examples.

Much of the last decade's progress came from more data, but more data doesn't always mean a better model. Lower-quality data, such as outdated examples or wrong labels, can make performance worse.

Quality and quantityA lot of the rest of the book is about data: where it comes from (Chapter 3), how to sample and label it (Chapter 4), and how to engineer features from it (Chapter 5).
Code lab · Python

Add 8,000 examples: help or harm?

Step 14 starts with 2,000 clean examples and adds 8,000 more whose labels are 0%, 20% or 40% wrong.

Python · step 14 · more data, worse model
X_clean, y_clean = make(2000, 1)
X_extra, y_extra = make(8000, 2)
for flip in [0.0, 0.2, 0.4]:
    noisy = y_extra ^ (rng.random(len(y_extra)) < flip)       # flip a share of the new labels
    X_all = np.vstack([X_clean, X_extra])
    y_all = np.r_[y_clean, noisy]
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test2, HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_all, y_all).predict(X_test2))
    print(f"2,000 clean + 8,000 extra with {flip:.0%} wrong labels -> accuracy {acc:.3f}")
acc_clean = accuracy_score(y_test2, HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_clean, y_clean).predict(X_test2))
print(f"2,000 clean examples only                         -> accuracy {acc_clean:.3f}")
Output
2,000 clean + 8,000 extra with 0% wrong labels -> accuracy 0.885
2,000 clean + 8,000 extra with 20% wrong labels -> accuracy 0.873
2,000 clean + 8,000 extra with 40% wrong labels -> accuracy 0.815
2,000 clean examples only                         -> accuracy 0.865
How to read it

Clean extra data helps (0.885 vs 0.865 with the clean 2,000 alone). With 20% wrong labels the extra data still helps a little. With 40% wrong it makes the model worse than not adding it at all (0.815). Before adding data, know how good its labels are.

Book / Chapter 2 / Recap
Chapter 2 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Every project starts with why. For a business, ML must be driven by business objectives translated into ML objectives. Good systems are reliable, scalable, maintainable and adaptable; building them is an iterative cycle; and the way you frame a problem shapes everything after. Whatever the outcome of the mind-versus-data debate, data matters, so the next chapters zoom into it, starting with data engineering.

Eight takeaways

1. Start with whyTie ML metrics to a business metric, and prove the link with experiments.
2. Big tests for small liftsDecide the A/B sample size up front; small effects need many users.
3. Fail loudlyML fails silently. Guard inputs and watch outputs.
4. Scale three waysModel size, traffic and model count; automate as you grow.
5. Reproducible by defaultVersion code, data and configs so anyone can rebuild a model.
6. It's a cycleScope, data, model, deploy, monitor, analyse, repeat.
7. Frame it wellInputs, outputs, loss. Score items rather than enumerate them; decouple competing goals.
8. Data matters, quality tooMore data often beats a smarter model, unless the data is bad.

Chapter 3 · Broad summary

Data Engineering Fundamentals

ML grew up alongside big data, and big data systems are full of acronyms and fast-changing tools. This chapter gives you solid ground: where data comes from, how it's stored (formats), how it's structured (data models), which databases process it, how it flows between services, and how it's processed in batches or as a stream. Every idea comes with runnable Python: files, SQL, JSON documents, a graph, a transaction, an ETL job and a tiny message broker.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Sources. User input (messy, needs speed), system logs and behaviour data (huge volume), internal databases, and first-, second- and third-party data.
  2. Formats. JSON is everywhere. Row-major (CSV) suits writing whole records; column-major (Parquet) suits reading a few columns. Binary formats are smaller and faster than text.
  3. Data models. Relational tables and SQL (declarative), documents (self-contained, flexible), graphs (relationships first). Structured data fixes the schema on write; unstructured data leaves it to the reader.
  4. Storage and processing. Transactional databases (fast, ACID) vs analytical ones (aggregate columns); the line is blurring. ETL cleans data before storing; ELT dumps first, transforms later.
  5. Dataflow. Pass data through databases, through service requests, or through a real-time transport like Kafka. Batch processing makes static features; stream processing makes dynamic ones.

Each section has its own summary, sub-sections and code labs.

Book / Chapter 3 / Section 1
Section 1 of 5 · Summary

Data Sources

ML systems draw on many sources, each with its own quirks and processing needs. User input is messy and needs fast handling. System-generated data, logs and behaviour events, is huge but well-formed. Internal databases hold the business's own records. And third-party data can be bought, though privacy changes are shrinking it.

1.1User input1.2Logs & behaviour1.3Internal & third-party
1.1

User input data

Watch · What users actually type

Our examples. If users can enter something wrong, some will.

Text, images, videos, uploaded files: data users give you directly. If it's at all possible to enter something wrong, someone will: text that's too long or too short, words where numbers belong, files in the wrong format. User input needs heavy checking.

And it's urgentPeople expect results immediately after they submit something, so user input usually needs fast processing too.
Code lab · Python

Validate sign-ups before they reach the model

Setup creates a scratch folder for the files later labs write. Step 1 checks five sign-up records: name length, age, a six-digit Indian PIN code and the photo's file type.

Python · step 0 · setup
import json, os, re, sqlite3, tempfile, time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pd.set_option("display.width", 100)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()            # scratch folder for the files we write
print("writing files to a temporary folder")
Output
writing files to a temporary folder
Python · step 1 · never trust user input
signups = [
    {"name": "Priya Sharma", "age": "29", "pincode": "400076", "photo": "priya.jpg"},
    {"name": "", "age": "34", "pincode": "560001", "photo": "a.png"},
    {"name": "Rahul", "age": "twenty", "pincode": "1100", "photo": "rahul.pdf"},
    {"name": "Aisha Khan", "age": "212", "pincode": "600 042", "photo": "aisha.jpeg"},
    {"name": "x" * 300, "age": "41", "pincode": "700019", "photo": "x.jpg"},
]

def validate(rec):
    problems = []
    if not 1 <= len(rec["name"].strip()) <= 80:
        problems.append("name empty or too long")
    if not rec["age"].isdigit() or not 0 < int(rec["age"]) < 120:
        problems.append(f"age {rec['age'][:10]!r} invalid")
    pin = rec["pincode"].replace(" ", "")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[1-9]\d{5}", pin):
        problems.append(f"PIN {rec['pincode']!r} invalid")
    if not rec["photo"].lower().endswith((".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")):
        problems.append("photo must be jpg or png")
    return problems

for rec in signups:
    issues = validate(rec)
    print(f"{rec['name'][:14]:<14} {'OK' if not issues else 'REJECT: ' + '; '.join(issues)}")
Output
Priya Sharma   OK
               REJECT: name empty or too long
Rahul          REJECT: age 'twenty' invalid; PIN '1100' invalid; photo must be jpg or png
Aisha Khan     REJECT: age '212' invalid
xxxxxxxxxxxxxx REJECT: name empty or too long
How to read it

Only one of five records is clean. Each rejection says why, which you can show the user straight away so they fix it at the source, the cheapest place to fix bad data. Note the 300-character name: limits matter for storage and for models too.

1.2

System-generated data: logs and behaviour

Watch · Signal in the noise

Our illustration: thousands of routine lines, one that matters.

Systems generate logs (memory use, services called, job results) and outputs such as model predictions. Logs give visibility for debugging; mostly you ignore them, until something is on fire. They're rarely malformed, and can often be processed hourly or daily, though fast processing helps you get alerted.

  • Because ML is hard to debug, teams log everything, so volume explodes. Two problems: finding the signal (tools like Logstash, Datadog and Logz.io, often ML-powered, help) and storing it all. Keep logs only as long as they're useful; move rarely read ones to cheaper, slower storage.
  • Behaviour data (clicks, scrolls, ignored pop-ups, long pauses) is system-generated but still user data, and may fall under privacy law.
Code lab · Python

Parse 5,000 log lines and find the one that matters

Step 2 generates a morning's worth of log lines, hides one real incident among them, parses every line with a regular expression into a table, and summarises.

Python · step 2 · logs: lots of noise, a few signals
levels = rng.choice(["INFO", "INFO", "INFO", "DEBUG", "WARN", "ERROR"], 5000, p=[.5, .2, .1, .15, .04, .01])
services = rng.choice(["predict", "features", "auth"], 5000)
lines = [f"2025-03-04T10:{i // 100 % 60:02d}:{i % 60:02d} {lv:<5} service={sv} latency_ms={int(rng.lognormal(4, .4))}"
         for i, (lv, sv) in enumerate(zip(levels, services))]
lines[4321] = "2025-03-04T10:43:21 ERROR service=predict latency_ms=4120 msg='feature store timeout'"
print(lines[0], "\n...", len(lines), "lines\n")

pattern = re.compile(r"(\S+) (\w+)\s+service=(\w+) latency_ms=(\d+)")
logs = pd.DataFrame([pattern.match(l).groups() for l in lines], columns=["ts", "level", "service", "latency_ms"])
logs["latency_ms"] = logs["latency_ms"].astype(int)
print(pd.crosstab(logs["service"], logs["level"]))
print("\nslowest request:", lines[logs["latency_ms"].idxmax()])
Output
2025-03-04T10:00:00 INFO  service=predict latency_ms=67 
... 5000 lines

level     DEBUG  ERROR  INFO  WARN
service                           
auth        253     18  1321    74
features    250     15  1353    74
predict     264     19  1313    46

slowest request: 2025-03-04T10:43:21 ERROR service=predict latency_ms=4120 msg='feature store timeout'
How to read it

The table shows counts by service and level: mostly INFO and DEBUG. The incident is found not by reading but by asking a question of the parsed data (the slowest request), which points straight at a feature-store timeout. Turning unstructured text into a table is the first step of most log analysis.

1.3

Internal databases and third-party data

Play · First, second or third party?

Our clinic-chain examples.

Internal databases run the business: inventory, customers, users. ML components use them constantly; a search for "frozen" might mean frozen peas or the film, and either way the system must check stock before ranking results.

Third-party data is collected by companies about people who aren't their customers. Phones once had advertiser IDs (Apple's IDFA, Android's AAID) that tied activity together, making it easy to buy data as granular as "men, 25–34, in tech, in one city". Vendors sell it cleaned and processed.

Privacy is shrinking itIn 2021 Apple made IDFA opt-in, sharply cutting third-party data on iPhones and pushing companies towards their own first-party data. Some advertisers sought workarounds, such as device fingerprinting.
BACKChapter 3 overviewNEXT · SECTION 2Data Formats
Book / Chapter 3 / Section 2
Section 2 of 5 · Summary

Data Formats

Storing ("persisting") data means serialising it: converting it into a form that can be saved or sent and rebuilt later. Choose a format by how the data will be used: is it human-readable, text or binary, and will you read whole records or a few columns? Three formats show the main trade-offs: JSON, row-major CSV and column-major Parquet.

2.1Serialisation & JSON2.2Row vs column2.3Text vs binary
2.1

Serialisation and JSON

FormatTypeTypical use
JSONText, readableAPIs, configs, everywhere
CSVText, readableSpreadsheets, exports
ParquetBinaryData lakes, warehouses
AvroBinary (mostly)Hadoop, streaming
ProtobufBinary (mostly)Google services, TFRecord
PickleBinaryPython objects, PyTorch

Our summary. Wikipedia's "Comparison of data-serialization formats" lists many more.

Questions to ask before choosing: how to store multimodal samples (images plus text)? Where is storage cheap yet fast? How to store models so they load and run on different hardware?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is language-independent, readable, and its key-value pairs handle data from highly structured to a single blob of text.

JSON's painOnce records follow a schema, changing it later is painful, and text files take a lot of space (2.3).
Code lab · Python

Structured JSON vs a text blob

Step 3 stores one patient two ways, reads the city back from each, then adds a record that lacks a field.

Python · step 3 · JSON: structured or a blob
patient_structured = {"name": "Meera Iyer", "age": 41, "allergies": ["penicillin"],
                      "address": {"city": "Chennai", "pincode": "600042"}}
patient_blob = {"text": "Meera Iyer, 41, allergic to penicillin, lives in Chennai 600042"}

for label, obj in [("structured", patient_structured), ("blob", patient_blob)]:
    s = json.dumps(obj)
    print(f"{label:<10} {len(s):>3} chars  {s[:70]}{'...' if len(s) > 70 else ''}")

# Reading: the structured one answers questions directly; the blob needs parsing
print("\ncity (structured):", patient_structured["address"]["city"])
print("city (blob):      ", re.search(r"in (\w+)", patient_blob["text"]).group(1), "(regex, fragile)")

# Schema change: a new field arrives. Old records don't have it.
records = [patient_structured, {"name": "Arjun Rao", "age": 35, "address": {"city": "Pune"}}]
print("allergies per record:", [r.get("allergies", "MISSING") for r in records])
Output
structured 115 chars  {"name": "Meera Iyer", "age": 41, "allergies": ["penicillin"], "addres...
blob        75 chars  {"text": "Meera Iyer, 41, allergic to penicillin, lives in Chennai 600...

city (structured): Chennai
city (blob):       Chennai (regex, fragile)
allergies per record: [['penicillin'], 'MISSING']
How to read it

The blob is shorter, but getting the city out needs a regular expression that breaks as soon as someone writes "Chennai" differently. The structured version answers directly. The last line is schema change in miniature: the older record has no allergies field, and every reader must cope with "MISSING".

2.2

Row-major vs column-major

Play · How values sit in memory

CSV is row-major: consecutive values in a row are stored next to each other. Parquet is column-major: consecutive values in a column are. Computers read sequential memory much faster than scattered memory.

  • Row-major is better for reading or writing whole examples, e.g. appending each new ride as it happens, or loading today's examples.
  • Column-major is better for reading a few features from many examples. With 1,000 features you can read just the four you need (time, location, distance, price) without touching the rest.
pandas is columnarA DataFrame is built around columns (inspired by R's data frame), while a NumPy array is row-major by default. Looping over a DataFrame row by row is famously slow; convert to NumPy if you must work by row.
Code lab · Python

Time it: by column, by row

Step 4 sums a 20,000 × 10 DataFrame by column and by row, then sums each row of a 2,000 × 2,000 NumPy array stored both ways. Real timings from the build machine; yours will differ.

Python · step 4 · row-major vs column-major
df = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(20_000, 10)), columns=[f"f{i}" for i in range(10)])

def timed(fn, repeat=3):
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(repeat):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return best

t_cols = timed(lambda: [df[c].sum() for c in df.columns])                 # 10 columns
t_rows = timed(lambda: [row.sum() for _, row in df.iloc[:2000].iterrows()], 1) * 10  # scaled to 20k rows
big_c = rng.normal(size=(2000, 2000))                  # NumPy default: C order (row-major)
big_f = np.asfortranarray(big_c)                       # same numbers, Fortran order (column-major)
t_np_rows_c = timed(lambda: [big_c[i].sum() for i in range(2000)])
t_np_rows_f = timed(lambda: [big_f[i].sum() for i in range(2000)])

print(f"pandas, by column:            {t_cols * 1000:8.1f} ms")
print(f"pandas, by row (iterrows):    {t_rows * 1000:8.1f} ms   ({t_rows / t_cols:,.0f}x slower)")
print(f"\n2000 x 2000 NumPy array, summing each row:")
print(f"  stored row-major:             {t_np_rows_c * 1000:8.1f} ms")
print(f"  stored column-major:          {t_np_rows_f * 1000:8.1f} ms   ({t_np_rows_f / t_np_rows_c:.1f}x slower)")
Output
pandas, by column:                 0.4 ms
pandas, by row (iterrows):       457.9 ms   (1,101x slower)

2000 x 2000 NumPy array, summing each row:
  stored row-major:                  2.1 ms
  stored column-major:               5.1 ms   (2.4x slower)
How to read it

Iterating a DataFrame by row is around a thousand times slower than working by column, because each row is assembled from separate columns. In NumPy the same numbers are faster to read row by row when stored row-major, since each row is one contiguous block. Match your access pattern to the layout.

2.3

Text vs binary

Compare · Storing 1,000,000

CSV and JSON are text: open them in any editor and read them. Parquet is binary: raw bytes that only a program knowing the layout can interpret. Binary is more compact.

AWS recommends Parquet for its data lake exports, citing up to 2× faster unloads and up to 6× less storage in S3 than text formats.

Some practitioners dislike CSV for anything but simple text: it can silently lose floating-point precision, and quoting rules vary between tools.

Code lab · Python

The same 100,000 rides as CSV, JSON and Parquet

Step 5 writes 100,000 synthetic rides with 20 columns in three formats, compares file sizes, and times reading just four columns. Step 6 shows how text can lose precision.

Python · step 5 · text vs binary on disk
n = 100_000
rides = pd.DataFrame({
    "ride_id": np.arange(n),
    "ts": pd.Timestamp("2025-03-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 30 * 86400, n), unit="s"),
    "city": rng.choice(["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Bengaluru", "Pune"], n),
    "distance_km": rng.gamma(2, 3, n).round(3),
    "fare_inr": rng.normal(240, 60, n).round(2),
    "surge": rng.choice([1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0], n, p=[.7, .15, .1, .05]),
    **{f"feat_{i}": rng.normal(size=n).astype("float32") for i in range(14)},
})
paths = {"CSV": os.path.join(workdir, "rides.csv"), "JSON lines": os.path.join(workdir, "rides.jsonl"),
         "Parquet": os.path.join(workdir, "rides.parquet")}
rides.to_csv(paths["CSV"], index=False)
rides.to_json(paths["JSON lines"], orient="records", lines=True)
rides.to_parquet(paths["Parquet"], index=False)

sizes = {k: os.path.getsize(p) / 1e6 for k, p in paths.items()}
want = ["ts", "city", "distance_km", "fare_inr"]
pd.read_parquet(paths["Parquet"], columns=["city"])     # warm-up: the first call loads the Parquet library
read_csv = timed(lambda: pd.read_csv(paths["CSV"], usecols=want))
read_pq = timed(lambda: pd.read_parquet(paths["Parquet"], columns=want))
for k, mb in sizes.items():
    print(f"{k:<11} {mb:6.1f} MB")
print(f"\nread 4 of {rides.shape[1]} columns: CSV {read_csv * 1000:.0f} ms, Parquet {read_pq * 1000:.0f} ms")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.4))
ax.barh(list(sizes), list(sizes.values()), color=["#D97E06", "#D63E74", "#0E9466"])
ax.set(xlabel="file size (MB) for the same 100,000 rides")
ax.invert_yaxis()
Output
CSV           20.3 MB
JSON lines    42.0 MB
Parquet       10.8 MB

read 4 of 20 columns: CSV 85 ms, Parquet 4 ms
Python · step 6 · text can lose detail
x = 0.12345678901232323
pd.DataFrame({"x": [x]}).to_csv(os.path.join(workdir, "p.csv"), index=False, float_format="%.10f")
back = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(workdir, "p.csv"))["x"][0]
print("original:  ", repr(x))
print("via CSV:   ", repr(back), " (as written with 10 decimals)")
print("number 1000000 as text:", len("1000000"), "bytes; as int32:", np.int32(1000000).nbytes, "bytes")
Output
original:   0.12345678901232322
via CSV:    0.123456789  (as written with 10 decimals)
number 1000000 as text: 7 bytes; as int32: 4 bytes
How to read it

JSON lines repeats every column name in every record, so it's the largest; CSV is about half that; Parquet about half again, thanks to binary encoding and per-column compression. Reading four columns, Parquet skips the other sixteen entirely and is many times faster. (Its first-ever read in a session also loads the library, which is why the code does one warm-up read before timing.) And a float written as text keeps only the digits you asked for.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1Data SourcesNEXT · SECTION 3Data Models
Book / Chapter 3 / Section 3
Section 3 of 5 · Summary

Data Models

A data model describes how data is represented, and it shapes what your system can easily do. A car can be described by make, model, year and price (handy for buyers) or by owner, number plate and address history (handy for police). The relational model and NoSQL models (documents and graphs) look opposite but are converging. A related split: structured vs unstructured data.

3.1Relational3.2SQL is declarative3.3Documents3.4Graphs3.5Structured vs unstructured
3.1

The relational model and normalisation

Play · Duplicate or split?

Our clinic data.

Invented by Edgar F. Codd in 1970, the relational model is still thriving. Data lives in relations (tables): sets of tuples (rows). Order doesn't matter: shuffle rows or columns and it's the same relation.

Normalisation (first normal form, second normal form, and so on) removes duplication: move repeated details, like a branch's name and city, into their own table and refer to them by ID. Changes then happen in one place, and spellings stay consistent.

The costNormalised data is spread across tables, and joining large tables back together can be expensive.
Code lab · Python

Two tables, one join, one update

Step 7 builds a normalised clinic database in SQLite (in memory): branches in one table, visits in another pointing to their branch. It joins them, renames a branch once, and joins again.

Python · step 7 · normalise, then join
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE branch (branch_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT);
CREATE TABLE visit (visit_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, patient TEXT, treatment TEXT,
                    fee_inr INTEGER, branch_id INTEGER REFERENCES branch(branch_id));
INSERT INTO branch VALUES (1, 'Smile Studio Andheri', 'Mumbai'), (2, 'Smile Studio Koramangala', 'Bengaluru');
INSERT INTO visit VALUES
  (1, 'Asha', 'Cleaning', 1200, 1), (2, 'Vikram', 'Filling', 1500, 1), (3, 'Meera', 'Root canal', 6500, 2),
  (4, 'Rohan', 'Cleaning', 1200, 2), (5, 'Asha', 'Whitening', 4000, 1);
""")
query = """SELECT v.patient, v.treatment, v.fee_inr, b.name AS branch
           FROM visit v JOIN branch b USING (branch_id) ORDER BY v.visit_id"""
print(pd.read_sql(query, db).to_string(index=False))

# The branch is renamed: one update in one table, every visit sees it
db.execute("UPDATE branch SET name = 'Smile Studio Andheri West' WHERE branch_id = 1")
print("\nafter renaming branch 1:")
print(pd.read_sql(query, db).head(2).to_string(index=False))
Output
patient  treatment  fee_inr                   branch
   Asha   Cleaning     1200     Smile Studio Andheri
 Vikram    Filling     1500     Smile Studio Andheri
  Meera Root canal     6500 Smile Studio Koramangala
  Rohan   Cleaning     1200 Smile Studio Koramangala
   Asha  Whitening     4000     Smile Studio Andheri

after renaming branch 1:
patient treatment  fee_inr                    branch
   Asha  Cleaning     1200 Smile Studio Andheri West
 Vikram   Filling     1500 Smile Studio Andheri West
How to read it

The branch name appears in every joined row, but it's stored only once. Renaming it was a single UPDATE on one row, and both of Asha's and Vikram's visits immediately show the new name. In a single denormalised table you'd have to update every matching row and hope you didn't miss one.

3.2

SQL is declarative

Imperative (Python)Declarative (SQL)
You writeThe stepsThe result you want
Who plansYouThe query optimiser
RiskSlow if you loop badlyHuge unreadable queries

SQL is the dominant query language for relational databases (its model differs slightly from pure relations; for example, tables may hold duplicate rows). Crucially, it's declarative: you state which tables, conditions, joins, groupings and sorts you want, and the database decides how. Finding the fastest plan is the job of the query optimiser, one of the hardest problems in databases (ML is even used to improve it). The upside: one optimiser serves every application.

Declarative ML?Frameworks such as Uber's Ludwig and H2O AutoML let you declare features and a task and get a model. Useful, but they automate model building, often the easier part. The hard parts of production ML (features, data processing, evaluation, drift, continual learning) remain.
Code lab · Python

The same answer, two ways

Step 8 totals fees by treatment with a Python loop and with one SQL statement, then asks SQLite how it would run a lookup by patient once an index exists.

Python · step 8 · say what, not how
rows = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM visit", db).to_dict("records")

# Imperative (Python): you spell out every step
totals = {}
for r in rows:
    totals[r["treatment"]] = totals.get(r["treatment"], 0) + r["fee_inr"]
print("imperative:", dict(sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])))

# Declarative (SQL): you describe the result; the database plans the steps
sql = "SELECT treatment, SUM(fee_inr) AS total FROM visit GROUP BY treatment ORDER BY total DESC"
print("declarative:", dict(db.execute(sql).fetchall()))

db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_patient ON visit(patient)")
for row in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM visit WHERE patient = 'Asha'"):
    print("query plan:", row[-1])
Output
imperative: {'Root canal': 6500, 'Whitening': 4000, 'Cleaning': 2400, 'Filling': 1500}
declarative: {'Root canal': 6500, 'Whitening': 4000, 'Cleaning': 2400, 'Filling': 1500}
query plan: SEARCH visit USING INDEX idx_patient (patient=?)
How to read it

Same result both ways. In Python you wrote the loop; in SQL you described the answer. The query plan shows the optimiser choosing the index on patient by itself: you never told it how to search.

3.3

The document model

Compare · One patient's record

NoSQL began as a meetup hashtag and is now read as "Not Only SQL". A 2014 Couchbase survey found frustration with schema management was the top reason people adopted its non-relational database.

A document (JSON, XML or binary BSON) holds everything about one thing under a unique key. A collection of documents is like a table, but documents in it can have different fields.

  • "Schemaless" is misleading: the reader still assumes a structure. Responsibility just moves from writer to reader.
  • Better locality: one lookup returns the whole record.
  • Worse joins: questions across documents mean scanning them all.

PostgreSQL and MySQL now support both relational tables and JSON documents.

Code lab · Python

Fast to fetch, slow to search across

Step 9 stores three patient documents, fetches one by key, then asks a question across all of them.

Python · step 9 · documents: everything about one thing, together
docs = {
    "doc-101": {"patient": "Asha", "branch": {"name": "Andheri", "city": "Mumbai"},
                "visits": [{"treatment": "Cleaning", "fee": 1200}, {"treatment": "Whitening", "fee": 4000}]},
    "doc-102": {"patient": "Meera", "branch": {"name": "Koramangala", "city": "Bengaluru"},
                "visits": [{"treatment": "Root canal", "fee": 6500}], "insurance": "Star Health"},
    "doc-103": {"patient": "Rohan", "branch": {"name": "Koramangala", "city": "Bengaluru"},
                "visits": [{"treatment": "Cleaning", "fee": 1200}]},
}
print("one lookup gets a whole record:", json.dumps(docs["doc-102"])[:90], "...")

# A cross-document question means reading every document
scanned, cheap = 0, []
for key, d in docs.items():
    scanned += 1
    if any(v["fee"] < 2000 for v in d["visits"]):
        cheap.append(d["patient"])
print(f"patients with a visit under ₹2,000: {cheap}  (read {scanned} of {len(docs)} documents)")
print("fields differ between documents:", sorted(set().union(*[d.keys() for d in docs.values()])))
Output
one lookup gets a whole record: {"patient": "Meera", "branch": {"name": "Koramangala", "city": "Bengaluru"}, "visits": [{" ...
patients with a visit under ₹2,000: ['Asha', 'Rohan']  (read 3 of 3 documents)
fields differ between documents: ['branch', 'insurance', 'patient', 'visits']
How to read it

Fetching Meera is one lookup that returns her branch, visits and insurance together. Finding everyone with a cheap visit meant opening every document (3 of 3; imagine 3 million). And only Meera's document has an insurance field: flexible for the writer, extra checks for every reader.

3.4

The graph model

Play · Who was born in India?

Our example graph, the same one as the code lab.

A graph has nodes (people, cities, companies) and edges (born in, within, friend of). Where documents prioritise content, graphs prioritise relationships, and queries that follow relationships are fast.

Finding everyone born in a country is a short walk backwards from the country node along "within" and "born_in" edges. In SQL it's awkward, because the number of hops varies: Pune → Maharashtra → India is one hop longer than Bengaluru → India.

Pick the model for the queryMany queries that are easy in one model are hard in another. Choosing well can make your life much easier.
Code lab · Python

Variable-length paths with networkx

Step 10 builds the graph and, for each person, searches for a path from their birthplace to India, however many hops it takes.

Python · step 10 · graphs: relationships first
import networkx as nx
G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_edges_from([
    ("Ananya", "Pune", {"rel": "born_in"}), ("Pune", "Maharashtra", {"rel": "within"}),
    ("Maharashtra", "India", {"rel": "within"}), ("Kabir", "Bengaluru", {"rel": "born_in"}),
    ("Bengaluru", "India", {"rel": "within"}), ("Lena", "Munich", {"rel": "born_in"}),
    ("Munich", "Germany", {"rel": "within"}), ("Ananya", "Lena", {"rel": "friend_of"}),
])
people = [n for n, _, d in G.edges(data=True) if d["rel"] == "born_in"]
for p in people:
    place = next(v for _, v, d in G.out_edges(p, data=True) if d["rel"] == "born_in")
    path = nx.shortest_path(G, place, "India") if nx.has_path(G, place, "India") else None
    print(f"{p:<7} born in India? {'yes' if path else 'no ':<4} {' -> '.join([p] + path) if path else ''}")
Output
Ananya  born in India? yes  Ananya -> Pune -> Maharashtra -> India
Kabir   born in India? yes  Kabir -> Bengaluru -> India
Lena    born in India? no
How to read it

Ananya's path has three hops, Kabir's two, and the same code handles both. Lena's birthplace never reaches India. Graph databases such as Neo4j run this kind of traversal at scale.

3.5

Structured vs unstructured data

StructuredUnstructured
SchemaDefined up frontNone required
StrengthEasy to search and analyseArrives fast, from any source
PainSchema changes ripple everywhereReaders must guess the structure
Lives inData warehouseData lake

Our summary.

Structured data follows a schema (e.g. name: up to 50 characters; age: integer 0–200), so analysing it is easy. But change the schema and you must update all old data, which breeds odd bugs. In one real case the book describes, missing ages were stored as 0 and the model learned about "zero-year-old" customers.

Unstructured data (text, logs, images, audio) has no enforced schema, though it may have patterns you can extract. It's flexible to store: everything can become bytes.

Who carries the structure?Structured: the code that writes data. Unstructured: the code that reads it. Warehouses store processed, structured data; lakes store raw data.
Code lab · Python

Find structure on read, and the "age 0" bug

Step 11 parses "name, age" lines that mostly follow a pattern, then shows what storing missing ages as 0 does to the numbers.

Python · step 11 · structure on read, and a schema bug
raw_text = """Lisa, 43
Jack, 23
Huyen, 59
note: call back after 5pm
Ravi,
Neha, 31"""
parsed, rejected = [], []
for line in raw_text.splitlines():
    m = re.fullmatch(r"\s*([A-Za-z]+),\s*(\d+)\s*", line)
    (parsed if m else rejected).append(m.groups() if m else line)
print("parsed:", parsed)
print("rejected:", rejected)

# The 'missing age becomes 0' bug
ages = pd.Series([34, None, 52, None, 29], name="age")
print("\nmean age if nulls are stored as 0:", ages.fillna(0).mean())
print("mean age ignoring nulls:          ", ages.mean())
print("share of 'zero-year-old' customers:", (ages.fillna(0) == 0).mean())
Output
parsed: [('Lisa', '43'), ('Jack', '23'), ('Huyen', '59'), ('Neha', '31')]
rejected: ['note: call back after 5pm', 'Ravi,']

mean age if nulls are stored as 0: 23.0
mean age ignoring nulls:           38.333333333333336
share of 'zero-year-old' customers: 0.4
How to read it

Four lines fit the pattern; a free-text note and a line with no age are set aside rather than guessed. Below, filling two missing ages with 0 drags the average from about 38 to 23 and invents a 40% share of newborn customers. A missing value should stay missing (or use an impossible marker such as −1 with care).

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2Data FormatsNEXT · SECTION 4Storage & Processing
Book / Chapter 3 / Section 4
Section 4 of 5 · Summary

Data Storage Engines and Processing

Formats and models are the interface; storage engines (databases) are how data is actually kept and retrieved. Databases are tuned for two workloads: transactional (many small, fast reads and writes) and analytical (big aggregations over columns). And you'll meet ETL everywhere: extract, transform, load.

4.1Transactions & ACID4.2Analytics & decoupling4.3ETL vs ELT
4.1

Transactional processing and ACID

Play · Tap each guarantee
Tap a letter.

Our ride-hailing examples.

Digitally, a transaction is any action: a post, a ride booking, a model upload. Transactions are inserted as they happen, sometimes updated, sometimes deleted: online transaction processing (OLTP). Users are waiting, so it must be fast and always available; if the system is down, the transaction doesn't happen.

Transactional databases are often associated with ACID. Not all are; systems that relax it are sometimes called BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency), a definition Martin Kleppmann notes is even vaguer.

Because each transaction is handled as a unit, transactional databases are often row-major.

Code lab · Python

All or nothing: a ride booking

Step 12 adds a wallet table (balance can't go negative) and books rides inside a transaction: create the ride and charge the wallet, or do neither.

Python · step 12 · atomicity: all or nothing
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE wallet (user TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER CHECK (balance >= 0));
CREATE TABLE ride (ride_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user TEXT, driver TEXT);
INSERT INTO wallet VALUES ('asha', 150), ('vikram', 900);
""")

def book_ride(user, fare, driver):
    try:
        with db:                                     # one transaction: commit both or neither
            db.execute("INSERT INTO ride (user, driver) VALUES (?, ?)", (user, driver))
            db.execute("UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - ? WHERE user = ?", (fare, user))
        return "booked"
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
        return f"rolled back ({e})"

print("vikram:", book_ride("vikram", 320, "Driver 7"))
print("asha:  ", book_ride("asha", 320, "Driver 9"))
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM ride", db).to_string(index=False))
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM wallet", db).to_string(index=False))
Output
vikram: booked
asha:   rolled back (CHECK constraint failed: balance >= 0)
 ride_id   user   driver
       1 vikram Driver 7
  user  balance
  asha      150
vikram      580
How to read it

Vikram's booking commits both steps. Asha can't afford ₹320, so charging her wallet breaks the rule, and the database rolls back the whole transaction, including the ride row it had already inserted. No ride without payment: that's atomicity.

4.2

Analytical processing, and why the labels are fading

Play · How fast can you get the data?

Questions like "average fare for all rides in Mumbai in September" aggregate a column across many rows. Analytical databases (OLAP) are built for that. But both labels are fading, for three reasons:

  1. The split was a technology limit, now closing: transactional databases that handle analytics (CockroachDB) and analytical ones that handle transactions (Apache Iceberg, DuckDB).
  2. Storage and compute are being decoupled: keep data in one place, with processing layers on top tuned for different queries (BigQuery, Snowflake, IBM, Teradata).
  3. "Online" is overloaded: connected to the internet, in production, or how fast data is available (online, nearline, offline).
4.3

ETL vs ELT

Play · Transform before or after storing?
ExtractPull data from every source; validate it and reject what fails, telling the source. Getting this right saves time downstream.
TransformThe heavy part: join sources, clean, standardise values (one source says "Male/Female", another "M/F" or "1/2"), deduplicate, sort, aggregate, derive features, validate again.
LoadDecide how and how often to write the result to a file, database or warehouse.

As data volume and variety exploded, some companies flipped the order: dump everything raw into a data lake first and let each application transform what it needs, ELT. Fast arrival, but searching a huge lake of raw data gets inefficient. Meanwhile cloud infrastructure standardised schemas again. Vendors now offer lakehouses (Databricks, Snowflake) that combine a lake's flexibility with a warehouse's management.

Code lab · Python

A small ETL job

Step 13 merges patients from two branches that use different column names, date formats and gender codes: it rejects a bad date, standardises gender, derives age, and loads the result into a database table.

Python · step 13 · extract, transform, load
branch_a = pd.DataFrame({"pid": [1, 2, 3], "gender": ["Male", "Female", "Female"], "dob": ["1990-05-01", "1985-11-23", "bad"]})
branch_b = pd.DataFrame({"patient_id": [10, 11, 12], "sex": ["M", "F", "2"], "birth": ["12/02/1979", "03/07/2001", "30/09/1995"]})

# Extract: read, and reject what fails validation
a = branch_a.rename(columns={"pid": "patient_id", "dob": "birth"}).assign(source="A")
b = branch_b.rename(columns={"sex": "gender"}).assign(source="B")
a["birth"] = pd.to_datetime(a["birth"], errors="coerce", format="%Y-%m-%d")
b["birth"] = pd.to_datetime(b["birth"], errors="coerce", format="%d/%m/%Y")
both = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)
rejected = both[both["birth"].isna()]
both = both.dropna(subset=["birth"])

# Transform: one vocabulary for gender, derive age
both["gender"] = both["gender"].map({"Male": "M", "M": "M", "1": "M", "Female": "F", "F": "F", "2": "F"})
both["age"] = ((pd.Timestamp("2025-03-01") - both["birth"]).dt.days // 365).astype(int)

# Load: into the warehouse table
both.to_sql("patients", db, index=False, if_exists="replace")
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT patient_id, gender, age, source FROM patients", db).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nrejected {len(rejected)} row(s); tell the source:", rejected[["patient_id", "source"]].to_dict("records"))
Output
 patient_id gender  age source
          1      M   34      A
          2      F   39      A
         10      M   46      B
         11      F   23      B
         12      F   29      B

rejected 1 row(s); tell the source: [{'patient_id': 3, 'source': 'A'}]
How to read it

Five patients from two very different files now share one schema, with gender as M/F everywhere and age computed the same way. Patient 3's "bad" date was rejected and reported back to branch A rather than loaded as garbage. That's the whole idea of ETL in twenty lines.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 3Data ModelsNEXT · SECTION 5Dataflow & Streaming
Book / Chapter 3 / Section 5
Section 5 of 5 · Summary

Modes of Dataflow, Batch and Stream

In production, data must pass between processes that don't share memory: a dataflow. There are three main modes: through databases, through services (REST or RPC requests), and through a real-time transport such as Apache Kafka or Amazon Kinesis. Data at rest is processed in batches; data in motion is processed as a stream, and ML often needs features from both.

5.1Databases & services5.2Real-time transport5.3Batch vs stream5.4Static & dynamic features
5.1

Through databases and through services

Play · Three services that need each other's data

Our ride-hailing pricing example.

Through a database is simplest: A writes, B reads. But both must reach the same database (hard across companies), and database reads and writes are often too slow for consumer apps.

Through services: A sends B a request and B answers over the network. This is the service-oriented way, and when one app is split into many services it's a microservice architecture. Ride-hailing pricing, for instance, needs predicted drivers and predicted ride requests from two other services every time someone asks for a ride.

  • REST was designed for requests over networks and dominates public APIs. (HTTP is one implementation of REST, not the same thing.)
  • RPC makes a remote call look like a local function, common between services inside one organisation.
The web problemRequests are synchronous: if the driver service is down, pricing keeps retrying until it times out, and failures cascade. With hundreds of services, the web of requests becomes a bottleneck.
5.2

Real-time transport: pub/sub and message queues

Pub/subMessage queue
Who readsAnyone subscribed to the topicIntended consumers
Producer knows consumers?NoYes, roughly
RetentionKept for a while (e.g. 7 days), then deleted or archivedUntil delivered
ExamplesApache Kafka, Amazon KinesisRabbitMQ, Apache RocketMQ

Instead of every service calling every other, put a broker in the middle. Whenever the driver service makes a prediction, it broadcasts it; anyone who needs it reads the latest from the broker. A database could be the broker, but it's too slow, so real-time transports use in-memory storage.

Each broadcast item is an event, so this is event-driven architecture, and the transport is sometimes called an event bus. Request-driven suits logic-heavy systems; event-driven suits data-heavy ones. It sits between databases and services: asynchronous, with fairly low latency.

Code lab · Python

Build a tiny pub/sub broker

Step 14 writes a 20-line broker: topics hold the last few events (retention), and each subscriber remembers how far it has read (its offset). Driver and ride services publish; the pricing service subscribes.

Python · step 14 · a tiny pub/sub broker
from collections import defaultdict, deque

class Broker:
    def __init__(self, retention=5):
        self.topics = defaultdict(lambda: deque(maxlen=retention))  # keep the last N events per topic
        self.offsets = defaultdict(int)                             # where each subscriber has read up to
        self.published = defaultdict(int)

    def publish(self, topic, event):
        self.topics[topic].append((self.published[topic], event))
        self.published[topic] += 1

    def poll(self, subscriber, topic):
        start = self.offsets[(subscriber, topic)]
        new = [e for i, e in self.topics[topic] if i >= start]
        self.offsets[(subscriber, topic)] = self.published[topic]
        return new

bus = Broker(retention=5)
for minute in range(3):
    bus.publish("drivers_available", {"minute": minute, "area": "Bandra", "drivers": int(rng.integers(20, 60))})
    bus.publish("ride_requests", {"minute": minute, "area": "Bandra", "requests": int(rng.integers(30, 90))})

# The pricing service subscribes to both topics; it never calls the other services directly
drivers = bus.poll("pricing", "drivers_available")
requests = bus.poll("pricing", "ride_requests")
for d, r in zip(drivers, requests):
    surge = max(1.0, round(r["requests"] / d["drivers"], 1))
    print(f"minute {d['minute']}: {r['requests']} requests / {d['drivers']} drivers -> surge {surge}x")
print("polling again returns only new events:", bus.poll("pricing", "drivers_available"))
Output
minute 0: 35 requests / 50 drivers -> surge 1.0x
minute 1: 59 requests / 27 drivers -> surge 2.2x
minute 2: 38 requests / 44 drivers -> surge 1.0x
polling again returns only new events: []
How to read it

The pricing service computed a surge for each minute without calling the driver or ride services at all; it only read their events. Polling again returns nothing new, because its offset has moved forward. Kafka works on the same ideas (topics, retention, offsets), distributed across machines and built to survive failures.

5.3

Batch processing vs stream processing

Watch · Every day, recompute everything, or just add today?

Data in databases, lakes and warehouses is historical, processed by periodic batch jobs (once a day, say), using engines like MapReduce and Spark. Data in Kafka or Kinesis is streaming, processed every few minutes or whenever it's needed.

  • Stream processing can give low latency: process data as it arrives, before it's even stored.
  • It isn't inherently less efficient: engines like Apache Flink are distributed and scalable, and streaming shines at stateful computation, updating a running result instead of recomputing from scratch.
  • It's harder: data is unbounded and arrives at varying speeds. Making a stream processor do batch is easier than the reverse, and Flink's maintainers argue batch is just a special case of streaming.
Code lab · Python

Thirty days of a free trial, two ways

Step 15 totals each of 1,000 trial users' minutes over 30 days: the batch way recomputes over all days so far, every day; the streaming way keeps a running total and adds only the new day.

Python · step 15 · batch vs stream
days = 30
daily_minutes = rng.poisson(25, (days, 1000))          # 1,000 trial users, minutes used per day

# Batch: every day, recompute over all days so far
t0 = time.perf_counter()
batch_ops = 0
for d in range(1, days + 1):
    total = daily_minutes[:d].sum(axis=0)
    batch_ops += d * 1000
batch_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

# Stream: keep running state and add only today's numbers
t0 = time.perf_counter()
state = np.zeros(1000)
stream_ops = 0
for d in range(days):
    state += daily_minutes[d]
    stream_ops += 1000
stream_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

print("same answer:", np.array_equal(total, state))
print(f"batch:  {batch_ops:>7,} values processed")
print(f"stream: {stream_ops:>7,} values processed ({batch_ops / stream_ops:.1f}x fewer)")
Output
same answer: True
batch:  465,000 values processed
stream:  30,000 values processed (15.5x fewer)
How to read it

Identical totals, but batch touched 465,000 values while the stateful stream touched 30,000, 15.5 times fewer. The gap grows with the window: a 90-day window would be about 45 times fewer. That saving is the point of stateful stream processing.

5.4

Static and dynamic features

Batch (static) featuresStream (dynamic) features
ChangeSlowlyBy the minute
ExampleDriver's 90-day ratingRide requests in the last minute
Computed withSpark, MapReduceFlink, KSQL, Spark Streaming

Batch jobs compute features that change slowly, such as a driver's rating after hundreds of rides: static features. Stream processing computes fast-changing ones, such as drivers available now, requests in the last minute, or the median price of the last 10 rides nearby: dynamic features. Good pricing needs both, joined at prediction time (Chapter 7 returns to this).

Streaming features get complexFraud detection or credit scoring can use hundreds or thousands of streaming features with joins and aggregations. Kafka's built-in processing is limited; tools like Apache Flink and KSQL (both with SQL interfaces) or Spark Streaming do the heavy lifting.
Code lab · Python

Assemble one prediction's features

Step 16 keeps a nightly table of driver ratings (batch) and a rolling buffer of ride requests (stream), then builds the feature vector for one pricing request.

Python · step 16 · static + dynamic features at prediction time
driver_ratings = pd.DataFrame({"driver": ["D1", "D2", "D3"], "rating_90d": [4.8, 4.3, 4.9]})   # batch, updated nightly

events = deque(maxlen=1000)                                                 # stream of ride requests
now = 600.0
for t in np.sort(rng.uniform(0, now, 120)):
    events.append({"t": t, "area": rng.choice(["Bandra", "Andheri"])})

def requests_last(seconds, area):
    return sum(1 for e in events if e["area"] == area and now - e["t"] <= seconds)

request = {"driver": "D2", "area": "Bandra"}
features = {
    "rating_90d (batch)": float(driver_ratings.set_index("driver").loc[request["driver"], "rating_90d"]),
    "requests_last_60s (stream)": requests_last(60, request["area"]),
    "requests_last_300s (stream)": requests_last(300, request["area"]),
}
print("feature vector for this prediction:", features)
Output
feature vector for this prediction: {'rating_90d (batch)': 4.3, 'requests_last_60s (stream)': 8, 'requests_last_300s (stream)': 26}
How to read it

The rating comes from yesterday's batch job and won't change today. The two request counts come from the live stream and change every second: a handful in the last minute, more over the last five. The model sees both side by side. Keeping these consistent between training and serving is a big topic for later chapters.

Chapter 3 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Choose formats for how data will be used: row-major vs column-major, text vs binary. Relational, document and graph models each make certain questions easy. Structured vs unstructured comes down to who assumes the structure: the writer or the reader. Transactional and analytical databases are converging as storage and compute separate. Data moves through databases, services or real-time transports, and is processed in batches (static features) or streams (dynamic features). Next: turning this data into training data.

Eight takeaways

1. Know your sourcesUser input: messy and urgent. Logs: huge. Third-party: shrinking with privacy rules.
2. Format follows accessRow-major for writing whole records, column-major for reading a few features.
3. Binary is smallerParquet is far smaller and faster to read selectively than CSV or JSON.
4. pandas is columnarWork by column; avoid row-by-row loops.
5. Model for the questionTables and joins, self-contained documents, or relationship-first graphs.
6. Who holds the schema?Structured: the writer. Unstructured: the reader. Never store missing as 0.
7. Transactions and ETLACID keeps records consistent; ETL validates and standardises before loading.
8. Events and streamsBrokers decouple services; streams compute dynamic features with running state.

Book / Chapter 4
Chapter 4 · Broad summary

Training Data

Courses spend their time on models; real projects spend it on data. This chapter is about getting good training data: all the data used to build a model, including train, validation and test splits. It covers sampling the right data, getting labels (by hand, naturally, or with clever shortcuts when labels are scarce), coping with class imbalance, and augmenting data you don't have enough of. "Training data", not "dataset": in production it's never finished or fixed. And a warning that bears repeating: data is full of biases, so use it, but don't trust it too much.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Sampling. Convenience samples are biased. Random, stratified, weighted, reservoir and importance sampling each solve a specific problem.
  2. Labelling. Hand labels are expensive, slow and risky for privacy, and annotators disagree. Track where every label came from. Natural labels (clicks, arrival times) are free but arrive late.
  3. Few labels. Weak supervision writes rules instead of labels; semi-supervision spreads a few labels; transfer learning reuses a model trained on another task; active learning labels the most useful examples first.
  4. Class imbalance. It's the norm. Use the right metrics, then resample the data or reweight the loss.
  5. Augmentation. Make more data with label-preserving transforms, perturbations and synthesis.
