Book / Chapter 4 / Section 1
Section 1 of 5 · Summary

Sampling

Sampling happens all over an ML project: picking real-world data to train on, splitting data into train, validation and test, picking events to monitor. Sometimes it's forced (you can't access or process everything); often it's just faster and cheaper, such as trying a new model on a small subset first. Knowing the methods helps you avoid sampling bias and pick data efficiently. There are two families: non-probability and random sampling.

1.1Non-probability1.2Random & stratified1.3Weighted1.4Reservoir1.5Importance
1.1

Non-probability sampling

Play · Four shortcuts

Our clinic examples.

Here, data isn't chosen by any probability rule. It's quick and easy, which is why ML data so often comes this way, but it's riddled with selection bias.

  • Language models train on what's easy to collect (Wikipedia, Common Crawl, Reddit), not on all text.
  • Sentiment datasets often come from IMDB and Amazon reviews, which only represent people who post reviews online.
  • Early self-driving data came mostly from sunny Phoenix and the Bay Area. Waymo added rainy Kirkland, Washington in 2016, but sunny data still dominates.

Fine for getting a project off the ground; for reliable models, move to probability-based sampling.

Code lab · Python

Online reviews vs a random sample

Setup loads the libraries and scikit-learn's digits. Step 1 invents 100,000 clinic patients with a satisfaction score; very happy and very unhappy patients are more likely to post a review.

Python · step 0 · setup
import random, re, itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
                             confusion_matrix, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score)
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

pd.set_option("display.width", 100)
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
digits = load_digits()                  # 1,797 tiny 8x8 handwritten digits, bundled with scikit-learn
print("digits:", digits.data.shape)
Output
digits: (1797, 64)
Python · step 1 · convenience sampling is biased
# 100,000 clinic patients. Only some leave online reviews, and they skew happy or furious.
n = 100_000
satisfaction = rng.normal(3.6, 0.9, n).clip(1, 5)
p_review = 0.02 + 0.10 * (np.abs(satisfaction - 3) > 1.2)    # extremes are more likely to review
reviewed = rng.random(n) < p_review
print(f"true average satisfaction:        {satisfaction.mean():.2f}")
print(f"average among online reviewers:   {satisfaction[reviewed].mean():.2f}   ({reviewed.sum():,} reviews)")
print(f"random sample of 2,000 patients:  {rng.choice(satisfaction, 2000, replace=False).mean():.2f}")
print(f"share of 1-2 star views, all vs reviewers: {(satisfaction < 2).mean():.1%} vs {(satisfaction[reviewed] < 2).mean():.1%}")
Output
true average satisfaction:        3.58
average among online reviewers:   4.05   (4,715 reviews)
random sample of 2,000 patients:  3.57
share of 1-2 star views, all vs reviewers: 3.7% vs 6.7%
How to read it

Reviewers average 4.05 when the true average is 3.58, and they show nearly twice the share of very unhappy patients. A random sample of just 2,000 patients gets the average almost exactly (3.57). The convenient data was 2.4 times bigger and much more wrong.

1.2

Simple random and stratified sampling

Play · Draw a sample

Our illustration: 400 dots, 4 of them rare (pink); each draw takes 10%.

Simple randomEvery item has the same chance. Easy, but a rare class (say 0.01% of data) may not appear at all in a 1% sample, and the model would think it doesn't exist.
StratifiedSplit the population into groups you care about (strata) and sample each separately, e.g. 1% of class A and 1% of class B. Rare groups are guaranteed to appear.

Stratifying isn't always possible, for example in multilabel tasks where one sample belongs to several groups.

Code lab · Python

Ten random samples vs one stratified sample

Step 2 builds 200,000 cases where only 0.05% are rare, takes ten simple 1% samples, then one stratified 1% sample.

Python · step 2 · simple random vs stratified
population = pd.DataFrame({"label": rng.choice(["normal", "rare"], 200_000, p=[0.9995, 0.0005])})
print("rare cases in the population:", (population["label"] == "rare").sum())

simple_counts = [(population.sample(frac=0.01, random_state=s)["label"] == "rare").sum() for s in range(10)]
strat = population.groupby("label", group_keys=False).apply(lambda g: g.sample(frac=0.01, random_state=0))
print("rare cases in ten 1% simple random samples:", simple_counts)
print("rare cases in a 1% stratified sample:      ", (strat["label"] == "rare").sum(),
      "(always 1% of each class)")
Output
rare cases in the population: 89
rare cases in ten 1% simple random samples: [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1]
rare cases in a 1% stratified sample:       1 (always 1% of each class)
How to read it

The ten random samples contain anywhere from 0 to 2 rare cases; two of them have none at all. The stratified sample always gets its exact share. In practice train_test_split(..., stratify=y) does this for you, and you should almost always use it for classification.

1.3

Weighted sampling and sample weights

Play · Correct a skewed dataset

Data: 25% red, 75% blue. Reality: 50/50.

In weighted sampling each item gets a weight that sets its chance of selection. It lets you use domain knowledge (recent data matters more, so weight it up) and correct data whose mix differs from reality: if red is 25% of your data but 50% of the world, give red three times the weight.

Sample weights are differentWeighted sampling decides which examples get picked. Sample weights decide how much each picked example counts in the loss. Raise the weight on some examples and the model's decision boundary moves towards fitting them.
Code lab · Python

Weighted draws, reweighting and a moving boundary

Step 3 draws 10,000 items with weights 60/30/10, corrects a 25/75 red-blue mix to 50/50, and trains the same classifier with minority weight 1 and 5.

Python · step 3 · weighted sampling and sample weights
random.seed(1)
draws = random.choices(["recent", "last year", "older"], weights=[0.6, 0.3, 0.1], k=10_000)
print("weighted draws:", {k: f"{v / 100:.0f}%" for k, v in Counter(draws).items()})

# Our data is 25% red, 75% blue, but reality is 50/50: weight red 3x to correct it
colours = np.array(["red"] * 250 + ["blue"] * 750)
w = np.where(colours == "red", 3.0, 1.0)
fixed = rng.choice(colours, 10_000, p=w / w.sum())
print("after reweighting:", {k: f"{v / 100:.0f}%" for k, v in Counter(fixed).items()})

# Sample weights during training shift the decision boundary
X2 = np.vstack([rng.normal([0, 0], 1, (200, 2)), rng.normal([2.2, 2.2], 1, (40, 2))])
y2 = np.r_[np.zeros(200), np.ones(40)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.scatter(*X2[y2 == 0].T, s=10, alpha=.5, label="majority")
ax.scatter(*X2[y2 == 1].T, s=16, alpha=.8, label="minority")
xs = np.linspace(-3, 5, 50)
for weight, style in [(1, "--"), (5, "-")]:
    m = LogisticRegression().fit(X2, y2, sample_weight=np.where(y2 == 1, weight, 1))
    ax.plot(xs, -(m.intercept_[0] + m.coef_[0][0] * xs) / m.coef_[0][1], style, color="#161A2E",
            label=f"boundary, minority weight {weight}")
ax.set(xlim=(-3, 5), ylim=(-3, 5))
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper left")
Output
weighted draws: {'recent': '60%', 'last year': '29%', 'older': '10%'}
after reweighting: {'red': '49%', 'blue': '51%'}
How to read it

The draws match their weights; the tripled red weight restores a 50/50 mix. In the chart, giving the minority (orange) points five times the weight pushes the boundary into the majority's territory: the model now accepts more majority errors to get the minority right.

1.4

Reservoir sampling

Play · Keep 3 items from a stream

Production data arrives as a stream: you don't know how many items will come and can't hold them all. You want a sample of k where every item had an equal chance, and you can stop at any moment.

  1. Put the first k items in the reservoir.
  2. For the n-th item, pick a random whole number i from 1 to n.
  3. If i ≤ k, replace reservoir slot i with the new item; otherwise skip it.

Each new item enters with probability k/n, and every item in the reservoir has the same k/n chance of being there.

Code lab · Python

Implement it, then check it's fair

Step 4 implements the three steps, samples 5 from a stream of 1,000, then runs 20,000 times on a 20-item stream to check every item is equally likely to survive.

Python · step 4 · reservoir sampling a stream
def reservoir_sample(stream, k, seed=None):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    reservoir = []
    for n, item in enumerate(stream, start=1):
        if n <= k:
            reservoir.append(item)            # 1. keep the first k items
        else:
            i = r.randint(1, n)               # 2. pick a random position from 1..n
            if i <= k:
                reservoir[i - 1] = item       # 3. if it lands in the reservoir, replace that slot
    return reservoir

print("one sample of 5 from a stream of 1,000 tweets:", reservoir_sample(range(1, 1001), 5, seed=7))

# Is every item equally likely? Run it many times on a stream of 20 items.
counts = Counter(x for s in range(20_000) for x in reservoir_sample(range(20), 4, seed=s))
share = np.array([counts[i] for i in range(20)]) / 20_000
print("chance each of 20 items was kept (should all be 4/20 = 0.20):")
print(np.round(share, 3))
Output
one sample of 5 from a stream of 1,000 tweets: [930, 990, 361, 754, 58]
chance each of 20 items was kept (should all be 4/20 = 0.20):
[0.196 0.203 0.202 0.198 0.201 0.2   0.199 0.204 0.201 0.2   0.202 0.199
 0.197 0.2   0.199 0.197 0.2   0.2   0.203 0.2  ]
How to read it

Every one of the 20 items ends up in the reservoir about 20% of the time (4 slots ÷ 20 items), whether it arrived first or last. That's the guarantee: a fair sample from a stream of unknown length, in memory for only k items.

1.5

Importance sampling

Watch · Sample from Q, reweight to P

Our waiting-time example, the same as the code lab.

Sometimes the distribution you need, P(x), is expensive or impossible to sample from, but a similar one, Q(x), is easy. Sample from Q and weight each sample by P(x)/Q(x). On average this gives the same answer as sampling from P, provided Q(x) > 0 wherever P(x) isn't zero. Q is called the proposal or importance distribution.

In ML it appears in policy-based reinforcement learning: rewards collected under the old policy are reweighted to estimate a nearby new policy, avoiding costly new rollouts.

Code lab · Python

Estimate a mean you can't sample directly

Step 5 targets a gamma distribution of waiting times (mean 20 minutes), but draws from an easy exponential with mean 25.

Python · step 5 · importance sampling
# Target P: patients' waiting time ~ Gamma(shape 2, scale 10) minutes. Pretend we can't sample it.
# Proposal Q: an easy exponential with mean 25. Weight each draw by P(x)/Q(x).
from scipy import stats
P = stats.gamma(a=2, scale=10)
Q = stats.expon(scale=25)
x = Q.rvs(size=50_000, random_state=1)
w = P.pdf(x) / Q.pdf(x)
print(f"true mean of P:                   {P.mean():.2f} min")
print(f"plain mean of Q samples (wrong):  {x.mean():.2f} min")
print(f"importance-weighted estimate:     {np.mean(w * x):.2f} min")
Output
true mean of P:                   20.00 min
plain mean of Q samples (wrong):  24.94 min
importance-weighted estimate:     19.98 min
How to read it

Averaging the proposal's samples gives the proposal's mean (about 25), which is wrong. Weighting each sample by P/Q recovers the target's mean (19.98 vs 20.00), using samples that never came from the target.

BACKChapter 4 overviewNEXT · SECTION 2Labelling
Book / Chapter 4 / Section 2
Section 2 of 5 · Summary

Labelling

Most production models are supervised, so they need labels, and their quality depends heavily on those labels. Labelling has become a core function of ML teams: Andrej Karpathy, asked how long he'd need an in-house labelling team at Tesla, replied by asking how long they'd need an engineering team. Labels come from people (hand labels) or from the system itself (natural labels).

2.1Hand labels & disagreement2.2Data lineage2.3Natural labels
2.1

Hand labels and label multiplicity

Play · Three annotators, one sentence

Our sentence. Task: mark every named entity.

  • Expensive: spam labels need a crowd trained in 15 minutes; chest X-rays need board-certified radiologists.
  • Privacy: someone must look at the data. Medical records may not leave the building.
  • Slow: phonetic transcription can take 400× the audio's length, so an hour of speech is about 400 hours of work. Slow labels mean slow iteration: if PR suddenly wants an ANGRY class, you relabel and wait while the old model decays.
Label multiplicityAnnotators disagree, more so when more expertise is needed. If experts can't agree, what does "human-level" even mean? Fix it with a clear problem definition (e.g. "choose the longest span") and train every annotator on it.
Code lab · Python

Measure annotator agreement

Step 6 has three annotators mark 12 patient messages URGENT or ROUTINE, then measures raw agreement and Cohen's kappa, which discounts agreement expected by chance.

Python · step 6 · when annotators disagree
# Three annotators label 12 patient messages as URGENT or ROUTINE
labels = pd.DataFrame({
    "A": ["U", "R", "R", "U", "U", "R", "R", "U", "R", "R", "U", "R"],
    "B": ["U", "R", "U", "U", "R", "R", "R", "U", "R", "U", "U", "R"],
    "C": ["U", "U", "U", "U", "R", "R", "R", "U", "R", "R", "U", "U"],
})
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
for a, b in itertools.combinations(labels.columns, 2):
    agree = (labels[a] == labels[b]).mean()
    print(f"{a} vs {b}: agree {agree:.0%}, Cohen's kappa {cohen_kappa_score(labels[a], labels[b]):.2f}")
labels["majority"] = labels.mode(axis=1)[0]
labels["unanimous"] = labels[["A", "B", "C"]].nunique(axis=1) == 1
print(f"\nunanimous on {labels['unanimous'].sum()} of {len(labels)} messages; the rest need a tie-break or a clearer guideline")
Output
A vs B: agree 75%, Cohen's kappa 0.50
A vs C: agree 67%, Cohen's kappa 0.35
B vs C: agree 75%, Cohen's kappa 0.50

unanimous on 7 of 12 messages; the rest need a tie-break or a clearer guideline
How to read it

Raw agreement of 67–75% sounds decent, but kappa (0 = chance, 1 = perfect) is only 0.35–0.50: moderate at best. All three agree on just 7 of 12 messages. Before training on these labels, tighten the guideline ("urgent means needs care within 24 hours") and relabel the disputed ones.

2.2

Data lineage

Watch · Every label remembers where it came from

Mixing data from many sources and annotators without checking quality can make a model fail mysteriously. A common story: a decent model on 100,000 samples; you pay for a million more; performance drops, because the new labels were crowdsourced and far less accurate, and now the two are mixed together.

Track the origin of every sample and labelThat's data lineage. It helps flag biases and debug: if the model fails mostly on recently acquired data, look at how that data was acquired. The author's teams found more than once that the problem was bad labels, not the model.
Code lab · Python

More labels, worse model, and how lineage finds out why

Step 7 trains a digit classifier on 400 careful in-house labels, then adds a vendor batch in which about 45% of labels are wrong. Each row keeps its source.

Python · step 7 · data lineage finds the bad batch
X, y = digits.data, digits.target
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0, stratify=y)
src = np.where(np.arange(len(y_tr)) < 400, "in-house", "vendor_batch_2")   # where each label came from
y_noisy = y_tr.copy()
bad = (src == "vendor_batch_2") & (rng.random(len(y_tr)) < 0.45)            # the vendor got many wrong
y_noisy[bad] = rng.integers(0, 10, bad.sum())

for name, mask in [("in-house only", src == "in-house"), ("in-house + vendor", np.ones(len(y_tr), bool))]:
    acc = accuracy_score(y_te, LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_tr[mask], y_noisy[mask]).predict(X_te))
    print(f"train on {name:<18} -> test accuracy {acc:.3f}")

# Because we kept lineage, we can audit by source: how often do labels disagree with a model trained elsewhere?
audit = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_tr[src == "in-house"], y_noisy[src == "in-house"])
disagree = audit.predict(X_tr) != y_noisy
print(pd.Series(disagree).groupby(src).mean().rename("label disagreement rate").round(2).to_string())
Output
train on in-house only      -> test accuracy 0.954
train on in-house + vendor  -> test accuracy 0.853
in-house          0.00
vendor_batch_2    0.44
How to read it

Adding the vendor's data drops accuracy from 0.954 to 0.853. Because every row carries its source, a quick audit (compare each label with a model trained only on trusted data) shows the in-house labels agree almost perfectly while 44% of the vendor's don't. Without lineage, you'd only know "the new model is worse".

2.3

Natural labels and feedback loop length

Play · How long do you wait before calling it "no click"?

Same click-delay pattern as the code lab.

Some tasks label themselves. Google Maps learns the true trip time when you arrive; a stock model learns the price two minutes later; a recommender learns whether you clicked. Labels inferred from behaviour are behavioural labels. You can also design for feedback (a Like button, "suggest a better translation"). In the author's survey of 86 companies, 63% worked on tasks with natural labels, probably because those are easier to start with.

  • Implicit labels are presumed (no click = negative); explicit ones are stated (a downvote).
  • Feedback loop length: minutes for product clicks, hours for long videos, weeks for clothes (Stitch Fix), one to three months for card disputes.
  • Feedback types differ: clicks are plentiful but weak; purchases are rarer but stronger and closer to revenue.
Window trade-offA short window gives labels fast but marks late clicks as negatives. Twitter's ads team found most clicks come in five minutes, but some come hours later, so measured click-through rates run low.
Code lab · Python

The cost of a short label window

Step 8 shows 50,000 ads with a true 4% click rate, where click delays follow a long-tailed distribution, and measures the click rate with different windows.

Python · step 8 · natural labels arrive late
n_ads = 50_000
clicked = rng.random(n_ads) < 0.04                                  # true click-through rate 4%
delay_min = rng.lognormal(mean=1.2, sigma=1.4, size=n_ads)          # most clicks come fast, some much later
for window in [2, 5, 15, 60, 24 * 60]:
    seen = clicked & (delay_min <= window)
    print(f"label window {window:>5} min: measured CTR {seen.mean():.2%}  (catches {seen.sum() / clicked.sum():.0%} of clicks)")
Output
label window     2 min: measured CTR 1.42%  (catches 35% of clicks)
label window     5 min: measured CTR 2.43%  (catches 61% of clicks)
label window    15 min: measured CTR 3.42%  (catches 85% of clicks)
label window    60 min: measured CTR 3.94%  (catches 98% of clicks)
label window  1440 min: measured CTR 4.01%  (catches 100% of clicks)
How to read it

A 2-minute window reports 1.4% when the truth is 4%; 15 minutes still misses 15% of clicks; an hour gets nearly all. Faster labels let you catch problems sooner, but they're biased low. Choose the window with that trade-off in mind, and correct for it if you can.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1SamplingNEXT · SECTION 3Handling the Lack of Labels
Book / Chapter 4 / Section 3
Section 3 of 5 · Summary

Handling the Lack of Labels

Good labels are scarce, so four families of techniques help you need fewer of them. Weak supervision writes heuristics instead of labels. Semi-supervision spreads a few labels using structure in the data. Transfer learning reuses a model trained on another task. Active learning spends the labelling budget on the most useful examples.

3.1Weak supervision3.2Semi-supervision3.3Transfer learning3.4Active learning
3.1

Weak supervision

Hand labellingProgrammatic labelling
CostExpensive, especially expertsExpertise written once, reused
PrivacyPeople see the dataWrite rules on a cleared sample
SpeedGrows with every label1K to 1M samples, same effort
ChangeRelabel everythingRe-run the functions

Our summary of the trade-offs.

People label with heuristics, so write the heuristics down as labeling functions (LFs) and let them label data. The best-known tool is Snorkel from Stanford. LFs can be keyword rules, regular expressions, database lookups, or other models' outputs.

LFs are noisy and can conflict, so their votes are combined, denoised and reweighted into the most likely labels. A few hand labels help check accuracy and inspire better LFs.

It worksIn a Stanford Medicine study, one radiologist's eight hours writing LFs produced labels whose models matched those trained on almost a year of hand labelling, and some LFs were reused across chest and extremity X-rays. You still train a model afterwards, because LFs don't cover every case.
Code lab · Python

Label triage notes with four functions

Step 9 writes four labeling functions for clinic triage notes, applies them all, and takes a majority vote of whichever functions didn't abstain.

Python · step 9 · weak supervision with labeling functions
notes = [
    "pt c/o severe chest pain radiating to arm", "routine scaling and polishing, no complaints",
    "swelling of face and fever since 2 days", "requests teeth whitening before wedding",
    "bleeding not stopping after extraction", "follow up for braces adjustment",
    "difficulty breathing after anaesthesia", "sensitivity to cold drinks, mild",
    "knocked out tooth in accident, child", "wants quote for implant",
    "abscess with high fever", "check-up, last visit 6 months ago",
]
truth = ["EMERGENT", "ROUTINE", "EMERGENT", "ROUTINE", "EMERGENT", "ROUTINE",
         "EMERGENT", "ROUTINE", "EMERGENT", "ROUTINE", "EMERGENT", "ROUTINE"]
ABSTAIN = None

def lf_red_flags(note):        # keyword heuristic
    return "EMERGENT" if re.search(r"bleeding|breathing|chest pain|knocked out", note) else ABSTAIN
def lf_infection(note):        # fever + swelling/abscess
    return "EMERGENT" if "fever" in note and re.search(r"swelling|abscess", note) else ABSTAIN
def lf_cosmetic(note):         # cosmetic or admin requests
    return "ROUTINE" if re.search(r"whitening|quote|braces|check-up|polishing", note) else ABSTAIN
def lf_mild(note):
    return "ROUTINE" if "mild" in note else ABSTAIN

lfs = [lf_red_flags, lf_infection, lf_cosmetic, lf_mild]
votes = pd.DataFrame({lf.__name__: [lf(n) for n in notes] for lf in lfs})
votes["weak_label"] = votes.apply(lambda r: Counter(v for v in r if v).most_common(1)[0][0] if r.notna().any() else ABSTAIN, axis=1)
covered = votes["weak_label"].notna()
correct = (votes["weak_label"] == pd.Series(truth))[covered]
print(f"coverage: {covered.mean():.0%} of notes got a label; accuracy on those: {correct.mean():.0%}")
print(votes.assign(note=[n[:34] for n in notes])[["note", "weak_label"]].to_string(index=False))
Output
coverage: 100% of notes got a label; accuracy on those: 100%
                              note weak_label
pt c/o severe chest pain radiating   EMERGENT
routine scaling and polishing, no     ROUTINE
swelling of face and fever since 2   EMERGENT
requests teeth whitening before we    ROUTINE
bleeding not stopping after extrac   EMERGENT
   follow up for braces adjustment    ROUTINE
difficulty breathing after anaesth   EMERGENT
  sensitivity to cold drinks, mild    ROUTINE
knocked out tooth in accident, chi   EMERGENT
           wants quote for implant    ROUTINE
           abscess with high fever   EMERGENT
 check-up, last visit 6 months ago    ROUTINE
How to read it

Four short functions labelled all twelve notes, and agreed with the true labels here. Be suspicious of a perfect score on a toy set, since the rules were written while looking at these very notes. On real data expect gaps (notes no rule covers) and conflicts, which is exactly why you then train a model on the weak labels and check it against a small hand-labelled set.

3.2

Semi-supervision

Watch · A few labels spread to their neighbours

Semi-supervision starts from a small set of real labels and uses assumptions about the data's structure to label more.

  • Self-training: train on the labels, predict the unlabelled data, add confident predictions as labels, retrain, repeat.
  • Similarity: similar samples share labels. Hashtags that appear in the same profile as #AI are probably about computing too; in general, clustering or nearest neighbours find the similar samples.
  • Perturbation: a slightly altered sample keeps its label (more in Section 5).
Mind the evaluation setWith few labels, a tiny evaluation set picks the model that overfits it; a big one eats your training labels. Many teams use a reasonably large evaluation set to pick the best model, then continue training it on that set.
Code lab · Python

50 labels, spread across 1,000 images

Step 10 keeps labels for only 50 of about 1,080 digit images. It trains a normal classifier on the 50, then uses label spreading, which passes labels along to similar-looking images.

Python · step 10 · semi-supervision: spread a few labels
from sklearn.semi_supervised import LabelSpreading
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(digits.data / 16, digits.target, test_size=0.4, random_state=1, stratify=digits.target)
labelled = np.zeros(len(y_tr), bool)
labelled[rng.choice(len(y_tr), 50, replace=False)] = True          # only 50 of ~1,080 have labels
y_partial = np.where(labelled, y_tr, -1)                            # -1 means "unlabelled"

sup = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_tr[labelled], y_tr[labelled])
print(f"supervised, 50 labels only:            {accuracy_score(y_te, sup.predict(X_te)):.3f}")
spread = LabelSpreading(kernel="rbf", gamma=8).fit(X_tr, y_partial)   # similar images get similar labels
print(f"label spreading, 50 labels + unlabelled: {accuracy_score(y_te, spread.predict(X_te)):.3f}")
filled = spread.transduction_[~labelled]
print(f"labels it inferred for the other {len(filled)} images: {accuracy_score(y_tr[~labelled], filled):.1%} correct")
Output
supervised, 50 labels only:            0.719
label spreading, 50 labels + unlabelled: 0.846
labels it inferred for the other 1028 images: 83.9% correct
How to read it

Using the unlabelled images lifts accuracy from 0.72 to 0.85 with the same 50 labels, and the labels it inferred for the other images are about 84% right. The unlabelled data told the model where the clusters are; the few labels told it what to call them.

3.3

Transfer learning

Watch · Learn once, reuse

Train a model on a base task with cheap, abundant data, then reuse it as the starting point for your downstream task. Language modelling (predict the next token) is ideal as a base: any text works, no labels needed.

  • Sometimes the base model works directly (zero-shot); often you finetune it a little on your data, or shape inputs with a prompt template so it produces the output you need.
  • Much production ML is transfer learning: object detectors pretrained on ImageNet, text classifiers built on BERT or GPT-3.
  • Bigger base models tend to transfer better, but cost tens of millions of dollars to train, so only a few companies may train them while everyone else adapts them.
Code lab · Python

Reuse a digit recogniser's hidden layer

Step 11 trains a small neural network to recognise all ten digits on 1,000 images. Then, on different images, a new task ("is the digit 5 or more?") is learned from just 20 or 40 labels, once from raw pixels and once from the network's hidden-layer features. Each result averages five random label draws.

Python · step 11 · transfer learning
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
import warnings
X01 = digits.data / 16
order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X01))
base_idx, down_idx = order[:1000], order[1000:]

# Base task: recognise all ten digits, trained on 1,000 labelled images
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    base_net = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=600, random_state=0).fit(X01[base_idx], digits.target[base_idx])

def embed(X):                         # reuse the base network's hidden layer as a feature extractor
    return np.maximum(0, X @ base_net.coefs_[0] + base_net.intercepts_[0])

# New downstream task on different images: "is the digit 5 or more?", with very few labels
Xd, yd = X01[down_idx], (digits.target[down_idx] >= 5).astype(int)
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(Xd, yd, test_size=0.5, random_state=0, stratify=yd)
for k in [10, 20]:
    raw_acc, tl_acc = [], []
    for seed in range(5):                                     # average over 5 random draws of the few labels
        r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        few = np.concatenate([r.choice(np.where(yd_tr == c)[0], k, replace=False) for c in [0, 1]])
        raw_acc.append(accuracy_score(yd_te, LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xd_tr[few], yd_tr[few]).predict(Xd_te)))
        tl_acc.append(accuracy_score(yd_te, LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(embed(Xd_tr[few]), yd_tr[few]).predict(embed(Xd_te))))
    print(f"{2 * k} labels: raw pixels {np.mean(raw_acc):.3f}   transferred features {np.mean(tl_acc):.3f}")
Output
20 labels: raw pixels 0.708   transferred features 0.773
40 labels: raw pixels 0.799   transferred features 0.850
How to read it

With the same handful of labels, the transferred features score about 6–7 points higher. The base network had already learned useful shapes (loops, strokes) while learning digits; the new task only had to learn how to combine them.

3.4

Active learning

Watch · Ask about the confusing cases

Our illustration: highlighted points sit near the decision boundary, where the model is least sure.

Instead of labelling random samples, let the model choose (it's sometimes called query learning). The hope: higher accuracy from fewer labels.

  • Uncertainty sampling: label the samples the model is least sure about.
  • Query-by-committee: train several models and label where they disagree most.
  • Others pick samples that would change the model most.

Candidates can be synthesised, picked from a pool of unlabelled data, or picked from a live stream. The author is most excited about the live case: a model that keeps choosing what to learn from as the world changes.

Code lab · Python

Random labelling vs uncertainty sampling

Step 12 starts with 30 random labels and buys 10 more at a time, up to 200, either at random or choosing the images where the model's top two guesses are closest. Each curve averages five runs.

Python · step 12 · active learning: label what the model is unsure about
X_pool, X_te, y_pool, y_te = train_test_split(digits.data / 16, digits.target, test_size=0.3, random_state=2, stratify=digits.target)

def run(strategy, seed, budget=200, start=30, step=10):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = list(r.choice(len(y_pool), start, replace=False))
    curve = {}
    while len(idx) <= budget:
        model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_pool[idx], y_pool[idx])
        curve[len(idx)] = accuracy_score(y_te, model.predict(X_te))
        rest = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y_pool)), idx)
        if strategy == "uncertainty":
            p = np.sort(model.predict_proba(X_pool[rest]), axis=1)
            margin = p[:, -1] - p[:, -2]                         # small gap between top two classes = unsure
            pick = rest[np.argsort(margin)[:step]]
        else:
            pick = r.choice(rest, step, replace=False)
        idx += list(pick)
    return curve

curves = {s: pd.DataFrame([run(s, seed) for seed in range(5)]).mean() for s in ["random", "uncertainty"]}
print(pd.DataFrame(curves).loc[[30, 60, 100, 150, 200]].round(3).rename_axis("labels").to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.2))
for s, mark in [("random", "o-"), ("uncertainty", "s-")]:
    ax.plot(curves[s].index, curves[s].values, mark, ms=3, label=f"{s} labelling")
ax.set(xlabel="labels paid for", ylabel="test accuracy (average of 5 runs)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
Output
        random  uncertainty
labels                     
30       0.681        0.681
60       0.816        0.870
100      0.883        0.916
150      0.905        0.943
200      0.914        0.951
How to read it

From the same 30-label start, uncertainty sampling pulls ahead immediately and stays ahead: about 0.92 at 100 labels versus 0.88 for random, and 0.95 versus 0.91 at 200. Put differently, it reaches random labelling's 200-label accuracy with roughly 100 labels.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2LabellingNEXT · SECTION 4Class Imbalance
Book / Chapter 4 / Section 4
Section 4 of 5 · Summary

Class Imbalance

Class imbalance means some classes have far more examples than others: 99.99% normal X-rays, 0.01% cancer. It also happens in regression, such as hospital bills, where the rare huge bills matter most. In school, datasets are balanced; at work, imbalance is the norm, because the rare events are often the interesting or dangerous ones. Three responses: the right metrics, data-level fixes (resampling) and algorithm-level fixes (changing the loss).

4.1Why it hurts4.2The right metrics4.3Resampling4.4Changing the loss
4.1

Why imbalance makes learning hard

Play · Tap each reason
Tap a reason.

Where it shows up: fraud (in 2018 about 6.8¢ of every $100 of card spending was fraud), churn, disease screening, CV screening (about 98% of applicants are cut at the first screen), even object detection, where most candidate boxes contain nothing.

It can also be caused by sampling: about 85% of all email was spam in 2021, but your company's mail database is mostly clean because filters removed the spam first. Or by labelling errors. Always look into why your data is imbalanced.

Simple, linearly separable problems barely care about imbalance; complex and multiclass problems care a lot. Very deep networks coped better than shallow ones in one 2017 study. Some argue a good enough model should just learn the real-world imbalance; until then, we need techniques.

Code lab · Python

A 98% accurate fraud model that catches nothing

Step 13 creates 20,000 transactions with about 2% fraud, and scores the laziest possible model: always say "not fraud".

Python · step 13 · the 99% accurate model that finds nothing
n = 20_000
Xf = rng.normal(size=(n, 6))
fraud = (Xf @ np.array([1.4, -1.0, 0.8, 0.5, 0, 0]) + rng.normal(0, 1, n)) > 4.4
print(f"fraud rate: {fraud.mean():.2%}")
always_no = np.zeros(n, bool)
print(f"'never fraud' accuracy: {accuracy_score(fraud, always_no):.2%}, frauds caught: {recall_score(fraud, always_no, zero_division=0):.0%}")
Output
fraud rate: 2.13%
'never fraud' accuracy: 97.87%, frauds caught: 0%
How to read it

97.9% accurate, 0% of fraud caught. Any model you build has to beat this trivial baseline on the metric that matters, which is clearly not accuracy. Gradient descent can get stuck near exactly this answer, because small random changes to it make accuracy worse.

4.2

Use the right evaluation metrics

Play · Same accuracy, different models

Our numbers: 2,000 scans, 200 with disease. The same as the code lab.

Accuracy and error rate treat every class equally, so the majority class dominates them. Better: metrics about the class you care about.

  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of those flagged, how many were right.
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the real cases, how many were caught.
  • F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall).

These are asymmetric: they change with which class you call positive (scikit-learn's f1_score uses label 1 by default). Per-class accuracy works too.

Curves, not one thresholdA model's score becomes a class through a threshold. The ROC curve plots recall against the false-positive rate for every threshold; its area (AUC) summarises it. Under heavy imbalance, the precision-recall curve (Davis and Goadrich) is often more informative.
Code lab · Python

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC and PR

Step 14 scores two models from their confusion-matrix counts, then trains a fraud model and plots its ROC and precision-recall curves.

Python · step 14 · the right metrics
def report(name, tp, fn, fp, tn):
    y_true = np.r_[np.ones(tp + fn), np.zeros(fp + tn)]
    y_pred = np.r_[np.ones(tp), np.zeros(fn), np.ones(fp), np.zeros(tn)]
    print(f"{name}: accuracy {accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred):.2f}  precision {precision_score(y_true, y_pred):.2f}  "
          f"recall {recall_score(y_true, y_pred):.2f}  F1 {f1_score(y_true, y_pred):.2f}")

# 2,000 scans, 200 truly show disease. Two models with the same accuracy:
report("model X", tp=30, fn=170, fp=30, tn=1770)
report("model Y", tp=170, fn=30, fp=170, tn=1630)

# ROC and precision-recall curves for a real model on the fraud data
Xf_tr, Xf_te, f_tr, f_te = train_test_split(Xf, fraud, test_size=0.4, random_state=0, stratify=fraud)
scores = LogisticRegression().fit(Xf_tr, f_tr).predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1]
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, precision_recall_curve
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(f_te, scores)
prec, rec, _ = precision_recall_curve(f_te, scores)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.2))
axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr); axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ":", color="#9AA0B8")
axes[0].set(title=f"ROC (AUC {roc_auc_score(f_te, scores):.2f})", xlabel="false positive rate", ylabel="recall")
axes[1].plot(rec, prec, color="#D97E06"); axes[1].axhline(f_te.mean(), ls=":", color="#9AA0B8")
axes[1].set(title=f"Precision-recall (AP {average_precision_score(f_te, scores):.2f})", xlabel="recall", ylabel="precision")
Output
model X: accuracy 0.90  precision 0.50  recall 0.15  F1 0.23
model Y: accuracy 0.90  precision 0.50  recall 0.85  F1 0.63
How to read it

Both models are 90% accurate, but model X finds 15% of the disease and Y finds 85%; F1 (0.23 vs 0.63) shows the difference immediately. In the charts the ROC curve looks very good (AUC near 1), while the precision-recall curve is more sober about how many flagged transactions are false alarms. The dotted PR baseline is the fraud rate: what random guessing would achieve.

4.3

Data-level methods: resampling

Play · Rebalance the training data
  • Undersampling removes majority examples; oversampling adds minority ones. The simplest versions do it at random.
  • Tomek links (1976) remove the majority point from each close opposite-class pair, clarifying the boundary, though the model then misses its subtleties.
  • SMOTE creates new minority points along lines between existing ones.
  • Both work mainly in low dimensions. Methods that need distances (Near-Miss, one-sided selection) get expensive in high dimensions.
Never evaluate on resampled dataTest on the real distribution, or you'll fool yourself. Undersampling throws data away; oversampling can overfit to copies. Refinements: two-phase learning (train on balanced data, then finetune on the original) and dynamic sampling (show more of what the model still gets wrong).
Code lab · Python

Five ways to treat the same fraud data

Step 15 uses imbalanced-learn to resample the training set four ways, trains the same model each time, and always evaluates on the untouched test set.

Python · step 15 · resampling: over, under, SMOTE, Tomek
from imblearn.over_sampling import RandomOverSampler, SMOTE
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks
rows = []
for name, sampler in [("none", None), ("random oversample", RandomOverSampler(random_state=0)),
                      ("random undersample", RandomUnderSampler(random_state=0)),
                      ("SMOTE", SMOTE(random_state=0)), ("Tomek links", TomekLinks())]:
    Xs, ys = (Xf_tr, f_tr) if sampler is None else sampler.fit_resample(Xf_tr, f_tr)
    pred = LogisticRegression().fit(Xs, ys).predict(Xf_te)          # always evaluate on the untouched test set
    rows.append({"method": name, "train rows": len(ys), "fraud share": f"{ys.mean():.1%}",
                 "recall": round(recall_score(f_te, pred), 2), "precision": round(precision_score(f_te, pred, zero_division=0), 2),
                 "F1": round(f1_score(f_te, pred), 2)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
Output
            method  train rows fraud share  recall  precision   F1
              none       12000        2.1%    0.41       0.70 0.51
 random oversample       23488       50.0%    0.98       0.20 0.34
random undersample         512       50.0%    0.97       0.20 0.34
             SMOTE       23488       50.0%    0.98       0.22 0.36
       Tomek links       11928        2.1%    0.48       0.68 0.56
How to read it

Balancing to 50/50 (over, under or SMOTE) pushes recall from 0.41 to about 0.98, but precision falls to about 0.20: most flags become false alarms. Tomek links nudge both recall and F1 up while keeping the original mix. None is "best": choose by the cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm. Note how undersampling trains on only 512 rows.

4.4

Algorithm-level methods: change the loss

Compare · A cost matrix
Actually normalActually fraud
Predicted normal0 (correct)₹ lost to fraud: high
Predicted fraudAnnoyed customer: low0 (correct)

Our example of a cost matrix with asymmetric costs.

Keep the data as it is and change how the model learns. The loss is usually the average over examples; reweight it so the examples you care about count more.

Cost-sensitive learningElkan (2001): a cost matrix sets the cost of each kind of mistake. Downside: you must choose the costs by hand.
Class-balanced lossWeight each class inversely to its frequency, so rare classes count more. Refined versions use the "effective number" of samples.
Focal lossLin et al. (2017): weight examples by how hard they still are, so easy, already-learned ones fade and the model focuses on what it gets wrong.

Ensembles also help with imbalance, but they're covered in Chapter 6.

Code lab · Python

Class weights, and what focal loss does

Step 16 retrains the fraud model with fraud mistakes counting 1×, 5× and "balanced" (about 46×), then plots focal loss against ordinary cross-entropy.

Python · step 16 · cost-sensitive learning and focal loss
for cw in [None, {False: 1, True: 5}, "balanced"]:
    pred = LogisticRegression(class_weight=cw).fit(Xf_tr, f_tr).predict(Xf_te)
    label = "no weights" if cw is None else ("balanced (1/frequency)" if cw == "balanced" else "fraud costs 5x")
    print(f"{label:<24} recall {recall_score(f_te, pred):.2f}  precision {precision_score(f_te, pred, zero_division=0):.2f}")

p = np.linspace(0.01, 1, 200)                 # model's probability for the true class
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
for gamma in [0, 1, 2, 5]:
    ax.plot(p, -(1 - p) ** gamma * np.log(p), label="cross-entropy" if gamma == 0 else f"focal, γ={gamma}")
ax.set(xlabel="probability given to the true class", ylabel="loss", ylim=(0, 4))
ax.legend()
Output
no weights               recall 0.41  precision 0.70
fraud costs 5x           recall 0.74  precision 0.42
balanced (1/frequency)   recall 0.98  precision 0.20
How to read it

The weight is a dial: 5× lifts recall from 0.41 to 0.74 at 0.42 precision, while "balanced" goes all the way to 0.98 recall at 0.20 precision, matching what oversampling did. In the chart, higher γ flattens the loss for examples the model already gets right (probability near 1), so training effort goes to the hard ones.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 3Handling the Lack of LabelsNEXT · SECTION 5Data Augmentation
Book / Chapter 4 / Section 5
Section 5 of 5 · Summary

Data Augmentation

Augmentation creates more training data from what you have. It started where data is scarce (medical imaging), but even with lots of data it makes models more robust to noise and to adversarial attacks. It's standard in computer vision and spreading into NLP. Three kinds: label-preserving transformations, perturbation and synthesis.

5.1Transformations5.2Perturbation5.3Synthesis
5.1

Label-preserving transformations

Play · Move a digit

An 8×8 handwritten "3". It's still a 3 wherever it sits.

Change the input without changing its label: crop, flip, rotate, erase part of an image. A rotated dog is still a dog. PyTorch, TensorFlow and Keras all support this. AlexNet generated its augmented images on the CPU while the GPU trained, making them effectively free.

In NLP, swap a word for a synonym, from a dictionary or from nearby words in an embedding space: "I'm so happy to see you" → "I'm so glad to see you". A quick way to double or triple text data.

Code lab · Python

Shift digits by one pixel

Step 17 trains on just 8 examples per digit, then adds four one-pixel-shifted copies of each. Both models are tested on centred digits and on the same digits written one pixel to the right. It also swaps synonyms in a sentence.

Python · step 17 · label-preserving transformations
def shift(img, dx, dy):
    """Move an 8x8 image by one pixel, filling the gap with blank."""
    im, out = img.reshape(8, 8), np.zeros((8, 8))
    out[max(dy, 0):8 + min(dy, 0), max(dx, 0):8 + min(dx, 0)] = im[max(-dy, 0):8 + min(-dy, 0), max(-dx, 0):8 + min(-dx, 0)]
    return out.ravel()

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(digits.data, digits.target, test_size=0.5, random_state=3, stratify=digits.target)
small = np.concatenate([np.where(y_tr == c)[0][:8] for c in range(10)])     # 8 examples per digit
X_small, y_small = X_tr[small], y_tr[small]
moves = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
X_aug = np.vstack([X_small] + [np.array([shift(im, dx, dy) for im in X_small]) for dx, dy in moves])
y_aug = np.tile(y_small, 5)
X_te_moved = np.array([shift(im, 1, 0) for im in X_te])                     # the same test digits, written 1 pixel to the right
for name, (Xa, ya) in [("80 originals", (X_small, y_small)), ("80 + 320 shifted copies", (X_aug, y_aug))]:
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(Xa, ya)
    print(f"{name:<24} centred test {accuracy_score(y_te, m.predict(X_te)):.3f}   off-centre test {accuracy_score(y_te, m.predict(X_te_moved)):.3f}")

random.seed(2)
SYN = {"pain": ["ache", "discomfort"], "tooth": ["molar", "teeth"], "severe": ["bad", "intense"]}
s = "severe pain in my tooth since morning"
print("\ntext augmentation by synonym swap:")
for _ in range(3):
    print("  ", " ".join(random.choice(SYN[w]) if w in SYN and random.random() < .7 else w for w in s.split()))
Output
80 originals             centred test 0.885   off-centre test 0.380
80 + 320 shifted copies  centred test 0.746   off-centre test 0.659

text augmentation by synonym swap:
   severe pain in my molar since morning
   bad pain in my teeth since morning
   bad ache in my tooth since morning
How to read it

A real trade-off. Without augmentation the model is great on centred digits (0.885) but collapses when they're slightly off-centre (0.380). With shifted copies it handles off-centre digits far better (0.659) but loses some accuracy on centred ones (0.746), because on 8×8 images one pixel is a big move. Augment with the variations your real data actually contains.

5.2

Perturbation

67.97%of CIFAR-10 test images misclassified by changing one pixel (Su et al.)
16.04%of ImageNet test images fooled the same way
15% → 1.5%BERT selects 15% of tokens and replaces 10% of those with random words: 1.5% overall

Perturbation also preserves labels, but deserves its own name because it's used to trick models. Neural networks are sensitive to noise; deliberately deceptive inputs are adversarial attacks, and they get easier as image resolution grows.

  • Training on noisy samples helps models find weak spots in their decision boundary. Noise can be random or searched for: DeepFool finds the smallest noise that causes a confident mistake (adversarial augmentation).
  • In NLP, random characters make gibberish, but small random replacement helps: BERT's "My dog is hairy" might become "My dog is apple", and that slight noise gave a small boost.

Chapter 6 uses perturbation to evaluate models, too.

Code lab · Python

Fool a digit classifier with a small nudge

Step 18 takes a correctly classified digit and nudges every pixel a little towards the class the model nearly chose, increasing the nudge until the prediction flips.

Python · step 18 · a tiny nudge flips the prediction
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
img = X_te[0]
pred = clf.predict([img])[0]
runner_up = np.argsort(clf.decision_function([img])[0])[-2]       # the class it almost chose
direction = np.sign(clf.coef_[runner_up] - clf.coef_[pred])        # nudge every pixel slightly towards it
for eps in np.arange(0, 16, 0.05):
    adv = np.clip(img + eps * direction, 0, 16)
    if clf.predict([adv])[0] != pred:
        break
print(f"true digit {y_te[0]}, model says {pred}")
print(f"nudge each pixel by up to {eps:.2f} (pixel values run 0-16, average change {np.abs(adv - img).mean():.2f}) "
      f"-> model says {clf.predict([adv])[0]}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6, 2.3))
for ax, im, t in zip(axes, [img, adv, adv - img], [f"original: {pred}", f"nudged: {clf.predict([adv])[0]}", "the nudge"]):
    ax.imshow(im.reshape(8, 8), cmap="Greys" if t != "the nudge" else "RdBu"); ax.set(title=t, xticks=[], yticks=[]); ax.grid(False)
Output
true digit 6, model says 6
nudge each pixel by up to 1.35 (pixel values run 0-16, average change 0.90) -> model says 8
How to read it

The 6 becomes an 8 after each pixel moves by at most 1.35 on a 0–16 scale, less than one shade of grey on average. To a person the two images look the same; the model sees a different digit. Training on such nudged examples teaches the model to ignore them.

5.3

Data synthesis: templates and mixup

Play · Generate queries from a template
Book a [SERVICE] with [DOCTOR] on [DAY] [TIME]
Play · Mixup

Collecting data is slow, costly and risky for privacy, so it would be a dream to synthesise it. We're far from fully synthetic training data, but partial synthesis helps.

  • Templates bootstrap NLP data: lists of services, doctors and times turn one template into many queries for a chatbot.
  • Mixup blends two images and their labels: 70% of a "3" plus 30% of an "8" gets the label (0.7, 0.3). It improves generalisation, reduces memorising corrupt labels, and adds robustness to adversarial examples.
  • Generative models: Sandfort et al. improved CT-scan segmentation by adding CycleGAN-generated images. Promising, but not yet common in production.
Code lab · Python

One template, 36 queries; and a mixup blend

Step 19 expands one booking template into every combination, then blends a "3" and an "8" at four mixing ratios.

Python · step 19 · templates and mixup
random.seed(3)
template = "Book a {service} with {doctor} on {day} {time}"
slots = {"service": ["cleaning", "root canal review", "braces check"], "doctor": ["Dr Rao", "Dr Mehta"],
         "day": ["Monday", "Saturday", "tomorrow"], "time": ["morning", "after 5 pm"]}
all_q = [template.format(**dict(zip(slots, combo))) for combo in itertools.product(*slots.values())]
print(f"{len(all_q)} training queries from one template, e.g.:")
for q in random.sample(all_q, 3):
    print("  ", q)

a = digits.data[digits.target == 3][0]
b = digits.data[digits.target == 8][0]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.4, 2.1))
for ax, lam in zip(axes, [1.0, 0.7, 0.3, 0.0]):
    ax.imshow((lam * a + (1 - lam) * b).reshape(8, 8), cmap="Greys")
    ax.set(title=f"{lam:.0%} '3' / {1 - lam:.0%} '8'", xticks=[], yticks=[]); ax.grid(False)
    ax.title.set_fontsize(8.5)
print("mixup label for the 70/30 image: [P(3)=0.7, P(8)=0.3]")
Output
36 training queries from one template, e.g.:
   Book a root canal review with Dr Rao on Saturday after 5 pm
   Book a braces check with Dr Mehta on tomorrow morning
   Book a cleaning with Dr Mehta on Saturday morning
mixup label for the 70/30 image: [P(3)=0.7, P(8)=0.3]
How to read it

Three services × two doctors × three days × two times = 36 phrasings with no labelling at all, though templates produce stiff language, so mix them with real queries. The mixup images move smoothly from a 3 to an 8, and each comes with a soft label saying how much of each it is.

Book / Chapter 4 / Recap
Chapter 4 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

However clever the algorithm, bad training data sinks it, so it pays to invest in curating and creating it. Sample deliberately, get labels you can trust (and track where they came from), use weak supervision, semi-supervision, transfer and active learning when labels are scarce, handle imbalance with the right metrics, resampling or loss changes, and augment what you have. Next: turning training data into features.

Eight takeaways

1. Convenience is biasedEasy-to-get data rarely represents reality. Sample randomly where you can.
2. Stratify and weightGuarantee rare classes appear; reweight data whose mix differs from reality.
3. Streams need reservoirsReservoir sampling gives a fair sample of unknown-length data.
4. Labels disagreeMeasure agreement, write clear guidelines, and track every label's lineage.
5. Natural labels are latePick the label window knowing it trades speed for accuracy.
6. Fewer labels, four waysLabeling functions, label spreading, transfer and active learning.
7. Imbalance needs careIgnore accuracy; use precision, recall, F1, PR curves; then resample or reweight.
8. Augment realisticallyTransform, perturb or synthesise, matching the variation your data really has.

Quick quiz

Book / Chapter 5
Chapter 5 · Broad summary

Feature Engineering

Facebook's 2014 ads paper said the right features matter most, and teams keep rediscovering it: once a model works, better features usually beat clever tuning. This chapter covers learned vs engineered features, the common operations (missing values, scaling, binning, encoding, crossing, positional features), the quiet disaster of data leakage, and how to tell a good feature by its importance and how well it generalises. Feature stores come later, in Chapter 10.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Learned vs engineered. Deep learning learns features from raw text and images, but most production models still need hand-built features from the rest of the data: users, context, history.
  2. Common operations. Handle missing values knowing why they're missing; scale and log-transform; bin sparingly; encode changing categories with the hashing trick; cross features for non-linear effects; encode positions with embeddings or Fourier features.
  3. Data leakage. When the label sneaks into the features in a way that won't exist at prediction time. Split by time and by group, split before scaling, deduplicate, and question any feature that looks too good.
  4. Good features. Keep the ones that matter (importance) and that will hold up on new data (coverage and value overlap). Remove the rest: they cost money, latency and risk.

Each section has its own summary, sub-sections and code labs.
