Book / Chapter 6 / Section 3
Section 3 of 4 · Summary

Developing Models

Training a model is mostly babysitting it. This section covers the habits that keep that sane: tracking experiments and versioning code and data so results can be reproduced; debugging models that fail silently; distributed training when data or models outgrow one machine; AutoML, from tuning hyperparameters to searching for architectures; and the four phases most teams move through.

3.1Tracking & versioning3.2Debugging3.3Distributed training3.4AutoML3.5Four phases
3.1

Experiment tracking and versioning

Play · What to track, and why data is hard to version

Tracking means recording what happens during each experiment: loss curves for every split, the metrics you care about, samples of predictions next to the true labels, speed, memory and GPU use, and how values like the learning rate change. It lets you spot problems early and compare experiments to learn what each change did.

Versioning means you can recreate any experiment later: the exact code, data and settings. Code versioning is routine. Data versioning is "like flossing": everyone agrees, few do it, partly because data is huge, diffs are unclear, and privacy laws may require deleting old data.

Even thenTracking and versioning help reproducibility but don't guarantee it: frameworks and hardware can add their own randomness.
Code lab · Python

A tracker in ten lines

Step 9 wraps training in run_experiment, which appends every run's settings and results as one JSON line to a log file, never overwriting. Four learning rates later, pandas reads the log back for comparison.

Python · step 9 · a minimal experiment tracker
log_path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "runs.jsonl")

def run_experiment(lr, hidden, seed=0):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    m = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=hidden, learning_rate_init=lr, max_iter=100, random_state=seed).fit(X_val_tr, y_val_tr)
    record = {"lr": lr, "hidden": hidden, "seed": seed, "val_acc": round(accuracy_score(y_val, m.predict(X_val)), 4),
              "final_loss": round(m.loss_, 4), "epochs": m.n_iter_, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)}
    with open(log_path, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")         # every run appended, never overwritten

for lr in [0.0005, 0.002, 0.003, 0.03]:
    run_experiment(lr, (32,))
runs = pd.read_json(log_path, lines=True)
print(runs.drop(columns="seconds").to_string(index=False))
print("\nbest run:", runs.loc[runs.val_acc.idxmax(), ["lr", "val_acc"]].to_dict())
Output
    lr hidden  seed  val_acc  final_loss  epochs
0.0005   [32]     0   0.8729      0.2926     100
0.0020   [32]     0   0.8871      0.2218     100
0.0030   [32]     0   0.8914      0.2010     100
0.0300   [32]     0   0.8729      0.1372      92

best run: {'lr': 0.003, 'val_acc': 0.8914000000000001}
How to read it

Every run is now a row you can sort and compare. A learning rate of 0.003 gave the best validation accuracy (0.891). Notice what the log reveals that one number wouldn't: the fastest learner (0.03) reached the lowest training loss but the worst validation accuracy, a sign of overfitting. The three slower runs used all 100 epochs, a hint they'd have kept improving.

3.2

Debugging ML models

Play · Where can it go wrong?
Pick a cause.

ML debugging is especially frustrating. Models fail silently: the code runs, loss goes down, predictions come out, and they're wrong. Checking a fix can mean hours of retraining. And the cause could sit with any of several teams: data, labels, features, algorithm, code or infrastructure.

Three tried-and-true habits: start simple and add one component at a time; overfit a single small batch (if the model can't memorise ten examples, something is broken); and set random seeds so you can tell a real improvement from luck.

Further readingAndrej Karpathy's blog post "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" is the classic list of these habits.
Code lab · Python

Overfit a tiny batch; measure seed noise

Step 10 trains a network on just 12 examples, once with the real features and once with a simulated upstream bug that zeroed them. Then it retrains one configuration with six different random seeds.

Python · step 10 · two debugging habits
tiny_X, tiny_y = X_tr[:12], y_tr[:12]
net = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(32,), max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(tiny_X, tiny_y)
print(f"overfit 12 examples, correct pipeline:  train accuracy {accuracy_score(tiny_y, net.predict(tiny_X)):.0%}")

buggy_X = np.zeros_like(tiny_X)                  # a bug: features replaced by zeros somewhere upstream
net_b = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(32,), max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(buggy_X, tiny_y)
print(f"overfit 12 examples, broken features:   train accuracy {accuracy_score(tiny_y, net_b.predict(buggy_X)):.0%}  <- can't even memorise: look for the bug")

scores = [accuracy_score(y_val, MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(32,), max_iter=100, random_state=s).fit(X_val_tr, y_val_tr).predict(X_val)) for s in range(6)]
print(f"\nsame model, 6 random seeds: {np.round(scores, 3)}  (range {max(scores) - min(scores):.3f})")
Output
overfit 12 examples, correct pipeline:  train accuracy 100%
overfit 12 examples, broken features:   train accuracy 75%  <- can't even memorise: look for the bug

same model, 6 random seeds: [0.881 0.89  0.89  0.891 0.89  0.893]  (range 0.011)
How to read it

With real features the network memorises all 12 examples (100%). With zeroed features it can't: it gets 75% only by always guessing the majority class. A model that can't even overfit is telling you there's a bug. And the seeds alone move validation accuracy from 0.881 to 0.893, so a "1-point improvement" from one run might be pure luck.

3.3

Distributed training

Play · Three ways to split the work

When data doesn't fit in memory (CT scans, genomes, huge text corpora), preprocessing, shuffling and batching must run out of core and in parallel. Tricks like gradient checkpointing trade extra compute for less memory.

Data parallelism: every machine has the whole model and trains on different data, then results are combined. In synchronous mode, everyone waits for the slowest machine (the straggler); in asynchronous mode, nobody waits, but updates can go stale. Huge combined batches can also make training unstable.

Model parallelism: different machines hold different parts of the model. Pipeline parallelism splits each batch into micro-batches so those parts can work at the same time. Big teams use several of these together.

Code lab · Python

Simulate synchronous steps with stragglers

Step 11 simulates workers whose step takes about 100 ms, with a 1% chance of being 2–4 times slower. A synchronous step takes as long as its slowest worker.

Python · step 11 · synchronous training and stragglers
def sync_step_time(workers, trials=2000):
    # each worker's step takes ~100 ms, but now and then one is slow (a straggler)
    t = rng.normal(100, 8, (trials, workers))
    slow = rng.random((trials, workers)) < 0.01
    t[slow] *= rng.uniform(2, 4, slow.sum())
    return t.max(axis=1).mean()                   # synchronous: everyone waits for the slowest

ws = [1, 2, 8, 32, 128, 512]
times = [sync_step_time(w) for w in ws]
for w, t in zip(ws, times):
    print(f"{w:>4} workers: average synchronous step {t:6.1f} ms  (batch {w * 1000:>7,} examples)")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3))
ax.plot(ws, times, "o-", color="#7351DA")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="workers", ylabel="time per step (ms)")
Output
   1 workers: average synchronous step  102.1 ms  (batch   1,000 examples)
   2 workers: average synchronous step  107.9 ms  (batch   2,000 examples)
   8 workers: average synchronous step  125.4 ms  (batch   8,000 examples)
  32 workers: average synchronous step  169.7 ms  (batch  32,000 examples)
 128 workers: average synchronous step  266.7 ms  (batch 128,000 examples)
 512 workers: average synchronous step  368.9 ms  (batch 512,000 examples)
How to read it

One worker averages 102 ms per step. With 512 workers each step takes 369 ms, more than three times as long, because with so many workers some are almost always stragglers. You still process 512 times more data per step, so it's a big win overall, just not 512 times faster. This is why asynchronous updates and straggler handling matter at scale.

3.4

AutoML

Play · Nine tries: grid or random?

Soft AutoML is hyperparameter tuning: searching for settings like learning rate, tree depth or batch size. Grid search, random search and Bayesian optimisation are the common methods, built into most frameworks. Some hyperparameters matter far more than others; tune those most carefully.

Hard AutoML goes further. Neural architecture search treats the model's structure as something to search over, using a search space, a quick way to estimate each candidate's performance, and a search strategy. Learned optimisers even learn the update rule itself. Both need huge compute, but the results (such as Google's EfficientNet family) can be reused by everyone.

Never tune on the test splitChoose hyperparameters on validation data; touch the test split once, for the final number.
Code lab · Python

Grid search vs random search, same budget

Step 12 gives grid search and random search the same budget: 9 settings each, with 3-fold cross-validation on a 1,500-row sample. Each winner is then scored once on the separate validation split.

Python · step 12 · grid search vs random search
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV
X_s, y_s = X_val_tr[:1500], y_val_tr[:1500]
grid = GridSearchCV(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0, max_iter=100),
                    {"learning_rate": [0.01, 0.1, 0.5], "max_leaf_nodes": [4, 16, 64]}, cv=3).fit(X_s, y_s)
rand = RandomizedSearchCV(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0, max_iter=100),
                          {"learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.5), "max_leaf_nodes": randint(4, 64)},
                          n_iter=9, cv=3, random_state=0).fit(X_s, y_s)
for name, s in [("grid, 9 combos  ", grid), ("random, 9 draws", rand)]:
    p = s.best_params_
    print(f"{name}: best CV {s.best_score_:.3f}  lr={p['learning_rate']:.3f} leaves={p['max_leaf_nodes']}"
          f"  -> validation {accuracy_score(y_val, s.best_estimator_.predict(X_val)):.3f}")
print("\n(the test split stays untouched until the very end)")
Output
grid, 9 combos  : best CV 0.865  lr=0.100 leaves=64  -> validation 0.864
random, 9 draws: best CV 0.873  lr=0.240 leaves=50  -> validation 0.867

(the test split stays untouched until the very end)
How to read it

Random search found slightly better settings (CV 0.873 vs 0.865), partly because it tried nine different learning rates while the grid only tried three. The margin is small, and on another day the grid might win, but it shows why random search is a strong default. The validation scores (0.864 and 0.867) are lower than the CV scores: picking the best of nine is a little optimistic, which is why you check on held-out data.

3.5

Four phases of model development

Play · Walk through the phases

Phase 1, before ML. Try a heuristic first. You may find you don't need ML yet. A common rule of thumb: if ML would give you a 100% boost, a heuristic gets you halfway.

Phase 2, simplest ML models. Logistic regression or boosted trees: easy to understand and deploy, so you can test the whole pipeline end to end.

Phase 3, optimise simple models. Better objectives, hyperparameter search, feature engineering, more data, ensembles.

Phase 4, complex models. Only when simple models hit their limit and the use case needs more. Then also find out how fast the model decays in production.

Code lab · Python

The four phases on clinic no-shows

Step 13 simulates 5,000 clinic appointments: missed visits before, how many days ahead it was booked, travel distance, age, and whether an SMS reminder went out. It predicts no-shows with each phase's solution and reports AUC on held-out appointments.

Python · step 13 · the four phases on one problem
# Predict whether a clinic patient will miss their next appointment
n = 5000
p = pd.DataFrame({"missed_before": rng.poisson(0.6, n), "days_ahead": rng.integers(0, 45, n),
                  "distance_km": rng.gamma(2, 3, n), "age": rng.integers(18, 80, n), "sms_reminder": rng.random(n) < 0.5})
logit = -2.2 + 0.9 * p.missed_before + 0.03 * p.days_ahead + 0.05 * p.distance_km - 0.9 * p.sms_reminder + 0.4 * (p.age < 25) + 0.5 * (p.days_ahead > 30) * (~p.sms_reminder)
noshow = rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))
Pa, Pb, na, nb = train_test_split(p, noshow, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=noshow)
results = {
    "1 · heuristic: 'missed before'": roc_auc_score(nb, Pb.missed_before),
    "2 · logistic regression": roc_auc_score(nb, LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Pa, na).predict_proba(Pb)[:, 1]),
    "3 · tuned boosted trees": roc_auc_score(nb, RandomizedSearchCV(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
                                 {"learning_rate": loguniform(0.02, 0.3), "max_leaf_nodes": randint(4, 32)}, n_iter=8, cv=3, scoring="roc_auc",
                                 random_state=0).fit(Pa, na).predict_proba(Pb)[:, 1]),
    "4 · neural network": roc_auc_score(nb, MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 64), max_iter=300, early_stopping=True, random_state=0).fit((Pa - Pa.mean()) / Pa.std(), na).predict_proba((Pb - Pa.mean()) / Pa.std())[:, 1]),
}
for k, v in results.items():
    print(f"{k:<32} AUC {v:.3f}")
Output
1 · heuristic: 'missed before'   AUC 0.679
2 · logistic regression          AUC 0.760
3 · tuned boosted trees          AUC 0.745
4 · neural network               AUC 0.756
How to read it

The one-line heuristic, "has this patient missed before?", already gets 0.679. Logistic regression jumps to 0.760. Then a surprise worth noticing: tuned boosted trees (0.745) and a neural network (0.756) do not beat it. On this data, phase 2 was the place to stop, and each phase was only worth it measured against the one before.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2EnsemblesNEXT · SECTION 4Offline Evaluation
Book / Chapter 6 / Section 4
Section 4 of 4 · Summary

Offline Evaluation

"How do I know our model is any good?" is a hard question. Ideally you'd evaluate the same way in development and in production, but in production you often lack labels, so you must check thoroughly beforehand. Start with baselines so the number means something. Then go beyond one overall score: perturbation, invariance and directional tests for robustness and fairness, calibration and confidence for trustworthy probabilities, and slice-based evaluation for the groups that matter.

4.1Baselines4.2Perturbation4.3Invariance & direction4.4Calibration4.5Confidence4.6Slices
4.1

Baselines

Play · How good is random guessing?

A guesser that says "positive" at the label rate. Its expected F1 equals that rate.

A metric alone means little. An engineer once proudly reported an F1 of 0.90, on a task where 90% of labels were positive: random guessing at that rate scores about the same. Always compare against baselines:

Random (uniform or at the label rate) · simple heuristic (e.g. most recent posts first) · zero rule (always predict the most common class) · human performance · existing solutions, including the system you're replacing.

And usefulnessBeating baselines isn't enough: a self-driving car that is 99% safe still isn't usable. Ask what level the product needs.
Code lab · Python

Score three baselines on an imbalanced task

Step 14 makes 100,000 labels with 10% positive and scores three dumb predictors: a coin flip, a guesser that says "positive" 10% of the time, and the zero rule. Then it flips the task to 90% positive.

Python · step 14 · baselines give metrics meaning
n = 100_000
truth = rng.random(n) < 0.10                          # 10% positive
uniform = rng.random(n) < 0.5
label_dist = rng.random(n) < 0.10
zero_rule = np.zeros(n, bool)
for name, pred in [("uniform random", uniform), ("random at label rate", label_dist), ("zero rule (always negative)", zero_rule)]:
    print(f"{name:<28} accuracy {accuracy_score(truth, pred):.3f}   F1 {f1_score(truth, pred, zero_division=0):.3f}")

flipped = ~truth                                      # now the positive class is 90%
print(f"\nif positives are 90%, random-at-label-rate F1 is {f1_score(flipped, rng.random(n) < 0.9):.2f}: an F1 of 0.90 might mean nothing")
Output
uniform random               accuracy 0.502   F1 0.171
random at label rate         accuracy 0.820   F1 0.099
zero rule (always negative)  accuracy 0.899   F1 0.000

if positives are 90%, random-at-label-rate F1 is 0.90: an F1 of 0.90 might mean nothing
How to read it

The zero rule scores 0.899 accuracy while never finding a single positive (F1 0). So accuracy of 0.90 on this task is worthless. Flip the task to 90% positive and blind guessing earns an F1 of 0.90, exactly the anecdote above. Write the baseline next to every metric you report.

4.2

Perturbation tests

Play · Add noise to the test inputs

Clean test sets flatter models. Real inputs are messy: a patient records a voice note on an old phone in a noisy waiting room, or types a symptom with a typo. A perturbation test adds small, realistic changes to the test inputs and checks how much performance drops.

The more sensitive a model is to noise, the harder it will be to maintain, and the easier it will be to fool on purpose (adversarial attacks). Sometimes a slightly less accurate but steadier model is the better choice.

BonusAdding noise to training data can make models more robust to noisy inputs.
Code lab · Python

Accuracy as noise grows

Step 15 trains three models on clean data, then adds Gaussian noise of growing strength to the test features only.

Python · step 15 · perturbation tests
Xn_tr, Xn_te, yn_tr, yn_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=3)
cands = {"deep tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), "boosted trees": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
         "logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)}
rows = []
for name, m in cands.items():
    m.fit(Xn_tr, yn_tr)
    row = {"model": name}
    for noise in [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]:
        noisy = Xn_te + rng.normal(0, noise, Xn_te.shape)       # like a cheap microphone or a typo
        row[f"noise {noise}"] = round(accuracy_score(yn_te, m.predict(noisy)), 3)
    rows.append(row)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
Output
              model  noise 0.0  noise 0.5  noise 1.0
          deep tree      0.784      0.764      0.701
      boosted trees      0.893      0.868      0.811
logistic regression      0.776      0.782      0.748
How to read it

Boosted trees stay the most accurate throughout but lose 8.2 points by noise 1.0. The deep tree loses 8.3. Logistic regression loses only 2.8, and at noise 0.5 it even scores a touch higher than on clean data (noise can do that). If your inputs will be noisy, the gap between models narrows, and robustness is a reason to choose.

4.3

Invariance and directional expectation tests

Play · Change one input, watch the price

An illustration in the spirit of the lab, not the lab's model.

Some changes to the input should not change the output. A flat's price shouldn't depend on the owner's religion; a loan decision shouldn't depend on gender. An invariance test changes only that attribute and checks the prediction stays put. If it moves, the model has learned a bias, often from biased history.

Other changes should move the output in a known direction. A bigger flat, all else equal, shouldn't be predicted cheaper. A directional expectation test checks that, and failures hint the model learned something wrong.

A simple fix for invarianceLeave sensitive attributes out of the features. But watch for proxies, such as neighbourhood, that carry the same information.
Code lab · Python

Test a house-price model for bias and direction

Step 16 simulates 3,000 flats whose historical prices were biased against one religious group, trains a model with that attribute included, and runs an invariance test. Then it retrains without the attribute and runs a directional test: add 200 sq ft.

Python · step 16 · invariance and directional expectation tests
n = 3000
homes = pd.DataFrame({"area_sqft": rng.integers(400, 2200, n), "floor": rng.integers(0, 25, n),
                      "age_years": rng.integers(0, 40, n), "owner_religion": rng.integers(0, 3, n)})
price = 9000 * homes.area_sqft * (1 + 0.004 * homes.floor) * (1 - 0.006 * homes.age_years) * rng.normal(1, 0.08, n)
price += np.where(homes.owner_religion == 2, -400_000, 0)     # biased historical prices
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
model = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(homes, price)

sample = homes.sample(500, random_state=1)
base_pred = model.predict(sample)
inv = model.predict(sample.assign(owner_religion=0))
print(f"invariance: changing only owner_religion moves the price by up to ₹{np.abs(inv - base_pred).max():,.0f}  -> FAIL")
fair = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(homes.drop(columns="owner_religion"), price)
print("fix: drop the sensitive feature, so the model cannot use it")

bigger = fair.predict(sample.drop(columns="owner_religion").assign(area_sqft=sample.area_sqft + 200))
smaller = fair.predict(sample.drop(columns="owner_religion"))
print(f"directional: +200 sq ft lowered the price for {(bigger < smaller).mean():.1%} of homes (should be 0%)")
Output
invariance: changing only owner_religion moves the price by up to ₹604,620  -> FAIL
fix: drop the sensitive feature, so the model cannot use it
directional: +200 sq ft lowered the price for 0.0% of homes (should be 0%)
How to read it

With the attribute available, changing only the owner's religion moves a prediction by up to ₹6 lakh: a clear fail, and a model that repeats past discrimination. With the attribute removed, there's nothing for that test to catch. The directional test passes: adding 200 sq ft never lowered a predicted price. In real data, check for proxies too.

4.4

Model calibration

Play · When the model says 70%, what happens?

A model is calibrated if, among the cases where it says 70%, about 70% really are positive. A forecaster who says 70% chance of rain should be right on about 70% of those days.

It matters whenever you use the probability itself, not just the yes/no. Our own example: a clinic expects 10 patients each with a 30% no-show risk, so it plans for about 3 empty slots when overbooking. If the model's "30%" really means 50%, the plan is wrong every day. Ad systems use predicted click rates in exactly this way to set bids.

Fixing itFit a small correction on held-out data: Platt scaling (a sigmoid) or isotonic regression. In scikit-learn: CalibratedClassifierCV.
Code lab · Python

Reliability curves before and after calibration

Step 17 bins each model's test predictions into ten probability ranges and compares the average prediction in each bin with the actual share of positives. Then it wraps naive Bayes in CalibratedClassifierCV.

Python · step 17 · calibration
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve, CalibratedClassifierCV
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ":", color="#9AA0B8", label="perfectly calibrated")
for name, m in [("naive Bayes", GaussianNB()), ("logistic regression", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
                ("naive Bayes + calibration", CalibratedClassifierCV(GaussianNB(), method="sigmoid", cv=5))]:
    prob = m.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    frac, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_te, prob, n_bins=10)
    ax.plot(mean_pred, frac, "o-", ms=4, label=name)
    gap = np.abs(frac - mean_pred).mean()
    print(f"{name:<26} average gap between predicted and actual rate: {gap:.3f}")
ax.set(xlabel="predicted probability", ylabel="actual fraction positive")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
Output
naive Bayes                average gap between predicted and actual rate: 0.070
logistic regression        average gap between predicted and actual rate: 0.026
naive Bayes + calibration  average gap between predicted and actual rate: 0.051
How to read it

The dotted diagonal is perfect calibration. Logistic regression hugs it (average gap 0.026). Naive Bayes strays further (0.070) because its independence assumption makes it overconfident. Sigmoid calibration narrows the gap to 0.051, an improvement but not a cure. Calibration fixes probabilities, not ranking: its accuracy stays the same.

4.5

Confidence measurement

Play · Raise the confidence bar

Overall accuracy averages over all predictions, but each prediction can be judged on its own. Confidence measurement asks: how sure is the model about this one, and is that sure enough to act on?

A system might auto-send reminders only for patients it's confident will miss, and route uncertain cases to a person. The lower-confidence ones aren't thrown away; they're handled differently. For this to work, confidence must be measured on validation data, and the probabilities should be calibrated.

A threshold per predictionThink of it as a usefulness bar for each individual answer, not just for the model overall.
Code lab · Python

Coverage vs accuracy as the threshold rises

Step 18 takes the boosted-tree probabilities and, for several thresholds, keeps only the predictions at least that confident. It reports how many cases are covered and the accuracy on those.

Python · step 18 · act only when confident
prob = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
conf = np.maximum(prob, 1 - prob)
pred = prob >= 0.5
for t in [0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95]:
    keep = conf >= t
    print(f"show only predictions with confidence ≥ {t:.2f}: covers {keep.mean():5.1%} of cases, accuracy {accuracy_score(y_te[keep], pred[keep]):.3f}")
Output
show only predictions with confidence ≥ 0.50: covers 100.0% of cases, accuracy 0.909
show only predictions with confidence ≥ 0.70: covers 88.8% of cases, accuracy 0.937
show only predictions with confidence ≥ 0.80: covers 81.9% of cases, accuracy 0.950
show only predictions with confidence ≥ 0.90: covers 69.0% of cases, accuracy 0.969
show only predictions with confidence ≥ 0.95: covers 54.4% of cases, accuracy 0.977
How to read it

Answering everything gives 0.909. Answer only at 90% confidence or more and accuracy rises to 0.969, but now 31% of cases go to a person. At 0.95, accuracy is 0.977 on just over half. There's no right threshold in the abstract: it depends on what a mistake costs compared with a human review.

4.6

Slice-based evaluation

Play · Overall vs by slice

One overall score can hide a model that fails an important group: a minority of users, a region, mobile users, severe cases. Slice-based evaluation scores each subgroup separately.

It can even reverse a conclusion. In Simpson's paradox, model A wins on every slice yet loses overall, because the slices are mixed differently. Slices also reveal where to improve, and whether a model is fair. Some slices are critical: paying customers, or patients at highest risk.

Finding slicesUse domain knowledge (heuristics), look at where errors cluster (error analysis), or use tools that search for weak slices automatically.
Code lab · Python

Simpson's paradox in four rows

Step 19 compares two versions of a symptom-triage app on mild and severe cases. Version B happened to be shown mostly mild cases.

Python · step 19 · slice-based evaluation and Simpson's paradox
# Two mobile-app versions; mild cases are easier than severe ones
data = pd.DataFrame({
    "model":  ["A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "slice":  ["mild", "severe", "mild", "severe"],
    "cases":  [120, 380, 400, 100],
    "solved": [114, 266, 360, 65],
})
data["rate"] = (data.solved / data.cases).round(3)
print(data.pivot(index="model", columns="slice", values="rate"))
overall = data.groupby("model")[["solved", "cases"]].sum()
print("\noverall:", (overall.solved / overall.cases).round(3).to_dict())
print("A wins on every slice, B wins overall, because B was mostly given the easy cases.")
Output
slice  mild  severe
model              
A      0.95    0.70
B      0.90    0.65

overall: {'A': 0.76, 'B': 0.85}
A wins on every slice, B wins overall, because B was mostly given the easy cases.
How to read it

A is better on mild cases (0.95 vs 0.90) and on severe ones (0.70 vs 0.65). Yet overall B wins, 0.85 to 0.76, because 80% of B's cases were the easy mild ones, while 76% of A's were severe. Report only the overall number and you'd ship the worse model. Always check the slices that matter.

Chapter 6 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Choosing, training and evaluating a model is the most fun part for many people, but its success rests on everything before it: good framing, data and features. Pick models with strategy rather than hype, record what you try, debug methodically, and evaluate beyond a single number before anything reaches users. Next: getting the model to users, with deployment and prediction services.

Eight takeaways

In our words.

1. Start simpleA simple model tests the whole pipeline and becomes the baseline to beat.
2. Equal effortGive every candidate the same tuning budget before declaring a winner.
3. Look aheadLearning curves hint which model will win as data grows.
4. Diverse ensemblesVoting helps only when members make different mistakes.
5. Log every runTrack experiments and version code and data, so results can be reproduced.
6. Overfit a batchIf a model can't memorise ten examples, look for a bug. Fix seeds.
7. Baseline every metricRandom, zero rule, heuristic, human, existing system.
8. Test beyond accuracyPerturbation, invariance, direction, calibration, confidence and slices.

Chapter 7 · Broad summary

Model Deployment and Prediction Service

"Deploying is easy if you ignore all the hard parts." Wrapping a predict function in an API takes an hour. Serving millions of users in milliseconds, keeping models fresh and fixing them fast is the real work, and it's an engineering problem more than an ML one. This chapter clears up four deployment myths, compares batch and online prediction, shows how to make models smaller with compression, and weighs running them in the cloud or on the edge, including compilers and the browser.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Deployment myths. Companies run many models, not one or two. Models decay even if nobody touches them. So the question isn't how often you should update, but how often you can. And most ML engineers do need to care about scale.
  2. Batch vs online. Batch prediction computes answers ahead of time and looks them up; online prediction computes them when asked. Batch is a workaround for slow or costly models, but it wastes work and goes stale. Moving online needs a fast pipeline and a fast model, and training and serving pipelines that compute features the same way.
  3. Model compression. Make models smaller and often faster: low-rank factorisation, knowledge distillation, pruning, and the most widely used, quantisation.
  4. Cloud and edge. The cloud is easy to start with but costs money and adds network delay. The edge (phones, browsers, devices) works offline and keeps data local, but needs capable hardware. Compilers and intermediate representations get models running fast on many chips, and WebAssembly runs them in any browser.

Book / Chapter 7 / Section 1
Section 1 of 4 · Summary

Deployment and Its Myths

To deploy a model means getting it running and reachable outside the development environment: in staging for tests, or in production for real users. "Production" is a spectrum, from charts in a notebook for the business team to a service answering millions of requests a day; this chapter is about the second end. People who haven't deployed models tend to believe four myths, and each one leads to infrastructure that won't cope.

1.1Export and serve1.2Many models, all decaying1.3Update as often as you can1.4Scale matters
1.1

The easy part: export and serve

Play · Follow one request

The quick version: export the trained model to a file, wrap a predict function in a POST endpoint (Flask or FastAPI), package its dependencies in a container, and push it to a cloud service. An app sends inputs to that endpoint and gets predictions back. With the right tools, that's an afternoon.

Exporting, also called serialisation, saves two things: the model's definition (its structure) and its learned parameter values. TensorFlow has SavedModel; PyTorch can export to ONNX; scikit-learn models are usually saved with joblib.

The hard partsMillisecond latency for millions of users, high uptime, alerting the right person when something breaks, finding out what broke, and shipping the fix without downtime.
Code lab · Python

Train, export, load and serve a no-show model

Setup first: a generator for clinic appointments whose patterns slowly change month by month (we'll need that later). Step 1 trains a scaled logistic regression, exports it with joblib, loads it back as a prediction service would, and answers a JSON request.

Python · step 0 · setup
import time, json, os, io, tempfile, warnings, dis, ast, pickle
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import joblib
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)
FEATURES = ["missed_before", "days_ahead", "distance_km", "age", "sms_reminder"]

def make_clinic(n, month=0, seed=0):
    """Appointments at a clinic chain. As months pass, behaviour slowly changes (more online
    bookings far ahead, SMS reminders matter less, distance matters more after a relocation)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = min(month / 12, 1.0)
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "missed_before": r.poisson(0.6, n),
        "days_ahead": r.integers(0, 31, n),
        "distance_km": r.gamma(2, 3, n),
        "age": r.integers(18, 80, n),
        "sms_reminder": (r.random(n) < 0.5 + 0.3 * d).astype(int),
    })
    logit = (-2.0 + 0.8 * df.missed_before + 0.03 * df.days_ahead * (1 - d) + 0.05 * df.distance_km * (1 + 3 * d)
             - (1.0 - 0.9 * d) * df.sms_reminder + 0.5 * (df.age < 25) * (1 - 2 * d))
    df["no_show"] = (r.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    return df

train = make_clinic(6000, month=0, seed=1)
print(train.head(3).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\n{len(train):,} past appointments, no-show rate {train.no_show.mean():.1%}")
Output
 missed_before  days_ahead  distance_km  age  sms_reminder  no_show
             0          25     2.677723   64             1        0
             1          16     2.555762   70             1        0
             1          26     3.254630   50             0        1

6,000 past appointments, no-show rate 25.2%
Python · step 1 · export the model, wrap it in a predict function
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(train[FEATURES], train.no_show)

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "noshow.joblib")
joblib.dump(model, path)                                  # export = definition + learned parameters
print(f"exported to {os.path.basename(path)}: {os.path.getsize(path):,} bytes")

served = joblib.load(path)                                # what the prediction service loads at start-up

def predict(request_body: str) -> str:
    """What a POST /predict endpoint does: JSON in, JSON out."""
    rows = pd.DataFrame(json.loads(request_body)["appointments"])[FEATURES]
    return json.dumps({"no_show_probability": served.predict_proba(rows)[:, 1].round(3).tolist()})

req = json.dumps({"appointments": [
    {"missed_before": 0, "days_ahead": 2, "distance_km": 3.0, "age": 45, "sms_reminder": 1},
    {"missed_before": 3, "days_ahead": 28, "distance_km": 14.0, "age": 22, "sms_reminder": 0}]})
print("request: ", req[:72] + "...")
print("response:", predict(req))
same = np.allclose(model.predict_proba(train[FEATURES]), served.predict_proba(train[FEATURES]))
print("loaded model gives identical predictions:", same)
Output
exported to noshow.joblib: 1,870 bytes
request:  {"appointments": [{"missed_before": 0, "days_ahead": 2, "distance_km": 3...
response: {"no_show_probability": [0.059, 0.897]}
loaded model gives identical predictions: True
How to read it

The whole model fits in under 2 KB. The service takes a JSON request for two appointments and returns probabilities: 6% for a regular patient booked two days ahead with a reminder, 90% for a young patient who has missed three times, lives far away, booked four weeks ahead and got no reminder. The loaded copy predicts exactly what the original did. That's the easy part done.

1.2

Many models, and all of them decay

Play · How many models does a clinic chain need?

Myth 1: you only deploy one or two models. Real applications have many features, each with its own model. A ride-hailing app predicts demand, driver supply, arrival times, prices, fraud and churn, and may need a set per country. Uber runs thousands of models; Booking.com reported 150+.

Myth 2: if you do nothing, performance stays the same. Software rots, and ML has an extra problem: the data the model sees in production drifts away from the data it was trained on (Chapter 8). A model is usually at its best right after training.

Code lab · Python

Watch a frozen model age

Step 2 scores the same deployed model on each month's appointments for a year, while patient behaviour slowly changes: reminders matter less, and distance matters more after the clinic moves.

Python · step 2 · myth: if we do nothing, performance stays the same
months = range(0, 13)
aucs = []
for m in months:
    live = make_clinic(4000, month=m, seed=100 + m)
    aucs.append(roc_auc_score(live.no_show, model.predict_proba(live[FEATURES])[:, 1]))
for m in [0, 3, 6, 9, 12]:
    print(f"month {m:>2}: AUC {aucs[m]:.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3))
ax.plot(list(months), aucs, "o-", color="#D63E74")
ax.set(xlabel="months since deployment", ylabel="AUC on that month's appointments")
Output
month  0: AUC 0.700
month  3: AUC 0.721
month  6: AUC 0.703
month  9: AUC 0.671
month 12: AUC 0.670
How to read it

Nobody touched the model, yet its AUC falls from 0.700 to 0.670 over the year. It isn't a smooth slide: it even rises for the first few months while the changes happen to suit it, which is exactly why decay goes unnoticed without monitoring. By the end of the year it's clearly worse than it was at launch.

1.3

Update as often as you can

Play · Choose how often to retrain

A sketch of the pattern: each retrain resets the slide.

Myth 3: you won't need to update your models much. The wrong question is "how often should I update?" The right one: "how often can I?" Since models decay, sooner is better.

Software teams learned this long ago: by 2015 Etsy deployed about 50 times a day and Netflix thousands of times. Many companies still update models monthly or quarterly, while some (Weibo, for example) update certain models every 10 minutes. Chapter 9 returns to retraining frequency.

Build for itFast updates need automated data pipelines, training, evaluation and deployment. Without them, retraining stays rare because it's painful.
Code lab · Python

Never, twice a year, quarterly or monthly

Step 3 replays the year four ways. Each policy retrains on the most recent month's data at its own cadence, and every month is scored on that month's appointments.

Python · step 3 · myth: you won't need to update much
def run(every):
    """Retrain on the latest month's data every `every` months (0 = never)."""
    current, scores = model, []
    for m in range(1, 13):
        if every and (m - 1) % every == 0 and m > 1:
            recent = make_clinic(4000, month=m - 1, seed=200 + m)
            current = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(recent[FEATURES], recent.no_show)
        live = make_clinic(4000, month=m, seed=100 + m)
        scores.append(roc_auc_score(live.no_show, current.predict_proba(live[FEATURES])[:, 1]))
    return np.array(scores)

for name, every in [("never update", 0), ("every 6 months", 6), ("every 3 months", 3), ("every month", 1)]:
    s = run(every)
    print(f"{name:<15} average AUC over the year {s.mean():.3f}   worst month {s.min():.3f}")
Output
never update    average AUC over the year 0.697   worst month 0.670
every 6 months  average AUC over the year 0.720   worst month 0.694
every 3 months  average AUC over the year 0.724   worst month 0.702
every month     average AUC over the year 0.726   worst month 0.702
How to read it

Never updating averages 0.697 and ends the year at 0.670. Retraining every six months lifts the average to 0.720; quarterly 0.724; monthly 0.726. Most of the gain comes from updating at all, and each step faster still helps a little, especially for the worst month. With faster-changing data, the gaps would be larger.

1.4

Most ML engineers do need to worry about scale

Play · Push traffic towards capacity

One server that can handle about 50 requests a second (20 ms each), textbook queue.

Myth 4: scale is only for Google-sized companies. True, there are few giants, but they, and other large firms, employ much of the software workforce. Developer surveys suggest over half of engineers work at companies with at least 100 employees, which are likely to serve real traffic: hundreds of queries a second or millions of users a month.

The trap is that latency doesn't grow evenly with load. A server at half capacity feels fast; the same server at 90% has requests waiting in line, and the slowest ones, the ones users notice, get dramatically worse.

Code lab · Python

Simulate a queue of prediction requests

Step 4 simulates 40,000 requests arriving at random to servers that take about 20 ms each, and reports the median (p50) and 99th-percentile (p99) wait plus service time.

Python · step 4 · myth: scale is someone else's problem
def latency(qps, servers=1, service_ms=20, n=40_000, seed=0):
    """Requests arrive at random; each server handles one at a time (about 20 ms each)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    arrivals = np.cumsum(r.exponential(1000 / qps, n))
    service = r.exponential(service_ms, n)
    free = np.zeros(servers)
    done = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        k = free.argmin()
        start = max(arrivals[i], free[k])
        free[k] = start + service[i]
        done[i] = free[k] - arrivals[i]
    return np.percentile(done, 50), np.percentile(done, 99)

print(f"{'requests/s':>10} {'servers':>8} {'p50 ms':>8} {'p99 ms':>8}")
for qps, s in [(10, 1), (30, 1), (45, 1), (48, 1), (48, 2), (90, 2)]:
    p50, p99 = latency(qps, s)
    print(f"{qps:>10} {s:>8} {p50:>8.0f} {p99:>8.0f}")
Output
requests/s  servers   p50 ms   p99 ms
        10        1       17      117
        30        1       35      249
        45        1      144      942
        48        1      359     1974
        48        2       19      116
        90        2       78      475
How to read it

At 10 requests a second, the median is 17 ms. At 45 the median jumps to 144 ms and p99 to almost a second; at 48, p99 is about 2 seconds. Adding one more server at the same 48 requests a second brings p99 back to 116 ms. Capacity planning is part of deploying ML, and it's the tail, not the average, that hurts users first.

BACKChapter 7 overviewNEXT · SECTION 2Batch vs Online Prediction
Book / Chapter 7 / Section 2
Section 2 of 4 · Summary

Batch Prediction vs Online Prediction

Making predictions is called inference. Online (synchronous, on-demand) prediction computes the answer as soon as a request arrives, like a translation app. Batch (asynchronous) prediction computes answers periodically, stores them, and looks them up when needed, like recommendations refreshed every few hours. Batch optimises for throughput, online for latency. Many apps use both, and the trend is towards online.

2.1Three modes2.2The cost of batch2.3Hybrid serving2.4One pipeline, not two
2.1

Three modes of prediction

Play · Pick a mode

If you remember one thing, remember three modes:

Batch prediction, which uses only batch features (computed from historical data). Online prediction with batch features, such as precomputed embeddings fetched at request time. And online prediction with batch and streaming features, also called streaming prediction.

A delivery-time estimate might combine a restaurant's average prep time (batch) with how many orders and riders are around in the last 10 minutes (streaming). Note that "online features" means any feature used online, including batch features kept in memory; "streaming features" come only from streaming data.

Code lab · Python

Precompute and look up, or compute on request

Step 5 runs a "nightly job" that scores 200,000 patients at once and stores the results in a dictionary. Then it serves 300 requests twice: by lookup, and by calling the model for each request.

Python · step 5 · batch prediction vs online prediction
patients = make_clinic(200_000, month=0, seed=7)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
table = dict(zip(range(len(patients)), model.predict_proba(patients[FEATURES])[:, 1]))   # nightly batch job
batch_s = time.perf_counter() - t0

ids = np.random.default_rng(1).integers(0, len(patients), 300)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for i in ids:
    _ = table[i]                                          # batch: just look the answer up
lookup_us = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(ids) * 1e6
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for i in ids:
    _ = model.predict_proba(patients.iloc[[i]][FEATURES])[0, 1]   # online: compute it now
online_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(ids) * 1e3
print(f"batch job: {len(patients):,} predictions in {batch_s:.2f} s  ({batch_s / len(patients) * 1e6:.1f} µs each)")
print(f"serving from the batch table: {lookup_us:.2f} µs per request")
print(f"online, one request at a time: {online_ms:.2f} ms per request")
Output
batch job: 200,000 predictions in 0.03 s  (0.1 µs each)
serving from the batch table: 1.37 µs per request
online, one request at a time: 0.70 ms per request
How to read it

The batch job is extremely efficient per prediction because it's vectorised. Serving from the table takes a few microseconds at most; calling the model one request at a time takes around a millisecond, hundreds of times slower (the exact ratio varies from run to run). That's batch prediction's appeal: it hides a model's latency. (Our model is tiny; with a large one, the online cost would be far higher.)

2.2

What batch prediction costs you

Play · How often does the batch job run?

Wasted work. If only 2% of users open the app each day, a daily batch for everyone throws away 98% of its predictions. Online prediction only computes for people who show up.

Staleness. Batch results can't react to what a user just did. Binge horror films, then search for comedy today, and your recommendations stay horror until the next batch run.

Unknown requests. You can precompute for known users, but not for every sentence someone might type into a translator.

When online is a mustFraud detection, voice assistants, face unlock, fall detection for the elderly: a late answer is a wrong answer.
Code lab · Python

Count the waste and the staleness

Step 6 counts how many of a million daily predictions are ever shown, then simulates 100,000 changes of taste at random times and measures how long recommendations stay stale under three batch schedules.

Python · step 6 · what batch prediction costs you
users, active_share = 1_000_000, 0.02
print(f"daily batch for every user: {users:,} predictions, {users * active_share:,.0f} ever shown "
      f"-> {1 - active_share:.0%} of the compute wasted")

# Staleness: a user's taste changes at a random moment; how long until the recommendations catch up?
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
change = r.uniform(0, 24, 100_000)                        # hour of the day the change happens
for every in [24, 4, 1]:
    wait = np.ceil(change / every) * every - change       # hours until the next batch run
    print(f"batch every {every:>2} h: recommendations stale for {wait.mean():4.1f} h on average after a change")
print("online prediction: stale for 0 h, if the features update in real time")
Output
daily batch for every user: 1,000,000 predictions, 20,000 ever shown -> 98% of the compute wasted
batch every 24 h: recommendations stale for 12.0 h on average after a change
batch every  4 h: recommendations stale for  2.0 h on average after a change
batch every  1 h: recommendations stale for  0.5 h on average after a change
online prediction: stale for 0 h, if the features update in real time
How to read it

980,000 of the million predictions are never used. Staleness is half the batch interval on average: 12 hours for a daily job, 2 for every 4 hours, 30 minutes for hourly. You can shrink it by running batches more often, but you pay for every run. Online prediction removes it, if features update in real time.

2.3

Hybrid: precompute the popular, compute the rest

Play · How many queries to precompute?

Batch and online aren't either/or. A food-delivery app can precompute restaurant recommendations in batch (too many restaurants to rank on the fly), then compute dish recommendations online once you open a restaurant.

Another hybrid: precompute answers for popular queries and compute rare ones online. Because query popularity is usually very uneven, a small cache covers much of the traffic.

Batch is a workaroundfor models that aren't fast or cheap enough online. As hardware and techniques improve, online prediction may become the default.
Code lab · Python

Cache coverage for uneven traffic

Step 7 draws a million search requests from a long-tailed (Zipf) distribution and measures how much traffic the top 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 queries cover.

Python · step 7 · precompute the popular queries, compute the rest online
r = np.random.default_rng(5)
queries = r.zipf(1.3, 1_000_000)                          # a few queries are very common, most are rare
counts = pd.Series(queries).value_counts()
print(f"{len(counts):,} distinct queries in 1,000,000 requests")
for k in [10, 100, 1_000, 10_000]:
    print(f"precompute the top {k:>6,}: covers {counts.iloc[:k].sum() / len(queries):.1%} of traffic")
Output
57,036 distinct queries in 1,000,000 requests
precompute the top     10: covers 58.1% of traffic
precompute the top    100: covers 78.8% of traffic
precompute the top  1,000: covers 89.4% of traffic
precompute the top 10,000: covers 95.0% of traffic
How to read it

There are 57,036 distinct queries, yet the top 10 cover 58% of all requests and the top 1,000 cover 89%. Precompute those, and online prediction only has to handle the remaining one request in ten. The long tail never ends, though: even 10,000 cached queries leave 5% to compute live.

2.4

Unify the batch and streaming pipelines

Play · One feature, two implementations

To go online you need two things: a near-real-time pipeline that computes streaming features and returns predictions, and a model fast enough for your users (often milliseconds).

Many companies built ML on batch systems like MapReduce and Spark, then added a separate streaming pipeline for serving. Now each feature is computed twice: in batch for training (say, average speed on a route over a month of data) and on a sliding window at serving time. When the two drift apart, often because different teams maintain them, the model sees different features in production than in training.

The fixOne definition of each feature, used by both: a stream processor such as Apache Flink for both, or a feature store (Chapter 10).
Code lab · Python

A one-line difference between pipelines

Step 8 trains on "missed appointments in the last year", computed in pandas. The serving team re-implements it and forgets the one-year window. Both versions are scored against the true outcomes.

Python · step 8 · two pipelines, two different features
r = np.random.default_rng(11)
n_pat = 6000
hist = pd.DataFrame({"patient": np.repeat(np.arange(n_pat), 12),
                     "days_ago": r.integers(1, 1500, n_pat * 12)})
hist["missed"] = r.random(len(hist)) < np.repeat(r.beta(1, 6, n_pat), 12)

def misses_last_year(h):          # training pipeline (written by the ML team, in pandas)
    return h[h.days_ago <= 365].groupby("patient").missed.sum().reindex(range(n_pat), fill_value=0)

def misses_serving(h):            # serving pipeline (rewritten by another team: forgot the window)
    return h.groupby("patient").missed.sum().reindex(range(n_pat), fill_value=0)

recent = misses_last_year(hist)
label = (r.random(n_pat) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-2.3 + 0.9 * recent)))).astype(int)
skew_model = LogisticRegression().fit(recent.to_frame("misses"), label)

for name, feat in [("same function as training", misses_last_year(hist)), ("separate serving pipeline", misses_serving(hist))]:
    p = skew_model.predict_proba(feat.to_frame("misses"))[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:<27} feature differs for {(feat != recent).mean():5.1%} of patients | "
          f"predicted no-show rate {p.mean():.1%} (actual {label.mean():.1%}) | AUC {roc_auc_score(label, p):.3f}")
Output
same function as training   feature differs for  0.0% of patients | predicted no-show rate 15.3% (actual 15.2%) | AUC 0.680
separate serving pipeline   feature differs for 59.7% of patients | predicted no-show rate 36.0% (actual 15.2%) | AUC 0.630
How to read it

With the same function, predictions match reality: 15.3% predicted vs 15.2% actual no-shows. With the re-implemented feature, 60% of patients get a different value, the model predicts 36% no-shows, more than double, and AUC drops from 0.680 to 0.630. No error is raised anywhere: the code runs and the predictions look plausible. A clinic overbooking on these numbers would pack its waiting room.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1Deployment MythsNEXT · SECTION 3Model Compression
Book / Chapter 7 / Section 3
Section 3 of 4 · Summary

Model Compression

A model too slow to serve can be made faster in three ways: optimise how it runs (inference optimisation, Section 4), run it on faster hardware, or make it smaller. Making it smaller is model compression. It started as a way to fit models on devices, but smaller models are often faster too. Four families come up most: low-rank factorisation, knowledge distillation, pruning and quantisation.

3.1Low-rank factorisation3.2Knowledge distillation3.3Pruning3.4Quantisation
3.1

Low-rank factorisation

Play · Replace one big matrix with two thin ones

The idea: replace large, high-dimensional weight tensors with smaller ones that do nearly the same job. A 64×256 layer can be approximated by a 64×k matrix times a k×256 one; with small k, that's far fewer weights.

For images, compact convolutional filters do this by design. SqueezeNet reached AlexNet-level accuracy with about 50 times fewer parameters. MobileNets split a K×K×C filter into a K×K×1 depthwise and a 1×1×C pointwise filter, using K²+C weights instead of K²C.

LimitsThese designs are specific to certain architectures and need deep know-how to create, so they aren't a general-purpose tool yet.
Code lab · Python

Factorise a trained layer with SVD

Step 9 trains a network whose first layer is 64×256, then swaps that layer for its best rank-k approximation (from a singular value decomposition) without any retraining. It ends with the MobileNet-style arithmetic.

Python · step 9 · low-rank factorisation
Xb, yb = make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=64, n_informative=24, n_redundant=10, random_state=4)
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
net = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(256,), max_iter=200, early_stopping=True, random_state=0).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
W = net.coefs_[0].copy()                                  # first layer: 64 x 256 weights
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(W, full_matrices=False)
print(f"full first layer: {W.size:,} weights, test accuracy {net.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
for k in [32, 16, 8, 4]:
    net.coefs_[0] = (U[:, :k] * S[:k]) @ Vt[:k]           # replace W with two thin matrices: 64xk and kx256
    print(f"rank {k:>2}: {k * (64 + 256):>6,} weights ({k * (64 + 256) / W.size:4.0%}), test accuracy {net.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
net.coefs_[0] = W

K, C = 3, 256
print(f"\nseparable 3x3 filter with {C} channels: {K * K * C} -> {K * K + C} weights ({K * K * C / (K * K + C):.1f}x fewer)")
Output
full first layer: 16,384 weights, test accuracy 0.963
rank 32: 10,240 weights ( 62%), test accuracy 0.922
rank 16:  5,120 weights ( 31%), test accuracy 0.872
rank  8:  2,560 weights ( 16%), test accuracy 0.795
rank  4:  1,280 weights (  8%), test accuracy 0.764

separable 3x3 filter with 256 channels: 2304 -> 265 weights (8.7x fewer)
How to read it

Rank 32 keeps 62% of the weights and loses 4 points of accuracy (0.963 to 0.922); rank 8 keeps 16% and falls to 0.795. Squeezing an already-trained layer hurts, which is why low-rank designs usually go in before training, so the network learns to work within them. The separable-filter arithmetic shows the payoff when you do: 2,304 weights become 265, 8.7 times fewer.

3.2

Knowledge distillation

Play · Teacher and students

A small student model is trained to mimic a large teacher model or ensemble, and only the student is deployed. Usually the teacher is trained first, though both can learn together. DistilBERT, a well-known example, is 40% smaller than BERT, about 60% faster, and keeps about 97% of its language understanding.

It works across architectures: a transformer can teach a random forest. The catch is that you need a teacher. If you have to train one first, that takes extra data and time, and results depend on the application, so it's less common in production.

Why it helpsThe teacher's soft probabilities carry more information than hard labels, and the teacher can label extra unlabelled data for the student to learn from.
Code lab · Python

Distil a 300-tree forest into one tree

Step 10 has 2,000 labelled rows and 18,000 unlabelled ones. A 300-tree random forest is the teacher. One depth-8 tree learns from the labels alone; another learns to copy the teacher's probabilities on all 20,000 rows.

Python · step 10 · knowledge distillation
Xd, yd = make_classification(n_samples=26_000, n_features=20, n_informative=10, flip_y=0.03, random_state=8)
X_lab, y_lab = Xd[:2000], yd[:2000]                       # the labelled data we have
X_unlab = Xd[2000:20_000]                                 # plenty of unlabelled data
X_test, y_test = Xd[20_000:], yd[20_000:]

teacher = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_lab, y_lab)
student_plain = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=8, random_state=0).fit(X_lab, y_lab)
soft = teacher.predict_proba(np.vstack([X_lab, X_unlab]))[:, 1]          # the teacher's soft answers
student_distilled = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=8, random_state=0).fit(np.vstack([X_lab, X_unlab]), soft)

size = lambda m: len(pickle.dumps(m))
print(f"teacher (300 trees):            accuracy {teacher.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}   size {size(teacher) / 1e6:5.1f} MB")
print(f"student trained on labels:      accuracy {student_plain.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}   size {size(student_plain) / 1e6:5.2f} MB")
acc = accuracy_score(y_test, student_distilled.predict(X_test) > 0.5)
print(f"student trained on the teacher: accuracy {acc:.3f}   size {size(student_distilled) / 1e6:5.2f} MB")
Output
teacher (300 trees):            accuracy 0.900   size  10.5 MB
student trained on labels:      accuracy 0.814   size  0.02 MB
student trained on the teacher: accuracy 0.859   size  0.04 MB
How to read it

The teacher is accurate (0.900) but weighs 10.5 MB. A single tree trained on the labels gets 0.814. The same-sized tree trained on the teacher's answers reaches 0.859, recovering more than half the gap, at well under 1% of the teacher's size. It doesn't match the teacher, and that's the usual trade.

3.3

Pruning

Play · Remove the smallest weights

Pruning began with decision trees: cut branches that don't help. Neural networks are over-parameterised too, so pruning means either removing whole nodes (changing the architecture) or, more commonly, setting the least useful weights to zero.

Zeroed weights don't reduce the parameter count, but sparse models need less storage and can run faster. Experiments have cut over 90% of non-zero weights without hurting accuracy. Researchers still debate why: some argue the value lies in the pruned architecture, which should be retrained from scratch; others found the pruned sparse model does better. Chapter 11 discusses how pruning can introduce bias.

Code lab · Python

Magnitude pruning, with and without retraining

Step 11 trains a 128×128 network, zeroes its smallest weights at several levels, and scores each. Then it prunes 90% and retrains the remaining weights for 15 epochs, keeping the pruned ones at zero.

Python · step 11 · pruning
big = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(128, 128), max_iter=60, random_state=0).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
orig = [w.copy() for w in big.coefs_]
total = sum(w.size for w in orig)
for share in [0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99]:
    cut = np.quantile(np.abs(np.concatenate([w.ravel() for w in orig])), share)   # global magnitude threshold
    big.coefs_ = [np.where(np.abs(w) < cut, 0, w) for w in orig]
    nonzero = sum((w != 0).sum() for w in big.coefs_)
    print(f"prune {share:4.0%} of weights: {nonzero:>6,} of {total:,} left, test accuracy {big.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")

# Prune 90%, then briefly retrain the weights that are left (the pruned ones stay at zero)
cut = np.quantile(np.abs(np.concatenate([w.ravel() for w in orig])), 0.9)
masks = [np.abs(w) >= cut for w in orig]
big.coefs_ = [w * m for w, m in zip(orig, masks)]
for epoch in range(15):
    big.partial_fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
    big.coefs_ = [w * m for w, m in zip(big.coefs_, masks)]
print(f"prune 90% then retrain 15 epochs: test accuracy {big.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
big.coefs_ = orig
Output
prune   0% of weights: 24,704 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.969
prune  50% of weights: 12,352 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.949
prune  80% of weights:  4,941 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.864
prune  90% of weights:  2,471 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.795
prune  95% of weights:  1,236 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.688
prune  99% of weights:    248 of 24,704 left, test accuracy 0.461
prune 90% then retrain 15 epochs: test accuracy 0.944
How to read it

Pruning half the weights costs 2 points. Cutting 90% in one go drops accuracy to 0.795. But give the surviving 10% a little retraining and it climbs back to 0.944, within 2.5 points of the full network, with a tenth of the weights. That's how the big published pruning ratios are reached: prune, then fine-tune.

3.4

Quantisation

Play · Store one weight with fewer bits

The most general and widely used method: store each parameter with fewer bits. 100 million parameters at 32 bits take 400 MB; at 16 bits (half precision), 200 MB; as 8-bit integers (fixed point), 100 MB. Some research even uses 1 bit per weight. Fewer bits also mean faster arithmetic and bigger batches.

The cost: fewer bits cover a smaller range of values, so numbers get rounded, can overflow, or underflow to zero, and small rounding errors can sometimes change results a lot. Quantisation can happen during training or after it. Post-training 8-bit inference is now standard, built into TensorFlow Lite, PyTorch Mobile and TensorRT.

A case studyRoblox served over a billion BERT requests a day on CPUs. Switching to DistilBERT and dynamic input shapes helped, but quantising to 8-bit integers gave the biggest win: about 7 times lower latency and 8 times higher throughput (they didn't report the effect on quality).
Code lab · Python

float32 → float16 → int8

Step 12 takes the 128×128 network from step 11, converts its weights to half precision and to 8-bit integers (one scale per layer), converts them back, and scores each. It ends with two range limits of float16.

Python · step 12 · quantisation
def int8(w):
    scale = np.abs(w).max() / 127                         # map the largest weight to ±127
    return np.round(w / scale).astype(np.int8), scale

for name, conv in [("float32 (default)", lambda w: w.astype(np.float32)),
                   ("float16 (half)", lambda w: w.astype(np.float16)),
                   ("int8 (fixed point)", lambda w: (lambda q, s: q.astype(np.float32) * s)(*int8(w)))]:
    big.coefs_ = [conv(w).astype(np.float64) for w in orig]
    nbytes = sum(w.size for w in orig) * {"float32": 4, "float16": 2, "int8 (f": 1}[name[:7]]
    err = max(np.abs(conv(w) - w).max() for w in orig)
    print(f"{name:<19} {nbytes / 1024:6.1f} KB   biggest rounding error {err:.1e}   test accuracy {big.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
big.coefs_ = orig
print("\nrange limits: float16(70000) =", np.float16(70000), "  float16(1e-8) =", np.float16(1e-8))
Output
float32 (default)     96.5 KB   biggest rounding error 2.0e-08   test accuracy 0.968
float16 (half)        48.2 KB   biggest rounding error 1.2e-04   test accuracy 0.968
int8 (fixed point)    24.1 KB   biggest rounding error 1.9e-03   test accuracy 0.967

range limits: float16(70000) = inf   float16(1e-8) = 0.0
How to read it

Half precision halves the size with no change in accuracy. Eight-bit integers make the weights four times smaller than float32 (96.5 KB down to 24.1 KB), with rounding errors of about 0.002 and accuracy within a tenth of a point. The last line is the warning: float16 can't hold 70,000 (it becomes infinity) or 0.00000001 (it becomes 0), which is why activations and scaling need care.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2Batch vs Online PredictionNEXT · SECTION 4ML on the Cloud and on the Edge
Book / Chapter 7 / Section 4
Section 4 of 4 · Summary

ML on the Cloud and on the Edge

Where should the computation happen? On the cloud, on public or private servers, or on the edge: browsers, phones, laptops, watches, cars, cameras and embedded chips. The cloud is the easy start; the edge saves money, works offline, cuts network delay and keeps data local. Running models well on so many kinds of hardware is where compilers, intermediate representations and optimisation come in, and the browser offers a shortcut to every device.

4.1Cloud vs edge4.2Compilers and IRs4.3Model optimisation4.4ML that optimises ML4.5ML in the browser
4.1

Cloud vs edge

Play · A patient app, two places to run the model

Illustrative numbers in the spirit of the lab.

Cloud. Package the model and use a managed service: the easiest start. But compute is expensive (big firms spend hundreds of millions of dollars a year on cloud bills, and one mistake can sink a startup), every request needs a network round trip, and user data travels and is stored centrally, which raises breach and regulatory risks.

Edge. Works without internet (rural areas, places with no-internet policies), skips network latency, and keeps sensitive data on the device, though a stolen device is its own risk. In return, the device needs enough compute, memory and battery: a full-size model can drain a phone fast.

Network often dominatesShaving inference from 30 ms to 20 ms means little if the network takes seconds.
Code lab · Python

Latency budget: fast server far away vs slow chip in your hand

Step 13 simulates 100,000 requests. Cloud: 12 ms of inference plus a patchy mobile round trip, and 4% of requests with no signal at all. Edge: 45 ms on a slower phone chip, no network.

Python · step 13 · cloud or edge: where does the time go?
r = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 100_000
network = r.lognormal(np.log(90), 0.7, n)                 # round trip on a patchy mobile connection
offline = r.random(n) < 0.04                              # no signal at all
cloud = np.where(offline, np.inf, network + 12)           # fast server: 12 ms of inference
edge = r.normal(45, 6, n)                                 # slower phone chip, but no network
for name, t in [("cloud (server + network)", cloud), ("edge (on the phone)", edge)]:
    ok = np.isfinite(t)
    print(f"{name:<25} median {np.median(t[ok]):5.0f} ms   p95 {np.percentile(t[ok], 95):5.0f} ms   failed {1 - ok.mean():.1%}")
Output
cloud (server + network)  median   102 ms   p95   296 ms   failed 4.0%
edge (on the phone)       median    45 ms   p95    55 ms   failed 0.0%
How to read it

The cloud server is almost four times faster at inference, yet the median cloud request takes 102 ms against 45 ms on the phone, and the slowest 5% take about 300 ms against 55. And 4% of cloud requests fail outright. For an app used in clinics with weak signal, the edge wins, provided the model fits the phone (Section 3).

4.2

Compilers and intermediate representations

Play · Lower a model, step by step

A framework only runs on hardware its vendor supports. PyTorch, for example, only gained TPU support about two and a half years after TPUs became publicly available. Every chip has its own compute primitives (CPUs historically worked on scalars, GPUs on vectors, TPUs on 2D tensors) and memory layouts, so supporting every framework on every chip by hand doesn't scale.

The answer is a middleman: an intermediate representation (IR). Frameworks translate to the IR; hardware vendors support the IR. Compilers lower code through a series of high- and low-level IRs to machine code. The high-level IR is usually the model's computation graph.

Lowering, not translatingThere's no one-to-one mapping between levels; each step makes choices.
Code lab · Python

See Python lower its own code

Step 14 takes a one-line scoring function and shows it at three levels: the source, a syntax tree (a high-level IR), and bytecode for Python's virtual machine (a lower-level IR). ML compilers do the same, with computation graphs and hardware instructions.

Python · step 14 · lowering: from code to IR to instructions
src = "def score(x):\n    return 1 / (1 + exp(-(w * x + b)))"
print("source:\n" + src)
tree = ast.parse(src).body[0].body[0].value
print("\nhigh-level IR (a syntax tree):\n" + ast.dump(tree)[:150] + " ...")
namespace = {"exp": np.exp, "w": 0.8, "b": -2.0}
exec(src, namespace)
print("\nlow-level IR (bytecode for Python's virtual machine):")
for ins in list(dis.get_instructions(namespace["score"]))[:9]:
    print(f"  {ins.opname:<14} {ins.argrepr}")
print("  ...")
Output
source:
def score(x):
    return 1 / (1 + exp(-(w * x + b)))

high-level IR (a syntax tree):
BinOp(left=Constant(value=1), op=Div(), right=BinOp(left=Constant(value=1), op=Add(), right=Call(func=Name(id='exp', ctx=Load()), args=[UnaryOp(op=USu ...

low-level IR (bytecode for Python's virtual machine):
  RESUME         
  LOAD_CONST     1
  LOAD_CONST     1
  LOAD_GLOBAL    NULL + exp
  LOAD_GLOBAL    w
  LOAD_FAST      x
  BINARY_OP      *
  LOAD_GLOBAL    b
  BINARY_OP      +
  ...
How to read it

The source is one line a person can read. The syntax tree breaks it into nested operations (divide, add, call exp, multiply). The bytecode is a flat list of simple steps: load a constant, load w, load x, multiply, load b, add. Each level is closer to what the machine executes, and each is a place where optimisations can be made.

4.3

Model optimisation

Play · Four local optimisations

Code that runs on a chip may still run slowly: it might ignore caches, or skip vector and parallel instructions. And ML workflows hop between pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and others with little optimisation across them; one study found typical NumPy/pandas/TensorFlow workloads ran 23 times slower than hand-optimised code.

Optimisation can be local (an operator or a few) or global (the whole graph). Four common local techniques: vectorisation, parallelisation, loop tiling (reorder loops to suit the memory layout) and operator fusion (do several operations in one pass). Bigger wins come from fusing larger parts of the graph, vertically or horizontally.

Who does this?Optimisation engineers with both ML and hardware skills: rare and expensive. Optimising compilers try to automate them.
Code lab · Python

Vectorise, fuse, and respect memory order

Step 15 computes a sigmoid score for a million values three ways: a Python loop, vectorised NumPy, and vectorised with one reused buffer instead of temporary arrays. Then it sums a 3,000×3,000 matrix by rows and by columns.

Python · step 15 · vectorisation, fusion and memory order
x = np.random.default_rng(0).random(1_000_000)
w, b = 0.8, -2.0

def timed(f, reps=3):
    best = min((lambda t0: (f(), time.perf_counter() - t0)[1])(time.perf_counter()) for _ in range(reps))
    return best * 1000

loop_ms = timed(lambda: [1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * v + b))) for v in x[:100_000]]) * 10
vec_ms = timed(lambda: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(w * x + b))))
buf = np.empty_like(x)
def fused():                                              # reuse one buffer instead of five temporary arrays
    np.multiply(x, -w, out=buf); np.subtract(buf, b, out=buf); np.exp(buf, out=buf); np.add(buf, 1, out=buf); np.reciprocal(buf, out=buf)
fused_ms = timed(fused)
print(f"python loop, one value at a time: {loop_ms:7.1f} ms")
print(f"vectorised numpy:                 {vec_ms:7.1f} ms   ({loop_ms / vec_ms:.0f}x faster)")
print(f"vectorised, one reused buffer:    {fused_ms:7.1f} ms")

M = np.random.default_rng(1).random((3000, 3000))         # stored row by row in memory
rows_ms = timed(lambda: [M[i, :].sum() for i in range(3000)])
cols_ms = timed(lambda: [M[:, j].sum() for j in range(3000)])
print(f"\nsum each row (memory in order):   {rows_ms:7.1f} ms")
print(f"sum each column (jumping around): {cols_ms:7.1f} ms   ({cols_ms / rows_ms:.1f}x slower, same arithmetic)")
Output
python loop, one value at a time:   604.7 ms
vectorised numpy:                    11.4 ms   (53x faster)
vectorised, one reused buffer:        3.0 ms

sum each row (memory in order):       3.8 ms
sum each column (jumping around):    13.8 ms   (3.6x slower, same arithmetic)
How to read it

Vectorisation is the big win: the same maths runs around a hundred times faster than the Python loop (the exact ratio varies from run to run). Reusing one buffer, a simple form of fusion, saves extra time by avoiding temporary arrays. And summing columns does exactly the same arithmetic as summing rows but takes several times longer, only because it jumps around memory: that's what loop tiling is about.

4.4

Using ML to optimise ML

Play · Search for the fastest way to run a graph

There are many ways to run one computation graph (fuse A with B, or B with C, or all three...). Hand-written heuristics are rarely optimal and must be redone for each new framework, chip or architecture. Trying every option is impossible.

So use ML: measure some options, learn a cost model that predicts how long others would take, and search where it's promising. cuDNN's autotune does this for convolutions; autoTVM does it for whole subgraphs, which it splits, searches separately, then stitches together.

Slow, but onceThe search can take hours or days, but the result is cached and reused on every device of that hardware type.
Code lab · Python

Autotune a batch size by measuring

Step 16 scores 40,000 appointments in chunks of different sizes, times each option, and picks the fastest: the core loop of every autotuner, without the learned cost model.

Python · step 16 · measure, don't guess: autotuning a batch size
rows = make_clinic(40_000, month=0, seed=9)[FEATURES].to_numpy()
scaler, lr = model.named_steps["standardscaler"], model.named_steps["logisticregression"]
def score_in_chunks(size):
    return np.concatenate([lr.predict_proba(scaler.transform(rows[i:i + size]))[:, 1] for i in range(0, len(rows), size)])

results = {size: timed(lambda: score_in_chunks(size), reps=5) for size in [16, 128, 1024, 8192, 40_000]}
for size, ms in results.items():
    print(f"chunk size {size:>6,}: {ms:7.1f} ms for 40,000 predictions")
print("autotuner picks:", min(results, key=results.get))
Output
chunk size     16:   105.8 ms for 40,000 predictions
chunk size    128:    13.6 ms for 40,000 predictions
chunk size  1,024:     2.2 ms for 40,000 predictions
chunk size  8,192:     0.8 ms for 40,000 predictions
chunk size 40,000:     0.5 ms for 40,000 predictions
autotuner picks: 40000
How to read it

Tiny chunks are far slower, because per-call overhead dominates. Larger chunks get much faster, but the gains flatten out, and neighbouring sizes can swap places from one run to the next as caches and memory behave differently. The autotuner doesn't need to know why; it measures and picks the fastest. Real autotuners add a learned cost model so they can skip measuring options that look hopeless.

4.5

ML in the browser

Play · This model is running in your browser

If a model runs in the browser, it runs on any device with one: laptops, phones, Chromebooks, whatever chip is inside. JavaScript tools (TensorFlow.js and others) exist, but JavaScript is slow and awkward for complex logic like feature extraction.

WebAssembly (WASM) is more promising: compile your model to an executable that runs in the browser. It's supported on over 90% of devices and much faster than JavaScript, though still slower than native apps (one study measured 45–55% slower).

The widget on the leftis the no-show model from 1.1, exported as a few numbers by the lab below. No server is involved: your browser computes every prediction.
Code lab · Python

Export a model the browser can run

Step 17 writes the scaler's means and scales and the model's coefficients to JSON, then re-implements prediction with plain arithmetic, exactly as the page's JavaScript does, and checks it against scikit-learn.

Python · step 17 · export a model the browser can run
scaler, lr = model.named_steps["standardscaler"], model.named_steps["logisticregression"]
web = {"features": FEATURES, "mean": scaler.mean_.round(4).tolist(), "scale": scaler.scale_.round(4).tolist(),
       "coef": lr.coef_[0].round(4).tolist(), "intercept": round(float(lr.intercept_[0]), 4)}
print(json.dumps(web))

def predict_like_js(row):                                 # the same arithmetic the page's JavaScript does
    z = web["intercept"] + sum(c * (v - m) / s for c, v, m, s in zip(web["coef"], row, web["mean"], web["scale"]))
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

sample = train[FEATURES].iloc[:500].to_numpy()
gap = np.abs(np.array([predict_like_js(r) for r in sample]) - model.predict_proba(train[FEATURES].iloc[:500])[:, 1]).max()
print(f"\n{len(json.dumps(web))} bytes of JSON; largest difference from scikit-learn over 500 rows: {gap:.4f}")
Output
{"features": ["missed_before", "days_ahead", "distance_km", "age", "sms_reminder"], "mean": [0.6105, 14.8355, 5.9653, 48.717, 0.505], "scale": [0.8032, 8.9578, 4.2274, 17.8556, 0.5], "coef": [0.6672, 0.2495, 0.2398, -0.0733, -0.5031], "intercept": -1.2579}

256 bytes of JSON; largest difference from scikit-learn over 500 rows: 0.0000
How to read it

The whole model is about 250 bytes of JSON: small enough to embed in a page. Using those numbers, the hand-written formula matches scikit-learn on 500 appointments to four decimal places. This works neatly for linear models; larger models need a real runtime such as TensorFlow.js or a WASM build, but the idea is the same: ship the model to the user instead of the user's data to the model.
