Book / Chapter 7 / Recap
Chapter 7 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Deployment is an engineering challenge more than an ML one. Online prediction keeps models responsive but needs low latency; batch prediction hides latency but goes stale. The cloud is easy but costs money and adds network delay; the edge needs capable devices. Many of these limits come from hardware, and as it improves, the book expects more prediction to move online and onto devices. A deployed model isn't the end of a project: next comes keeping it working, with monitoring for data distribution shifts.

Eight takeaways

In our words.

1. Export is the easy partServing fast, reliably and observably is the real work.
2. Expect many modelsBuild infrastructure for dozens or hundreds, not one.
3. Models decayAsk how often you can update, then make it faster.
4. Plan for the tailLatency explodes near capacity; watch p99, not the average.
5. Batch is a workaroundIt wastes work and goes stale; hybrids cover popular requests.
6. One feature definitionTraining and serving must compute features the same way.
7. Compress, then fine-tuneQuantise first; prune and distil when you need more.
8. Mind the networkThe edge avoids round trips, outages and data transfer.

Quick quiz

Book / Chapter 8
Chapter 8 · Broad summary

Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring

A grocery chain paid consultants for a demand-forecasting model, deployed it happily, and a year later found it over-ordering some items and under-ordering others until it was useless. Deployment isn't the end: models degrade in production. This chapter covers why ML systems fail (including edge cases and feedback loops), the kinds of data distribution shift, how to detect and address them, and how to monitor and observe a system so you notice problems before your users do.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Why systems fail. Many failures are ordinary software problems. ML-specific ones are rarer but harder to see: models fail silently. Production data differs from training data, rare edge cases can be catastrophic, and degenerate feedback loops let a model's own predictions shape its future training data.
  2. Kinds of shift. Covariate shift (inputs change), label shift (outcome rates change), concept drift (the same input now means a different outcome), plus feature changes and label schema changes.
  3. Detect and address. Compare distributions with statistics and two-sample tests, choose time windows carefully, and remember that significant isn't always important. Most companies address shifts by retraining on recent data, and design features and models to be robust.
  4. Monitoring. Track operational metrics and ML metrics: accuracy when labels arrive, predictions, features, raw inputs. Use logs, dashboards and alerts without causing alert fatigue, and make the system observable so you can find out why.

Sections

Each section has its own summary, sub-sections and code labs.

  • Silent failures
  • Edge cases and outliers
  • Feedback loops
Section 2

  • Covariate · label shift
  • Concept drift
  • Feature and schema changes
Section 3

Detecting and Addressing Shifts

Tests, windows and retraining.

  • Statistics vs two-sample tests
  • Time-scale windows
  • What to retrain on
Section 4

Monitoring and Observability

Know when, and why.

  • Operational metrics · SLAs
  • Predictions · features
  • Alerts · logs · observability

Book / Chapter 8 / Section 1
Section 1 of 4 · Summary

Why ML Systems Fail

A failure is when the system breaks an expectation. Ordinary software has operational expectations (answer within a second); ML adds performance expectations (be right 99% of the time). Operational failures announce themselves with timeouts and errors. Performance failures don't: the system keeps answering, wrongly. Google engineers reviewing 96 failures of one large ML pipeline found 60 were not ML problems at all, but the ML-specific ones are the hardest to spot.

1.1Silent failures1.2Edge cases and outliers1.3Degenerate feedback loops1.4Breaking the loop
1.1

Software failures and silent ML failures

Play · Which failures make a noise?
Pick a failure.

Software failures would hit any system: a dependency breaks, an old model binary gets deployed, a CPU overheats, a hosted server goes down. Fixing them takes engineering skill more than ML skill, which is why ML engineering is "mostly engineering".

ML-specific failures include bad data, poor hyperparameters, training and serving pipelines that disagree, shifting data, edge cases and feedback loops. They're a smaller share today, likely to grow as tooling matures, and much harder to see.

Not stationaryThe usual assumption that future data looks like training data is almost always false: training sets are finite and biased, and the world keeps changing, suddenly, gradually or seasonally.
Code lab · Python

A failure that returns HTTP 200

Setup first: a clinic no-show model trained on age, past misses and distance. Step 1 serves a normal day, then the same day after an upstream app update starts sending age in months.

Python · step 0 · setup
import re, json, warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp, spearmanr
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression, SGDClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, accuracy_score, mean_absolute_error, log_loss

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)

def clinic(n, seed):
    """Appointments: no-shows are likelier for young patients, past no-shows and long trips."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    df = pd.DataFrame({"age": r.integers(18, 80, n), "missed_before": r.poisson(0.6, n),
                       "distance_km": r.gamma(2, 3, n)})
    logit = -1.2 + 0.8 * df.missed_before + 0.06 * df.distance_km - 0.045 * (df.age - 18)
    df["no_show"] = (r.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    return df

F = ["age", "missed_before", "distance_km"]
train = clinic(8000, seed=1)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(train[F], train.no_show)
print(f"trained on {len(train):,} appointments; no-show rate {train.no_show.mean():.1%}")
Output
trained on 8,000 appointments; no-show rate 18.3%
Python · step 1 · ML systems fail silently
today = clinic(3000, seed=2)
broken = today.copy()
broken["age"] = broken.age * 12            # an upstream app update now sends age in months

for name, batch in [("normal day", today), ("after the upstream change", broken)]:
    p = model.predict_proba(batch[F])[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:<26} requests answered 3000/3000 (HTTP 200) | mean predicted no-show {p.mean():6.1%} "
          f"| actual {batch.no_show.mean():.1%} | AUC {roc_auc_score(batch.no_show, p):.3f}")
Output
normal day                 requests answered 3000/3000 (HTTP 200) | mean predicted no-show  18.3% | actual 19.2% | AUC 0.770
after the upstream change  requests answered 3000/3000 (HTTP 200) | mean predicted no-show   0.0% | actual 19.2% | AUC 0.721
How to read it

Both days, every request is answered. No error, no timeout. But after the change, the model thinks everyone is in their hundreds and predicts a 0% no-show rate, while 19% of patients actually miss. AUC only drops from 0.770 to 0.721, because the other features still rank patients, so even a ranking metric would barely notice. Only comparing predictions with reality, or checking the inputs, reveals it.

1.2

Edge cases and outliers

Play · 99.99% safe?

Would you ride in a self-driving car that's safe 99.99% of the time but occasionally catastrophic? Edge cases are inputs so extreme that the model makes catastrophic mistakes. In safety-critical work (medical diagnosis, traffic control) or brand-sensitive work (a chatbot that sometimes says something offensive), a few edge cases can make a model unusable.

Outliers are about data: examples very different from the rest. Edge cases are about performance: examples the model handles much worse. An outlier is only an edge case if the model gets it badly wrong. In training, removing outliers often helps; in production you can't ignore odd requests, so models must cope with them.

A warning signA sudden rise in poorly handled inputs may mean the distribution itself has shifted.
Code lab · Python

One typo bends the line

Step 2 fits waiting time against patients booked for 60 clinic sessions, once on clean data and once with a single typo (600 minutes instead of about 60).

Python · step 2 · outliers and edge cases
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
booked = r.integers(5, 40, 60)                               # patients booked for the session
wait = 4 + 1.5 * booked + r.normal(0, 4, 60)                 # average wait in minutes
wait_typo = wait.copy(); wait_typo[np.argmax(booked)] = 600  # one data-entry typo: 600 instead of ~60

clean_fit = LinearRegression().fit(booked.reshape(-1, 1), wait)
typo_fit = LinearRegression().fit(booked.reshape(-1, 1), wait_typo)
grid = np.arange(5, 40).reshape(-1, 1)
print(f"without the outlier: wait = {clean_fit.intercept_:5.1f} + {clean_fit.coef_[0]:.2f} x booked")
print(f"with one outlier:    wait = {typo_fit.intercept_:5.1f} + {typo_fit.coef_[0]:.2f} x booked")
truth = 4 + 1.5 * grid.ravel()
print(f"average error on new sessions: {np.abs(clean_fit.predict(grid) - truth).mean():.1f} min vs "
      f"{np.abs(typo_fit.predict(grid) - truth).mean():.1f} min")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3))
ax.scatter(booked, np.minimum(wait_typo, 120), s=14, color="#9AA0B8")
ax.plot(grid, clean_fit.predict(grid), color="#0E9466", label="fit without outlier")
ax.plot(grid, typo_fit.predict(grid), color="#D63E74", label="fit with one outlier (600, drawn at top)")
ax.set(xlabel="patients booked", ylabel="average wait (min)", ylim=(0, 125)); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
Output
without the outlier: wait =   5.1 + 1.42 x booked
with one outlier:    wait = -18.6 + 2.98 x booked
average error on new sessions: 0.8 min vs 14.9 min
How to read it

One bad row out of 60 doubles the slope (1.42 to 2.98 minutes per patient) and drags the intercept below zero, which would mean negative waits for small sessions. Average error on new sessions jumps from under a minute to 15 minutes. That's why cleaning outliers before training pays off, and why the model must still be checked on unusual inputs at serving time.

1.3

Degenerate feedback loops

Play · Rank by clicks, round by round

A degenerate feedback loop happens when a system's outputs shape its future inputs. A recommender ranks a song slightly higher, so more people see it and click it, so it ranks higher still. Two nearly equal songs end up far apart. The same effect goes by popularity bias, exposure bias, filter bubbles and echo chambers.

It can do real harm. A résumé screener that favours some feature X (a college, a former employer, a gender) only sends X candidates to interview, so only X candidates get hired, so the model leans on X even more.

Detecting itOffline, measure how diverse the outputs are (aggregate diversity, long-tail coverage) and compare accuracy across popularity buckets. Online, watch for recommendations becoming more uniform over time.
Code lab · Python

Rank 20 videos by total clicks

Step 3 has 20 health-tip videos with hidden true appeal. After a launch week of 50 random views each, a "most clicked" list shows the top 5 to 400 users per round, for 300 rounds. Higher slots get more clicks whatever is in them.

Python · step 3 · a degenerate feedback loop
POS = np.array([1.0, 0.6, 0.45, 0.35, 0.3])                  # people click higher slots more, whatever is there
r = np.random.default_rng(5)
appeal = r.uniform(0.03, 0.09, 20)                           # 20 health-tip videos; true appeal unknown to us
best = set(np.argsort(-appeal)[:5])

def simulate(score="clicks", explore=0.0, rounds=300, users=400, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    shows = np.full(20, 50.0)                                # launch week: 50 views each, in random slots
    clicks = r.binomial(50, appeal * POS.mean()).astype(float)
    exposure = shows * POS.mean()                            # position-weighted views
    first_top, changes, prev = None, 0, None
    for _ in range(rounds):
        s = clicks if score == "clicks" else clicks / exposure
        top = list(np.argsort(-s)[:5])
        if explore and r.random() < explore:                 # sometimes give the last slot to a random video
            top[4] = r.choice([v for v in range(20) if v not in top])
        first_top = first_top or set(top)
        changes += prev is not None and set(top) != prev
        prev = set(top)
        for slot, v in enumerate(top):
            shows[v] += users; exposure[v] += users * POS[slot]
            clicks[v] += r.binomial(users, appeal[v] * POS[slot])
    s = clicks if score == "clicks" else clicks / exposure
    return shows, set(np.argsort(-s)[:5]), first_top, changes

shows, top, first, changes = simulate("clicks")
print("ranking by total clicks, 300 rounds of 400 users:")
print(f"  rounds in which the 5 videos on screen changed: {changes}")
print(f"  videos never shown again after launch week: {(shows == 50).sum()} of 20")
print(f"  share of all views going to the 5 on screen: {np.sort(shows)[-5:].sum() / shows.sum():.0%}")
print(f"  of the 5 genuinely best videos, on screen now: {len(best & top)}")
Output
ranking by total clicks, 300 rounds of 400 users:
  rounds in which the 5 videos on screen changed: 0
  videos never shown again after launch week: 15 of 20
  share of all views going to the 5 on screen: 100%
  of the 5 genuinely best videos, on screen now: 2
How to read it

The top five never change, not even once in 300 rounds. Whatever led after launch week takes 100% of later views, and 15 videos are never shown again, so the system never learns that three of the five best videos are stuck among them. Every round's clicks seem to confirm the ranking, because the ranking caused them.

1.4

Breaking the loop: randomisation and positional features

Play · Do people click the song, or the slot?

Randomisation. Show some items regardless of their score, and use the feedback to learn their real quality. TikTok gives each new video a small initial pool of random viewers before deciding whether it earns a bigger one. Pure randomness hurts user experience; smarter exploration (such as contextual bandits, Chapter 9) balances the two.

Positional features. If the slot influences clicks, tell the model the slot during training (e.g. "shown first: yes/no"), then predict as if every item were in the same slot. A more refined version uses two models: one for whether a user sees an item at that position, one for whether they click once seen.

Code lab · Python

Three ranking policies, five runs each

Step 4 replays the simulation with three policies: total clicks; click rate per position-weighted view (a positional correction); and that rate plus a random video in the last slot 30% of the time.

Python · step 4 · break the loop: position-aware scores and exploration
for name, score, explore in [("total clicks", "clicks", 0.0), ("click rate per position-weighted view", "rate", 0.0),
                             ("position-aware rate + explore 30% of rounds", "rate", 0.3)]:
    found = [len(best & simulate(score, explore, seed=s)[1]) for s in range(5)]
    print(f"{name:<44} best videos on screen (5 runs): {found}  average {np.mean(found):.1f} of 5")
Output
total clicks                                 best videos on screen (5 runs): [2, 2, 3, 3, 1]  average 2.2 of 5
click rate per position-weighted view        best videos on screen (5 runs): [2, 3, 4, 3, 4]  average 3.2 of 5
position-aware rate + explore 30% of rounds  best videos on screen (5 runs): [4, 4, 3, 4, 4]  average 3.8 of 5
How to read it

Ranking by total clicks gets an average of 2.2 of the 5 best videos on screen. Correcting for position lifts that to 3.2: videos are judged by how they do given their slot. Adding exploration reaches 3.8, because overlooked videos finally get a chance to prove themselves. Neither fix is perfect, and exploration costs some clicks on weaker videos, but both loosen the loop.

BACKChapter 8 overviewNEXT · SECTION 2Kinds of Distribution Shift
Book / Chapter 8 / Section 2
Section 2 of 4 · Summary

Kinds of Data Distribution Shift

A model learns from a source distribution and makes predictions on a target distribution. When they differ, predictions suffer. With inputs X and outputs Y, the joint distribution splits two ways: P(X,Y) = P(Y|X)·P(X) = P(X|Y)·P(Y). Covariate shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) stays. Label shift: P(Y) changes, P(X|Y) stays. Concept drift: P(Y|X) changes, P(X) stays. In practice several happen at once, and teams care more about fixing a shift than naming it.

2.1Covariate shift2.2Label shift2.3Concept drift2.4Feature and schema changes
2.1

Covariate shift

Play · Who is in the data?

The inputs change, but the relationship between inputs and outcome doesn't. A breast-cancer model trained on clinic data sees mostly women over 40, because doctors send them for check-ups; the general public is younger. For any given age, the risk is the same.

Causes in development: sample selection bias, deliberate oversampling of rare classes, active learning. In production: a marketing campaign brings in a richer or younger crowd, or the app launches somewhere new.

Importance weightingIf you know (or can estimate) how production inputs differ, weight training examples by the density ratio Ptarget(x) / Psource(x) and retrain. The ratio can come from a classifier that tells source data from target data, no labels needed.
Code lab · Python

Reweight a check-up clinic's data for a young app audience

Step 5 trains on patients who are mostly older (mean age 57) and deploys to an app whose users are mostly young (mean 36). Risk by age is U-shaped and identical in both. A simple linear model is trained as is, then with importance weights from a source-vs-target classifier.

Python · step 5 · covariate shift and importance weighting
r = np.random.default_rng(11)
def patients(n, young_share):
    young = r.random(n) < young_share
    age = np.where(young, r.uniform(18, 40, n), r.uniform(40, 85, n))
    p = 0.08 + 0.35 * np.exp(-((age - 18) / 9) ** 2) + 0.25 * ((age - 40) / 45) ** 2   # U-shaped risk, same everywhere
    return age.reshape(-1, 1), (r.random(n) < p).astype(int)

X_src, y_src = patients(6000, young_share=0.15)   # training data from a check-up clinic: mostly older patients
X_tgt, y_tgt = patients(6000, young_share=0.80)   # the new app: mostly young users
print(f"training mean age {X_src.mean():.0f}, production mean age {X_tgt.mean():.0f} (same risk for any given age)")

# Estimate the density ratio with a classifier that tells source from target (needs no labels)
dom = LogisticRegression().fit(np.vstack([X_src, X_tgt]) / 100, np.r_[np.zeros(len(X_src)), np.ones(len(X_tgt))])
pt = dom.predict_proba(X_src / 100)[:, 1]
weights = pt / (1 - pt)

for name, m in [("trained as is", LogisticRegression().fit(X_src, y_src)),
                ("importance-weighted", LogisticRegression().fit(X_src, y_src, sample_weight=weights))]:
    p = m.predict_proba(X_tgt)[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:<20} on production: log loss {log_loss(y_tgt, p):.3f}, AUC {roc_auc_score(y_tgt, p):.3f}")
Output
training mean age 57, production mean age 36 (same risk for any given age)
trained as is        on production: log loss 0.553, AUC 0.348
importance-weighted  on production: log loss 0.523, AUC 0.652
How to read it

Trained as is, the model learns "risk rises with age" from the older patients. On the young audience that's backwards: AUC 0.348, worse than a coin toss. With importance weights, the young patients in the training data count for more, the model learns the slope that matters for its real users, and AUC rises to 0.652. Weighting helps most when, as here, the model can't fit every age range at once.

2.2

Label shift

Play · Monsoon arrives

One patient with a fever whose dry-season model score is 30%.

The share of each outcome changes, but each outcome still looks the same. In monsoon, far more fevers are dengue, but a dengue patient's temperature and platelet count look like they always did.

Covariate shift often causes label shift too (more older women in training also means more positive cases). But not always: a preventive drug that lowers everyone's risk changes P(Y|X), so it isn't covariate shift, yet a patient who has the disease still has the same age profile, so it is label shift.

Fixing itIf you know or can estimate the new outcome rate, adjust the model's odds by the ratio of new to old prior, as in the lab. Research methods such as Black Box Shift Estimation estimate it without labels.
Code lab · Python

A dry-season dengue model in the monsoon

Step 6 trains on fever cases where 5% are dengue, then predicts on monsoon cases where 30% are. Symptoms for each group come from the same distributions. It then updates the model's prior with Bayes' rule.

Python · step 6 · label shift
r = np.random.default_rng(12)
def fever_cases(n, pos_rate):
    y = (r.random(n) < pos_rate).astype(int)
    X = np.column_stack([r.normal(38.0 + 1.0 * y, 0.6), r.normal(180 - 70 * y, 40)])   # temperature, platelets (thousand)
    return X, y                                                                          # P(X | Y) never changes

X_dry, y_dry = fever_cases(10_000, 0.05)      # dry season: 5% of fever cases are dengue
X_mon, y_mon = fever_cases(10_000, 0.30)      # monsoon: 30%
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_dry, y_dry)
p = clf.predict_proba(X_mon)[:, 1]

def reprior(p, old, new):                     # Bayes: rescale the odds by the change in prior
    odds = p / (1 - p) * (new / (1 - new)) / (old / (1 - old))
    return odds / (1 + odds)

for name, q in [("dry-season model as is", p), ("same model, prior updated to 30%", reprior(p, 0.05, 0.30))]:
    flag = q >= 0.5
    print(f"{name:<34} mean predicted {q.mean():.1%} (actual {y_mon.mean():.1%}) | "
          f"dengue cases flagged {flag[y_mon == 1].mean():.0%} | false alarms {flag[y_mon == 0].mean():.1%}")
Output
dry-season model as is             mean predicted 17.0% (actual 29.6%) | dengue cases flagged 52% | false alarms 0.8%
same model, prior updated to 30%   mean predicted 29.5% (actual 29.6%) | dengue cases flagged 80% | false alarms 5.7%
How to read it

Unadjusted, the model expects 17% dengue when the true share is 30%, and flags only 52% of real cases: it's still tuned for a season when dengue was rare. Updating the prior brings the average prediction to 29.5% and catches 80% of cases, at the cost of more false alarms (0.8% to 5.7%). In monsoon, that's usually the right trade.

2.3

Concept drift

Play · Same trip, different season

Same input, different output. P(X) stays put while P(Y|X) changes. The book's example: the same apartment was worth far less once people left the city early in the pandemic. The houses didn't change; what they meant for the price did.

Concept drift is often cyclic or seasonal: ride fares on weekdays vs weekends, flight prices in holidays, travel times in the monsoon. Some companies keep separate models for each regime, for example one for weekdays and one for weekends.

Code lab · Python

Travel time to the clinic, dry season vs monsoon

Step 7 simulates trips whose distance and timing look the same all year, but each kilometre and each rush hour costs more in the monsoon. It trains on the dry season, then tests on the monsoon, and compares a separate model trained on last year's monsoon.

Python · step 7 · concept drift: same input, different output
r = np.random.default_rng(13)
def trips(n, monsoon):
    km = r.gamma(2.5, 3, n)
    hour = r.integers(7, 22, n)
    rush = ((hour >= 9) & (hour <= 11)) | ((hour >= 18) & (hour <= 20))
    minutes = 6 + km * (3.0 + 2.2 * monsoon) + rush * (8 + 10 * monsoon) + r.normal(0, 4, n)
    return pd.DataFrame({"km": km, "rush": rush.astype(int)}), minutes

X_dry, t_dry = trips(5000, monsoon=0)
X_wet, t_wet = trips(5000, monsoon=1)
print(f"input check: mean trip {X_dry.km.mean():.1f} km dry vs {X_wet.km.mean():.1f} km monsoon (inputs unchanged)")
dry_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_dry, t_dry)
X_wet_hist, t_wet_hist = trips(5000, monsoon=1)
wet_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_wet_hist, t_wet_hist)       # trained on last year's monsoon
print(f"dry-season model, dry season:      off by {mean_absolute_error(t_dry, dry_model.predict(X_dry)):5.1f} min")
print(f"dry-season model, monsoon:         off by {mean_absolute_error(t_wet, dry_model.predict(X_wet)):5.1f} min")
print(f"separate monsoon model, monsoon:   off by {mean_absolute_error(t_wet, wet_model.predict(X_wet)):5.1f} min")
Output
input check: mean trip 7.5 km dry vs 7.4 km monsoon (inputs unchanged)
dry-season model, dry season:      off by   3.2 min
dry-season model, monsoon:         off by  20.4 min
separate monsoon model, monsoon:   off by   3.2 min
How to read it

The inputs really don't change (7.5 km vs 7.4 km on average), so input monitoring would see nothing. Yet the dry-season model is off by 20 minutes a trip in the monsoon, against 3 minutes in its own season. A model built for the monsoon brings the error back to 3 minutes. Seasonal drift is predictable, so plan for it.

2.4

Feature changes and label schema changes

Play · What changed?
Pick a change.

Less studied, just as damaging. Feature change: features are added or removed, or their possible values change. Age in months instead of years; a pipeline bug that turns a feature into NaNs.

Label schema change: the set of possible outputs changes, so both P(Y) and P(X|Y) change. A credit-score range moves from 300–850 to 250–900; a disease is added to a diagnosis model; marketing splits NEGATIVE reviews into SAD and ANGRY. Often you must relabel data and retrain, sometimes with a new model structure. It's especially common with many-class tasks such as product categorisation.

AlsoMany apparent "shifts" on dashboards are internal errors: pipeline bugs, wrong model versions, features scaled with the wrong statistics, or an app change that alters user behaviour.
Code lab · Python

When three labels become four

Step 8 imagines a perfect 3-class sentiment model facing the new 4-class schema, then checks how many credit scores in the new range fall outside the old one.

Python · step 8 · feature change and label schema change
old_labels = ["POSITIVE", "NEGATIVE", "NEUTRAL"]
r = np.random.default_rng(14)
new_truth = r.choice(["POSITIVE", "NEUTRAL", "SAD", "ANGRY"], 2000, p=[0.45, 0.3, 0.15, 0.10])
old_pred = np.where(np.isin(new_truth, ["SAD", "ANGRY"]), "NEGATIVE", new_truth)   # even a perfect old model
print("old schema:", {k: i for i, k in enumerate(old_labels)})
print("new schema:", {k: i for i, k in enumerate(["POSITIVE", "NEUTRAL", "SAD", "ANGRY"])})
print(f"a perfect 3-class model scores {np.mean(old_pred == new_truth):.0%} on the 4-class task: "
      f"it can never say SAD or ANGRY ({np.isin(new_truth, ['SAD', 'ANGRY']).mean():.0%} of reviews)")

scores = r.integers(250, 901, 10)                         # credit-score range widened from 300-850 to 250-900
print("\nscores outside the range the old model was trained on:", int(((scores < 300) | (scores > 850)).sum()), "of", len(scores))
Output
old schema: {'POSITIVE': 0, 'NEGATIVE': 1, 'NEUTRAL': 2}
new schema: {'POSITIVE': 0, 'NEUTRAL': 1, 'SAD': 2, 'ANGRY': 3}
a perfect 3-class model scores 74% on the 4-class task: it can never say SAD or ANGRY (26% of reviews)

scores outside the range the old model was trained on: 1 of 10
How to read it

Even a model that was never wrong under the old schema scores only 74% on the new one, because it has no way to say SAD or ANGRY, which cover 26% of reviews. And the class-to-number mapping itself changed (NEUTRAL moved from 2 to 1), so mixing old and new code would silently misread every label. Schema changes need versioned schemas, relabelling and retraining.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1Why ML Systems FailNEXT · SECTION 3Detecting and Addressing Shifts
Book / Chapter 8 / Section 3
Section 3 of 4 · Summary

Detecting and Addressing Shifts

Shifts only matter if they hurt performance, so the first thing to watch is accuracy. But labels are often missing or late, so we also watch distributions: of inputs P(X), and, when labels exist, of P(Y) and the conditionals. In industry, most detection focuses on features, using summary statistics and two-sample tests, over carefully chosen time windows. Addressing a shift usually means retraining on recent data, plus designing features and models that are robust to change.

3.1Statistics and two-sample tests3.2Significant vs important3.3Time-scale windows3.4Addressing shifts
3.1

Summary statistics and two-sample tests

Play · Same mean and spread?

The simple approach: compare min, max, mean, median, variance, quantiles, skew and kurtosis between training data and production. Even TensorFlow's built-in data validation used only summary statistics (as of late 2021). It's a good start, but similar summaries don't prove the distributions match.

A two-sample test asks whether two samples could plausibly come from the same distribution. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test needs no assumptions about the distribution, but works on one dimension only, can be costly, and raises false alarms. Multivariate options include Least-Squares Density Difference and MMD; the open-source Alibi Detect library implements many of them. Tests work better on fewer dimensions, so reduce dimensions first.

Code lab · Python

Two distributions summary statistics can't tell apart

Step 9 compares a bell curve with a two-humped distribution built to have the same mean and spread, first by summary statistics, then with a KS test.

Python · step 9 · summary statistics vs a two-sample test
r = np.random.default_rng(15)
before = r.normal(0, 1, 5000)
after = np.where(r.random(5000) < 0.5, -0.9, 0.9) + r.normal(0, 0.436, 5000)   # two humps, same mean and spread
for name, s in [("training", before), ("production", after)]:
    print(f"{name:<11} mean {s.mean():+.2f}  std {s.std():.2f}  median {np.median(s):+.2f}")
res = ks_2samp(before, after)
print(f"\nKolmogorov-Smirnov test: statistic {res.statistic:.3f}, p-value {res.pvalue:.1e} -> the distributions differ")
Output
training    mean +0.01  std 1.00  median +0.03
production  mean +0.01  std 0.99  median +0.04

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: statistic 0.096, p-value 1.2e-20 -> the distributions differ
How to read it

Mean, standard deviation and median all match to two decimal places, so a summary-statistics check would pass. The KS test compares the whole shape and is certain they differ (p ≈ 10⁻²⁰). If your feature's histogram can change shape, a mean-and-variance check won't see it.

3.2

Significant is not the same as important

Play · Test many stable features at p < 0.05

"Statistically significant" means the difference probably isn't sampling noise. It doesn't mean the difference matters. With enough data, the tiniest shift becomes significant.

A useful rule of thumb from the book: if you can detect a difference from a fairly small sample, it's probably serious; if it only shows up with a huge sample, it's probably not worth worrying about.

And many tests means many false alarmsAt p < 0.05, about 1 in 20 tests of perfectly stable data will still "fail".
Code lab · Python

Sample size, and a month of false alarms

Step 10 runs a KS test on a tiny shift (2% of a standard deviation) at three sample sizes. Then it tests 200 features that never change, every day for 30 days.

Python · step 10 · significant is not the same as important
r = np.random.default_rng(16)
for n in [200, 2_000, 200_000]:
    a, b = r.normal(0, 1, n), r.normal(0.02, 1, n)          # a shift of 2% of a standard deviation
    print(f"n = {n:>7,}: p-value {ks_2samp(a, b).pvalue:.3f}  {'<- significant' if ks_2samp(a, b).pvalue < 0.05 else ''}")

alerts = []
for day in range(30):                                       # 200 features that never change at all
    pv = [ks_2samp(r.normal(0, 1, 2000), r.normal(0, 1, 2000)).pvalue for _ in range(200)]
    alerts.append(int(np.sum(np.array(pv) < 0.05)))
print(f"\n200 unchanged features, tested daily at p < 0.05: {np.mean(alerts):.1f} false alarms a day on average")
Output
n =     200: p-value 0.466  
n =   2,000: p-value 0.819  
n = 200,000: p-value 0.000  <- significant

200 unchanged features, tested daily at p < 0.05: 10.8 false alarms a day on average
How to read it

With 200 or 2,000 samples, the tiny shift is invisible; with 200,000 it's "significant". It's equally tiny either way, so the p-value alone can't tell you how much to care. And 200 unchanging features produce about 11 alerts a day, every one of them false. Section 4 shows what that does to a monitoring team.

3.3

Time-scale windows

Play · Compare day 15 with which window?

Shifts happen at different speeds: sudden ones are easy to spot, gradual ones hard. They can be spatial (new users, new devices) or temporal (over time). For temporal shifts, treat the data as a time series, and choose the window carefully: a window shorter than a weekly cycle will flag every weekly peak as a shift.

Sliding statistics are computed within a window (this hour); cumulative ones keep growing (since midnight). Cumulative numbers hide sudden dips. Many companies compare hourly or daily production data against the training distribution: shorter windows catch changes faster but raise more false alarms. Some platforms merge short windows into longer ones, or search across windows to find where a change began (root cause analysis).

Code lab · Python

A three-hour dip, and a weekly peak

Step 11 simulates a day where accuracy drops from 90% to about 62% between 16:00 and 19:00, and tracks it with sliding and cumulative accuracy. Then it checks day 15 of an orders series with a weekly peak against two different windows.

Python · step 11 · time windows: sliding vs cumulative
r = np.random.default_rng(17)
hours = np.arange(24)
acc_true = np.where((hours >= 16) & (hours < 19), 0.62, 0.90)
n = np.full(24, 500)
correct = r.binomial(n, acc_true)
sliding = correct / n
cumulative = correct.cumsum() / n.cumsum()
for h in [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]:
    print(f"hour {h}: sliding accuracy {sliding[h]:.2f}   cumulative {cumulative[h]:.2f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3))
ax.plot(hours, sliding, "o-", ms=3, color="#D63E74", label="sliding (this hour)")
ax.plot(hours, cumulative, "-", color="#1C7FD0", label="cumulative (since midnight)")
ax.set(xlabel="hour of day", ylabel="accuracy", ylim=(0.5, 1)); ax.legend(fontsize=8)

daily = 100 + 60 * (np.arange(1, 16) % 7 == 1) + r.normal(0, 6, 15)   # a weekly peak: days 1, 8, 15
print(f"\nday 15 orders {daily[14]:.0f}; days 9-14 averaged {daily[8:14].mean():.0f}, days 1-14 averaged {daily[:14].mean():.0f}")
print(f"z-score of day 15 against days 9-14: {(daily[14] - daily[8:14].mean()) / daily[8:14].std():+.1f}; "
      f"against the same weekday in earlier weeks: {(daily[14] - daily[[0, 7]].mean()) / 6:+.1f}")
Output
hour 14: sliding accuracy 0.90   cumulative 0.90
hour 15: sliding accuracy 0.91   cumulative 0.90
hour 16: sliding accuracy 0.60   cumulative 0.88
hour 17: sliding accuracy 0.66   cumulative 0.87
hour 18: sliding accuracy 0.65   cumulative 0.86
hour 19: sliding accuracy 0.91   cumulative 0.86
hour 20: sliding accuracy 0.90   cumulative 0.86

day 15 orders 167; days 9-14 averaged 98, days 1-14 averaged 106
z-score of day 15 against days 9-14: +14.9; against the same weekday in earlier weeks: +1.6
How to read it

The hourly view shows the dip clearly: 0.60 to 0.66. The cumulative view barely moves, from 0.90 to 0.86, and never recovers, so it hides when the problem started and when it ended. In the orders series, day 15 (167 orders) looks like a huge anomaly against days 9–14 (z = +15), but it's just the weekly peak: compared with the same weekday in earlier weeks it's ordinary. The window decides what counts as a shift.

3.4

Addressing data distribution shifts

Play · Robust by design

Three broad approaches. Massive training data, hoping production data falls inside what the model has seen (popular in research). Adapting without new labels, such as domain-invariant representations (little used in industry). And the industry default: retrain on labelled data from the new distribution.

Retraining raises two questions: from scratch (stateless) or continue from the last checkpoint (stateful, fine-tuning)? And on which data: the last day, week, six months, or since the drift began? Many teams pick a schedule by gut feeling; experiments are better (Chapter 9).

Not every drop needs MLMany failures are still human errors. Find and fix those first; finding the cause of a shift can be harder than detecting it.
Code lab · Python

Five ways to respond to a drifting week

Step 12 builds 9 weeks of data where the relationship between features and outcome shifts a little each week. It compares doing nothing, fine-tuning on the newest week, and retraining from scratch on the newest week, the last three weeks, or all nine, scoring each on the following week.

Python · step 12 · addressing shift: what to retrain, on what
r = np.random.default_rng(18)
def week(n, w):                                            # the relationship rotates a little each week
    X = r.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))
    beta = np.array([1.5, -1.0, 0.8, 0.0, 0.0]) + w * np.array([-0.25, 0.2, 0.0, 0.25, 0.2])
    return X, (r.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ beta)))).astype(int)

old = [week(4000, w) for w in range(8)]                    # 8 weeks of history
X_new, y_new = week(4000, 8)                               # the newest labelled week
X_next, y_next = week(4000, 9)                             # what we'll face next week

base = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0).fit(np.vstack([x for x, _ in old]), np.hstack([y for _, y in old]))
tuned = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0).fit(np.vstack([x for x, _ in old]), np.hstack([y for _, y in old]))
tuned.partial_fit(X_new, y_new)                        # stateful: continue from the old weights
options = {
    "do nothing": (base, 0),
    "fine-tune on the newest week": (tuned, 4000),
    "from scratch, newest week only": (SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0).fit(X_new, y_new), 4000),
    "from scratch, last 3 weeks": (SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0).fit(np.vstack([old[6][0], old[7][0], X_new]), np.hstack([old[6][1], old[7][1], y_new])), 12000),
    "from scratch, all 9 weeks": (SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0).fit(np.vstack([x for x, _ in old] + [X_new]), np.hstack([y for _, y in old] + [y_new])), 36000),
}
for name, (m, rows) in options.items():
    print(f"{name:<31} next-week AUC {roc_auc_score(y_next, m.predict_proba(X_next)[:, 1]):.3f}   rows trained {rows:>6,}")
Output
do nothing                      next-week AUC 0.763   rows trained      0
fine-tune on the newest week    next-week AUC 0.923   rows trained  4,000
from scratch, newest week only  next-week AUC 0.923   rows trained  4,000
from scratch, last 3 weeks      next-week AUC 0.920   rows trained 12,000
from scratch, all 9 weeks       next-week AUC 0.816   rows trained 36,000
How to read it

Doing nothing leaves AUC at 0.763. Fine-tuning on the newest week, or retraining on just the newest week, both reach about 0.923, from only 4,000 rows. Three weeks is nearly as good. Using all nine weeks is much worse (0.816): with steady drift, old data teaches the model a relationship that no longer holds. More data isn't always better data.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2Kinds of Distribution ShiftNEXT · SECTION 4Monitoring and Observability
Book / Chapter 8 / Section 4
Section 4 of 4 · Summary

Monitoring and Observability

Monitoring means tracking, measuring and logging metrics that tell you when something goes wrong. Observability means setting the system up (instrumenting it) so you can work out what went wrong: timers in functions, NaN counts in features, logs of unusual inputs. Monitor operational metrics (latency, throughput, uptime, CPU and memory) and ML metrics: accuracy, predictions, features and raw inputs. Then turn them into logs, dashboards and alerts people can act on.

4.1Operational metrics4.2Accuracy and predictions4.3Features4.4Alerts4.5Logs and observability
4.1

Operational metrics, uptime and SLAs

Play · How many nines?

ML systems are software systems first. Operational metrics cover the network, the machine and the application: latency, throughput, requests per minute, the share of successful (2xx) responses, CPU, GPU and memory use. If the system is down, the best model is worth nothing.

Availability is measured as uptime, and what counts as "up" is set in service level objectives or agreements (SLOs/SLAs), for example: median latency under 200 ms and 99th percentile under 2 s. Cloud providers promise uptime like 99.99% and refund credits if they miss it.

But up isn't enoughA system can be up and still serve garbage predictions, which is why ML metrics come next.
Code lab · Python

Downtime budgets and an hourly SLA check

Step 13 converts uptime targets into minutes a month, then checks a day of request logs against the SLA, hour by hour.

Python · step 13 · operational metrics and SLAs
for nines in ["99%", "99.9%", "99.99%", "99.999%"]:
    down = (1 - float(nines[:-1]) / 100) * 30 * 24 * 60
    print(f"uptime {nines:<8} allows {down:8.1f} minutes of downtime a month")

r = np.random.default_rng(19)
log = pd.DataFrame({"hour": np.repeat(np.arange(24), 2000)})
log["latency_ms"] = r.lognormal(np.log(120), 0.5, len(log)) * np.where(log.hour.isin([13]), 2.2, 1) \
                    + np.where(log.hour.isin([20]) & (r.random(len(log)) < 0.03), 4000, 0)
sla = log.groupby("hour").latency_ms.agg(median="median", p99=lambda s: s.quantile(0.99))
bad = sla[(sla["median"] >= 200) | (sla.p99 >= 2000)]
print("\nSLA: median < 200 ms and p99 < 2 s. Hours that broke it:")
print(bad.round(0).to_string())
Output
uptime 99%      allows    432.0 minutes of downtime a month
uptime 99.9%    allows     43.2 minutes of downtime a month
uptime 99.99%   allows      4.3 minutes of downtime a month
uptime 99.999%  allows      0.4 minutes of downtime a month

SLA: median < 200 ms and p99 < 2 s. Hours that broke it:
      median     p99
hour                
13     263.0   828.0
20     124.0  4127.0
How to read it

Each extra nine cuts the budget tenfold: from over 7 hours a month at 99% to about 4 minutes at 99.99%, and under 30 seconds at 99.999%. In the day's logs, two hours broke the SLA in different ways: at 13:00 everything slowed down (median 263 ms), while at 20:00 the median looked fine but a few very slow requests pushed p99 past 4 seconds. Checking only the median would have missed 20:00.

4.2

Monitoring accuracy and predictions

Play · Which signal arrives first?

Accuracy-related metrics are the most direct, so log every bit of user feedback: clicks, hides, purchases, votes, shares, watch time. Even feedback that isn't a label can reveal decline: if click-through holds steady but completion rate falls, recommendations are getting worse. Some products build feedback in, like up/down votes on a translation.

Predictions are the most commonly monitored artifact: low-dimensional, easy to plot and test. If the model hasn't changed, a shift in predictions usually means a shift in inputs. And odd patterns, such as a long run of the same answer, can be caught in minutes, while labels may take days.

Code lab · Python

Catch a stuck model from its predictions

Step 14 streams five predictions a minute. At 10:00 a bug blanks a feature and the model starts predicting "will attend" for everyone. A monitor compares the 15-minute share of "will miss" predictions with the morning's baseline.

Python · step 14 · monitoring predictions
r = np.random.default_rng(20)
minutes = np.arange(24 * 60)
rate = np.where(minutes < 600, 0.22, 0.0)                  # at 10:00 a bug blanks a feature; model says "no" to everyone
preds = r.random(len(minutes) * 5).reshape(-1, 5) < rate[:, None]   # 5 predictions a minute
pos_share = pd.Series(preds.mean(axis=1)).rolling(15).mean()
baseline = preds[:600].mean()
alarm = int(np.argmax((minutes >= 600) & (pos_share < baseline / 4)))
print(f"normal share of 'will miss' predictions: {baseline:.1%}")
print(f"prediction monitor (15-minute window) alarms at minute {alarm}: {alarm - 600} minutes after the bug")
print("accuracy monitor: needs labels; no-shows are known only after the appointment, often days later")
Output
normal share of 'will miss' predictions: 23.0%
prediction monitor (15-minute window) alarms at minute 612: 12 minutes after the bug
accuracy monitor: needs labels; no-shows are known only after the appointment, often days later
How to read it

Normally about 23% of predictions say "will miss". The prediction monitor raises an alarm 12 minutes after the bug, without needing a single label. An accuracy monitor would have to wait until appointments happen and no-shows are recorded, possibly days, while the clinic stops sending reminders to the people who need them.

4.3

Monitoring features

Play · Four worries about feature monitoring
Pick a worry.

Most industry monitoring tools focus on features: they're structured, with a known schema. The first step is feature validation, also called table testing or "unit tests for data": check that min, max and median are in range, values match a pattern, categories belong to an allowed set, and one column is always greater than another. Great Expectations and AWS's Deequ are common open-source tools.

Beyond validation, two-sample tests can check whether features have drifted. Raw inputs are harder: many sources and formats, often owned by a data platform team rather than the ML team.

Code lab · Python

Five expectations, two batches

Step 15 writes five checks in plain pandas, in the style of Great Expectations, and runs them on yesterday's clean batch and today's, which has four different upstream bugs.

Python · step 15 · feature validation ("unit tests for data")
def validate(df):
    checks = {
        "age between 0 and 120": df.age.between(0, 120).all(),
        "sms_reminder in {0, 1}": df.sms_reminder.isin([0, 1]).all(),
        "phone matches +91XXXXXXXXXX": df.phone.str.fullmatch(r"\+91\d{10}").all(),
        "appointment after booking": (df.appointment > df.booked_at).all(),
        "distance missing < 5%": df.distance_km.isna().mean() < 0.05,
    }
    return pd.Series(checks).map({True: "pass", False: "FAIL"})

r = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 500
good = pd.DataFrame({"age": r.integers(18, 80, n), "sms_reminder": r.integers(0, 2, n),
                     "phone": ["+91" + "".join(map(str, r.integers(0, 10, 10))) for _ in range(n)],
                     "booked_at": pd.Timestamp("2026-10-01") + pd.to_timedelta(r.integers(0, 600, n), "h"),
                     "distance_km": r.gamma(2, 3, n)})
good["appointment"] = good.booked_at + pd.to_timedelta(r.integers(24, 720, n), "h")
bad = good.copy()
bad["age"] = bad.age * 12                                          # months, not years
bad["phone"] = bad.phone.str[3:]                                   # country code dropped
bad.loc[:40, ["booked_at", "appointment"]] = bad.loc[:40, ["appointment", "booked_at"]].values   # swapped columns
bad.loc[r.random(n) < 0.2, "distance_km"] = np.nan
print(pd.DataFrame({"yesterday's batch": validate(good), "today's batch": validate(bad)}).to_string())
Output
                            yesterday's batch today's batch
age between 0 and 120                    pass          FAIL
sms_reminder in {0, 1}                   pass          pass
phone matches +91XXXXXXXXXX              pass          FAIL
appointment after booking                pass          FAIL
distance missing < 5%                    pass          FAIL
How to read it

Yesterday passes everything. Today fails four of five checks, each pointing at a specific bug: age in months, phone numbers missing the +91 country code, booking and appointment times swapped for 41 rows, and 20% of distances missing. The SMS column is fine, which narrows the search. Each check is one line, cheap enough to run on every batch before it reaches the model.

4.4

Alerts and alert fatigue

Play · Write an alert

An alert has three parts: a policy (the condition, e.g. accuracy under 90%, or latency over 1 s for 10 minutes), notification channels (email, a Slack channel, PagerDuty), and a description detailed enough to act on, ideally with a runbook of steps to take.

Alert fatigue is what happens when alerts fire too often: people stop reading them, and the critical one gets ignored along with the noise. Feature shifts happen all the time and most are harmless, so the hard part is deciding which shifts deserve an alert.

Dashboards tooA wiggly line is easy to plot and hard to interpret, and too many charts leads to "dashboard rot". Choose a few signals that mean something.
Code lab · Python

Naive alerts vs a smarter policy

Step 16 monitors 150 features for 30 days. Three real shifts are injected: two in features the model relies on, one in a feature it ignores. A naive rule alerts on any KS test with p < 0.05. A smarter one alerts only for important features whose population stability index (PSI) exceeds 0.1 for two days running.

Python · step 16 · alert fatigue
def psi(a, b, bins=10):
    edges = np.quantile(a, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)); edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    pa = np.histogram(a, edges)[0] / len(a) + 1e-6
    pb = np.histogram(b, edges)[0] / len(b) + 1e-6
    return float(np.sum((pb - pa) * np.log(pb / pa)))

r = np.random.default_rng(22)
n_feat, days = 150, 30
important = set(range(10))                                   # the 10 features the model leans on most
real = {(3, 12), (7, 20), (120, 5)}                          # real shifts: two important features, one unimportant
naive, smart, caught = 0, 0, set()
ref = r.normal(0, 1, (n_feat, 3000))
prev_flag = np.zeros(n_feat, bool)
for d in range(days):
    flag_today = np.zeros(n_feat, bool)
    for f in range(n_feat):
        shifted = any(f == rf and d >= rd for rf, rd in real)
        today = r.normal(0.5 if shifted else 0.03 * r.standard_normal(), 1, 3000)
        if ks_2samp(ref[f, :500], today[:500]).pvalue < 0.05:
            naive += 1
        flag_today[f] = psi(ref[f], today) > 0.1 and f in important
    for f in np.where(flag_today & prev_flag)[0]:            # alert only if it persists 2 days
        smart += 1; caught.add(int(f))
    prev_flag = flag_today
print(f"naive rule (any feature, KS p < 0.05): {naive} alerts in {days} days ({naive / days:.0f} a day)")
print(f"smarter rule (important features, PSI > 0.1, two days running): {smart} alerts; features caught: {sorted(caught)}")
Output
naive rule (any feature, KS p < 0.05): 433 alerts in 30 days (14 a day)
smarter rule (important features, PSI > 0.1, two days running): 26 alerts; features caught: [3, 7]
How to read it

The naive rule fires over 400 times in a month, about 14 a day, mostly about nothing; nobody reads that. The smarter policy fires 26 times, all for the two real shifts in important features (3 and 7), from the day after each began, and stays quiet about the shift in feature 120, which the model doesn't use. Fewer alerts, every one worth reading.

4.5

Logs, tracing and observability

Play · Follow one request through the services

Logs record events: containers starting, functions called, inputs and outputs, errors and stack traces. "If it moves, we track it," as an Etsy engineer put it. Volumes get huge (one dating app logged 20 billion events a day), and a single request may hop through 20–30 services, so the hard part is finding where something went wrong.

Distributed tracing gives each request an ID that every service logs, along with time, service, function and user. Logs can be processed in batch, or as a stream for real-time anomaly detection, and ML itself is used to spot unusual events.

Observability assumes you can infer a system's internal state from its outputs (telemetry), without shipping new code. It also allows finer questions than aggregate monitoring: which users, which inputs, which time period, which city.

Code lab · Python

Query structured logs by city and service

Step 17 logs 3,000 requests across three services (gateway, features, model), each event tagged with a request ID and city. One city's feature data source fails intermittently.

Python · step 17 · logs you can query: observability
r = np.random.default_rng(23)
n = 3000
req = pd.DataFrame({"request_id": [f"req-{i:05d}" for i in range(n)],
                    "city": r.choice(["Mumbai", "Pune", "Nashik", "Thane"], n, p=[0.5, 0.2, 0.15, 0.15])})
events = []
for row in req.itertuples():
    pune_bug = row.city == "Pune" and r.random() < 0.4      # a feature source for one city goes missing
    for service, ms in [("gateway", 5), ("features", 30), ("model", 15)]:
        status = "error" if (service == "features" and pune_bug) else "ok"
        events.append((row.request_id, row.city, service, round(r.gamma(4, ms / 4), 1), status))
        if status == "error":
            break
logs = pd.DataFrame(events, columns=["request_id", "city", "service", "ms", "status"])
print(f"{len(logs):,} log events; overall error rate {logs.groupby('request_id').status.apply(lambda s: (s == 'error').any()).mean():.1%}")
print("\nerrors by city and service:")
print(logs[logs.status == "error"].groupby(["city", "service"]).size().to_string())
bad_id = logs.loc[logs.status == "error", "request_id"].iloc[0]
print(f"\ntrace of {bad_id}:")
print(logs[logs.request_id == bad_id].to_string(index=False))
Output
8,732 log events; overall error rate 8.9%

errors by city and service:
city  service 
Pune  features    268

trace of req-00000:
request_id city  service   ms status
 req-00000 Pune  gateway  7.4     ok
 req-00000 Pune features 52.5  error
How to read it

The overall error rate, 8.9%, says something is wrong but not what. Grouping the errors by city and service answers it at once: every failure is in the features service, for Pune. The trace of one failed request shows it passing the gateway and stopping at the feature lookup. That's observability: answering a new question from logs you already have.

Chapter 8 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

ML systems fail silently, and the data they see keeps moving away from the data they learned from. Detecting shifts takes the right statistics, the right windows and judgement about what matters; monitoring takes operational and ML metrics, sensible alerts and observable systems. But monitoring only tells you something is wrong. Next: continual learning and testing in production, to keep models up to date.

Eight takeaways

In our words.

1. Expect silenceA model can answer every request and be wrong for all of them.
2. Watch for loopsWhen predictions shape future training data, explore and correct for position.
3. Name the shift if it helpsCovariate, label or concept drift each suggest a different fix.
4. Beyond the meanTwo-sample tests see shape changes that summary statistics miss.
5. Significant ≠ importantHuge samples make tiny shifts "significant"; many tests make false alarms.
6. Choose windows wiselySliding beats cumulative for dips; respect weekly and seasonal cycles.
7. Recent data firstUnder drift, retraining on recent data often beats using everything.
8. Alerts people readValidate features, alert on what matters, and log so you can ask why.

Book / Chapter 9
Chapter 9 · Broad summary

Continual Learning and Test in Production

Chapter 8 showed how to notice that a model is going stale. This chapter is about doing something about it: continually updating models, safely and efficiently. Continual learning is mostly an infrastructure problem, and companies reach it in four stages. Once updates are cheap, the question becomes how often to update, which depends on how much fresh data is worth. And because a fixed test set can't tell you how a model will do tomorrow, you also need to test in production: shadow deployments, A/B tests, canary releases, interleaving and bandits.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Continual learning. Not learning from every single example, but updating in micro-batches, with a copy (the challenger) that replaces the live model (the champion) only if it's better. It's less about how often you retrain and more about how: stateful fine-tuning is far cheaper than retraining from scratch. The hard parts are fresh labels, evaluation and algorithms that work on partial data.
  2. Four stages. Manual stateless retraining, then automated retraining, then automated stateful training, then fully continual learning triggered by time, performance, volume or drift.
  3. How often. Measure the value of data freshness: train on older and newer windows, test on today. And decide between iterating on data and iterating on the model.
  4. Test in production. Static test sets and backtests aren't enough. Shadow deployment is safest; A/B tests need randomisation and enough samples; canaries roll out gradually; interleaving and bandits need far less traffic.

Book / Chapter 9 / Section 1
Section 1 of 4 · Summary

Continual Learning

"Continual learning" makes people picture a model that updates with every example. Almost nobody does that: neural networks then suffer catastrophic forgetting (abruptly losing what they knew), and hardware is built for batches. Instead, companies update in micro-batches (say every 512 or 1,024 examples), on a copy of the model that replaces the live one only if it proves better. Continual learning is really about having the infrastructure to update whenever you need to, from scratch or by fine-tuning, and to deploy quickly.

1.1Champion and challenger1.2Stateless vs stateful1.3Why continual learning1.4Fresh data and labels1.5Evaluation and algorithms
1.1

Micro-batches, champion and challenger

Play · Feed the challenger batches

Never edit the live model directly. Make a replica, update it on the new micro-batch, evaluate it, and swap it in only if it beats the live model. The live model is the champion; the replica is the challenger.

Real systems are more complex: several challengers at once, and failed challengers studied rather than simply thrown away. And frequent updates aren't for everyone: with little traffic, or models that decay slowly, moving from weekly to daily updates may only add overhead.

The pointContinual learning isn't about how often you retrain. It's about being able to update quickly and safely whenever you need to.
Code lab · Python

40 micro-batches, one of them broken

Setup first: a food-delivery task (will this customer reorder within a week?) whose patterns drift a little each day. Step 1 starts from a model trained on day 0, then for each of 40 batches of 512 orders updates a copy, compares it with the champion on a fresh hold-out, and promotes it unless it's clearly worse. Batch 25 has every label flipped by a broken join.

Python · step 0 · setup
import copy, json, time, warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp, norm
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, accuracy_score

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)

BASE = np.array([1.4, -1.0, 0.8, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5])
DRIFT = np.array([-0.02, 0.015, 0.0, 0.02, 0.015, -0.01])

def day(d, n=2000, seed=None, shock=0.0):
    """One day of food-delivery orders: will this customer reorder within a week?
    The relationship drifts a little every day; `shock` adds a sudden change."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed if seed is not None else 1000 + d)
    X = r.normal(0, 1, (n, 6))
    beta = BASE + d * DRIFT + shock * np.array([-1.2, 0.8, 0, 0.9, 0, 0])
    y = (r.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ beta)))).astype(int)
    return X, y

def sgd():
    return SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", alpha=1e-4, random_state=0)

def auc(m, X, y):
    return roc_auc_score(y, m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])

X0, y0 = day(0, 20_000)
print(f"day-0 data: {X0.shape[0]:,} orders, reorder rate {y0.mean():.1%}")
Output
day-0 data: 20,000 orders, reorder rate 50.6%
Python · step 1 · micro-batches, champion and challenger
champion = sgd().fit(X0, y0)
frozen = copy.deepcopy(champion)
promoted, rejected = 0, 0
for b in range(1, 41):                                   # 40 micro-batches of 512 fresh orders
    Xb, yb = day(b, 512)
    if b == 25:
        yb = 1 - yb                                      # a broken label join flips every label in this batch
    challenger = copy.deepcopy(champion)                 # never touch the live model directly
    challenger.partial_fit(Xb, yb)
    Xh, yh = day(b, 2000, seed=5000 + b)                 # fresh hold-out from the same period
    gain = auc(challenger, Xh, yh) - auc(champion, Xh, yh)
    if gain > -0.02:                                     # allow for noise; block clear regressions
        champion, promoted = challenger, promoted + 1
    else:
        rejected += 1
        print(f"batch {b}: challenger AUC {gain:+.3f} vs champion -> rejected, champion stays live")
Xt, yt = day(41, 5000)
print(f"\npromoted {promoted}, rejected {rejected}")
print(f"next day: champion after 40 micro-batch updates AUC {auc(champion, Xt, yt):.3f}; never-updated model {auc(frozen, Xt, yt):.3f}")
Output
batch 25: challenger AUC -0.614 vs champion -> rejected, champion stays live

promoted 39, rejected 1
next day: champion after 40 micro-batch updates AUC 0.802; never-updated model 0.686
How to read it

39 challengers are promoted; the one trained on the broken batch scores 0.61 AUC lower and is rejected, so users never see it. After 40 small updates the champion scores 0.802 on the next day, against 0.686 for a model that was never updated. The evaluation gate is what makes frequent updates safe.

1.2

Stateless retraining vs stateful training

Play · What does each update train on?

Stateless retraining trains from scratch each time, on a large window (say the last three months). Stateful training, also called fine-tuning or incremental learning, continues from the last checkpoint using only new data (say yesterday's). Grubhub reported that moving from daily stateless to daily stateful training cut training compute 45-fold and raised purchase-through rate by 20%.

A bonus: if each example is used only once, you may not need to store it at all, which helps with privacy. Successful teams still retrain from scratch now and then, to recalibrate.

Data iteration vs model iterationStateful training works for refreshing a model with new data. Adding a feature or changing the architecture usually still means training from scratch.
Code lab · Python

30 days from scratch, or yesterday on top

Step 2 runs 30 daily updates two ways: retrain from scratch on the last 30 days, or continue the existing model on yesterday's orders only. It counts rows processed (rows × passes) and scores each model on the next day.

Python · step 2 · stateless retraining vs stateful training
stateless_auc, stateful_auc, rows_stateless, rows_stateful = [], [], 0, 0
history = {d: day(d) for d in range(0, 61)}
stateful = sgd().fit(np.vstack([history[d][0] for d in range(30)]), np.hstack([history[d][1] for d in range(30)]))
for d in range(30, 60):
    window = range(d - 29, d + 1)                        # stateless: last 30 days, from scratch, every day
    Xw = np.vstack([history[k][0] for k in window]); yw = np.hstack([history[k][1] for k in window])
    scratch = sgd().fit(Xw, yw); rows_stateless += len(yw) * scratch.n_iter_   # rows x passes over the data
    stateful.partial_fit(*history[d]); rows_stateful += len(history[d][1])   # stateful: yesterday only, one pass
    stateless_auc.append(auc(scratch, *history[d + 1])); stateful_auc.append(auc(stateful, *history[d + 1]))
print(f"stateless (30 days from scratch, daily): mean next-day AUC {np.mean(stateless_auc):.3f}, rows processed {rows_stateless:>9,}")
print(f"stateful  (yesterday only, daily):       mean next-day AUC {np.mean(stateful_auc):.3f}, rows processed {rows_stateful:>9,}")
print(f"compute ratio: {rows_stateless / rows_stateful:.0f}x less for stateful; it also never re-reads old orders")
Output
stateless (30 days from scratch, daily): mean next-day AUC 0.793, rows processed 23,940,000
stateful  (yesterday only, daily):       mean next-day AUC 0.813, rows processed    60,000
compute ratio: 399x less for stateful; it also never re-reads old orders
How to read it

Stateful training uses about 400 times less compute and still scores slightly better (0.813 vs 0.793): under steady drift, a 30-day window drags in stale patterns, while fine-tuning keeps nudging the model towards the present. Your ratio will differ, but the direction matches what Grubhub saw.

1.3

Why continual learning?

Play · A brand-new user, visit by visit

Sudden shifts. A big event on a usually quiet evening sends ride demand soaring; a model that can't react leaves riders waiting and drivers elsewhere.

Rare events. Black Friday or Singles Day happen once a year, so there's never enough history; learning during the day helps. Alibaba bought the team behind Apache Flink partly for this.

Continuous cold start. Not just new users, but users on a new device, users who aren't logged in, or who visit so rarely their history is stale. One search company found most shoppers on e-commerce sites visit fewer than three times a year. TikTok adapts to a new user within minutes.

Why not?Continual learning can do everything batch learning can, and more. The barrier is infrastructure, which is getting easier.
Code lab · Python

Adapt to a new user within one session

Step 3 simulates 5,000 new users with strong but unknown cuisine preferences. One recommender always suggests the most popular cuisine; the other starts there but updates after each dish the user opens.

Python · step 3 · continuous cold start: adapt within the session
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
CUISINES = ["biryani", "dosa", "pizza", "thali", "chinese", "desserts"]
popularity = np.array([0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05])
hits = {"most popular (no history)": np.zeros(8), "adapt within session": np.zeros(8)}
users = 5000
for u in range(users):
    taste = r.dirichlet(np.full(6, 0.4))                 # each new user has strong, unknown preferences
    counts = np.ones(6) * 0.5
    for step in range(8):
        choice = r.choice(6, p=taste)                    # what they actually want this time
        hits["most popular (no history)"][step] += choice == np.argmax(popularity)
        guess = np.argmax(counts + popularity)           # popularity as a prior, updated by this session
        hits["adapt within session"][step] += choice == guess
        counts[choice] += 1                              # learn from what they opened
for name, h in hits.items():
    print(f"{name:<26} hit rate at visit 1: {h[0] / users:.0%}   visit 3: {h[2] / users:.0%}   visit 8: {h[7] / users:.0%}")
Output
most popular (no history)  hit rate at visit 1: 16%   visit 3: 16%   visit 8: 16%
adapt within session       hit rate at visit 1: 16%   visit 3: 40%   visit 8: 50%
How to read it

On the first visit both are equally blind (16%). By the third pick, the adapting recommender is right 40% of the time and by the eighth, 50%, while "most popular" stays at 16% for ever. Learning within the session is how you serve users you know nothing about.

1.4

The fresh-data challenge

Play · How fast is a label ready?

To update hourly, you need new labelled data hourly. Pulling from a data warehouse is only as fast as data lands there; pulling from real-time transports (Kafka, Kinesis) is faster.

The best tasks have natural labels with short feedback loops: pricing, arrival times, ad clicks, recommendations. Even then, labels must be computed: a click at 10:33 p.m. has to be matched back to the recommendation that caused it. Doing that with stream processing gives labels in minutes; batch jobs add hours. Tools like Snorkel (programmatic labelling) or crowdsourcing can speed up labelling where there are no natural labels.

Code lab · Python

Compute labels by joining clicks to recommendations

Step 4 logs 6,000 recommendations and about 1,000 clicks over ten hours. Each click is matched to the latest recommendation of that dish to that user within 30 minutes (pandas.merge_asof); unmatched clicks are organic.

Python · step 4 · fresh data and label computation
r = np.random.default_rng(4)
recs = pd.DataFrame({"rec_id": range(6000), "user": r.integers(0, 800, 6000), "item": r.integers(0, 50, 6000),
                     "shown_at": np.sort(r.uniform(0, 600, 6000))})          # minutes since 10:00
clicked = recs.sample(frac=0.12, random_state=1)
clicks = pd.DataFrame({"user": clicked.user, "item": clicked.item,
                       "clicked_at": clicked.shown_at + r.exponential(4, len(clicked))})
organic = pd.DataFrame({"user": r.integers(0, 800, 300), "item": r.integers(0, 50, 300), "clicked_at": r.uniform(0, 600, 300)})
clicks = pd.concat([clicks, organic]).sort_values("clicked_at")

# Label computation: match each click to the latest recommendation of that item to that user, within 30 minutes
m = pd.merge_asof(clicks, recs.sort_values("shown_at"), left_on="clicked_at", right_on="shown_at",
                  by=["user", "item"], tolerance=30, direction="backward")
matched = m.dropna(subset=["rec_id"])
labels = recs.assign(label=recs.rec_id.isin(matched.rec_id).astype(int))
print(f"{len(clicks):,} click events; {len(matched):,} matched to a recommendation, {len(clicks) - len(matched):,} were organic")
print(f"labelled {len(labels):,} recommendations: {labels.label.mean():.1%} positive")
delay = matched.clicked_at - matched.shown_at
print(f"\nlabel ready after: stream processing ~{delay.median():.0f} min (as soon as the click arrives); "
      f"hourly batch job ~{delay.median() + 30:.0f} min on average; nightly warehouse job ~{delay.median() + 720:.0f} min")
Output
1,020 click events; 720 matched to a recommendation, 300 were organic
labelled 6,000 recommendations: 12.0% positive

label ready after: stream processing ~2 min (as soon as the click arrives); hourly batch job ~32 min on average; nightly warehouse job ~722 min
How to read it

720 clicks trace back to a recommendation and become positive labels; 300 were organic and must not be credited to the model. That leaves 6,000 labelled recommendations, 12% positive. With streaming, a label exists about 2 minutes after the click; an hourly batch adds about half an hour; a nightly warehouse job adds about 12 hours. That delay caps how fast the model can learn.

1.5

The evaluation and algorithm challenges

Play · Three challenges
Pick a challenge.

Evaluation is the biggest challenge: writing an update script is easy; making sure each update is safe isn't. More updates mean more chances to fail, and models that learn from live data can be manipulated: Microsoft's Tay chatbot was taught offensive language by trolls and pulled within 16 hours. Evaluation also takes time: one payments company needed about two weeks of traffic to see enough fraud to compare models, so it could only update fortnightly.

Algorithms are a softer challenge. Neural networks update on any batch size; matrix-factorisation and tree models usually need the whole dataset (incremental trees such as Hoeffding trees exist but are rare). Feature code needs care too: statistics like mean and variance must be computed online, not per batch.

Code lab · Python

Per-batch statistics vs running statistics

Step 5 streams skewed order values in batches of 64. It compares each batch's own mean with a StandardScaler updated by partial_fit, then scales one ₹300 order both ways.

Python · step 5 · the algorithm challenge: statistics on partial data
r = np.random.default_rng(5)
stream = r.lognormal(5, 1, 64 * 50)                      # order value in rupees: very skewed
batch_means, running_means = [], []
running = StandardScaler()
for b in range(50):
    chunk = stream[b * 64:(b + 1) * 64].reshape(-1, 1)
    batch_means.append(chunk.mean())
    running.partial_fit(chunk)                           # running statistics across all batches so far
    running_means.append(running.mean_[0])
print(f"true mean order value: ₹{stream.mean():.0f}")
print(f"per-batch means (64 orders each): ₹{min(batch_means):.0f} to ₹{max(batch_means):.0f}")
print(f"running mean after 10 batches ₹{running_means[9]:.0f}, after 50 batches ₹{running_means[-1]:.0f}")
z = [(300 - m) / s for m, s in [(np.mean(stream[b*64:(b+1)*64]), np.std(stream[b*64:(b+1)*64])) for b in range(50)]]
print(f"a ₹300 order scaled with per-batch stats becomes anything from {min(z):+.2f} to {max(z):+.2f}; "
      f"with running stats: {(300 - running.mean_[0]) / running.scale_[0]:+.2f}")
Output
true mean order value: ₹247
per-batch means (64 orders each): ₹186 to ₹327
running mean after 10 batches ₹240, after 50 batches ₹247
a ₹300 order scaled with per-batch stats becomes anything from -0.05 to +0.65; with running stats: +0.18
How to read it

The true average order is ₹247, but individual batches say anything from ₹186 to ₹327. Scale with per-batch statistics and the same ₹300 order becomes anything from −0.05 to +0.65 depending on which batch it arrived in: the model sees the same input as different values. Running statistics settle near the truth after ten batches and give one consistent value (+0.18).
