Book / Chapter 9 / Section 2
Section 2 of 4 · Summary

Four Stages of Continual Learning

Nobody starts with continual learning; teams grow into it. Stage 1: manual, stateless retraining, done when someone has time. Stage 2: a script retrains automatically on a schedule. Stage 3: the script fine-tunes from the last checkpoint instead of starting over. Stage 4: updates are triggered automatically by time, performance, data volume or drift, and the holy grail is models that keep learning on the device.

2.1Stages 1 and 22.2Stage 3: stateful2.3Stage 4: triggers
2.1

Stage 1, manual; stage 2, automated retraining

Play · The seven steps a retraining script automates

Stage 1. The team is busy building new models (fraud, recommendations, seller abuse, delivery time), so updates happen only when a model is doing harm and someone has time: every few months, or never. Each step is done by hand by different people, and changes made while retraining often never reach production. Most companies outside tech are here.

Stage 2. With 5–10 models live, maintenance becomes the priority, so a script runs the steps on a schedule (often chosen by gut feeling: "nightly seems right"). It needs a scheduler (Airflow, Argo), accessible data, and a model store that versions every artifact. Different models may need different schedules, and dependencies matter: when embeddings change, the ranking model that uses them must update too.

Log and waitReuse the features the prediction service already computed as training data: cheaper, and it guarantees training and serving features match.
Code lab · Python

A weekly retraining script with a gate and a model store

Step 6 automates pull, features, train, evaluate and deploy, and records each run in a minimal model store. Each new model must match the live model on the same fresh validation data. On the third run, an upstream column has gone blank.

Python · step 6 · stage 2: an automated retraining script with a model store
store = []                                              # the simplest model store: a list of versioned records

def retrain(run_day, window=14, corrupt=False):
    X = np.vstack([day(d)[0] for d in range(run_day - window, run_day)])       # 1. pull data
    y = np.hstack([day(d)[1] for d in range(run_day - window, run_day)])
    if corrupt:
        X[:, 0] = 0                                                            #    (an upstream column went blank)
    model = sgd().fit(X, y)                                                    # 2-5. features, labels, train
    Xv, yv = day(run_day, 3000, seed=9000 + run_day)
    score = auc(model, Xv, yv)                                                 # 6. evaluate, against the live
    live = next((s for s in reversed(store) if s["status"] == "live"), None)   #    model on the same fresh data
    live_score = auc(live["model"], Xv, yv) if live else 0
    ok = score >= live_score - 0.005
    for s in store:
        if ok and s["status"] == "live":
            s["status"] = "retired"
    store.append({"version": f"1.{len(store)}", "trained_on": f"days {run_day - window}-{run_day - 1}",
                  "auc": round(score, 3), "live_model_auc": round(live_score, 3) if live else None,
                  "status": "live" if ok else "blocked", "model": model})                     # 7. deploy (or not)

for run_day, corrupt in [(14, False), (21, False), (28, True), (35, False)]:
    retrain(run_day, corrupt=corrupt)
print(pd.DataFrame(store).drop(columns="model").to_string(index=False))
Output
version trained_on   auc  live_model_auc  status
    1.0  days 0-13 0.834             NaN retired
    1.1  days 7-20 0.815           0.811 retired
    1.2 days 14-27 0.736           0.773 blocked
    1.3 days 21-34 0.797           0.762    live
How to read it

Each run is compared with the live model on identical data, which matters: under drift, both scores fall over time, so comparing with an old score would wrongly block everything. Version 1.1 matches the live model and replaces it. Version 1.2, trained on the broken column, scores 0.736 against the live model's 0.773 and is blocked. Version 1.3 beats it and goes live. Every attempt stays in the store, so nothing is lost and everything can be audited.

2.2

Stage 3: automated, stateful training

Play · Pick a version, see where it came from

Why retrain on three months every day when you could continue from yesterday's checkpoint using just yesterday's data? Stage 3 changes the script to load the previous checkpoint and keep training. The biggest obstacle is habit: teams are used to handing over a freshly trained model each time.

The main new requirement is lineage: model 1.0 becomes 1.1, 1.2...; a new architecture starts 2.0, 2.1... To debug or reproduce any version, you need to know its base model and the data used at each step. The book notes no model store offered this at the time, so teams build it themselves. Pulling data from real-time transports may also mean upgrading the streaming pipeline.

Code lab · Python

A lineage register in a few lines

Step 7 records each version with its parent, the data used and how it was made, then walks back from any version to its origin.

Python · step 7 · stage 3: stateful training needs model lineage
lineage = {}
def register(version, parent, data, note=""):
    lineage[version] = {"parent": parent, "data": data, "note": note}

register("1.0", None, "orders Jan-Mar", "trained from scratch")
for i, wk in enumerate(["Apr wk1", "Apr wk2", "Apr wk3"], start=1):
    register(f"1.{i}", f"1.{i - 1}", f"orders {wk}", "fine-tuned")
register("2.0", None, "orders Jan-Apr", "new feature: delivery distance, from scratch")
register("2.1", "2.0", "orders May wk1", "fine-tuned")

def trace(v):
    chain = []
    while v:
        chain.append(f"{v} <- {lineage[v]['data']} ({lineage[v]['note']})")
        v = lineage[v]["parent"]
    return chain

print("how was model 1.3 made?")
print("\n".join("  " + c for c in trace("1.3")))
print("\nhow was model 2.1 made?")
print("\n".join("  " + c for c in trace("2.1")))
Output
how was model 1.3 made?
  1.3 <- orders Apr wk3 (fine-tuned)
  1.2 <- orders Apr wk2 (fine-tuned)
  1.1 <- orders Apr wk1 (fine-tuned)
  1.0 <- orders Jan-Mar (trained from scratch)

how was model 2.1 made?
  2.1 <- orders May wk1 (fine-tuned)
  2.0 <- orders Jan-Apr (new feature: delivery distance, from scratch)
How to read it

Model 1.3 is three fine-tunes on top of a January–March model; model 2.1 is one fine-tune on a model rebuilt from scratch when the delivery-distance feature was added (a model iteration). If 1.3 misbehaves, you can tell which week of data to inspect, and rebuild it exactly.

2.3

Stage 4: continual learning with triggers

Play · Four kinds of trigger

A fixed schedule is a guess: quiet weeks need fewer updates, busy weeks more. Stage 4 updates whenever it's needed, using a trigger: time (every five minutes), performance (accuracy drops), volume (labelled data grows 5%) or drift (a big distribution shift).

This needs solid monitoring (false alarms cause pointless updates) and a solid evaluation pipeline (Section 4). The holy grail: ship a model on a phone or watch that keeps adapting on the device, with no server cost and no user data leaving it.

Code lab · Python

Four triggers over 120 days with two sudden changes

Step 8 replays 120 days in which customer behaviour changes suddenly on days 40 and 85 (concept drift: same inputs, new meaning). Each policy retrains on the last week whenever its trigger fires: every 30 days, every 7 days, when AUC falls below 0.80, or when the prediction distribution shifts.

Python · step 8 · stage 4: what should trigger an update?
days = 120
shocks = {d: (1.0 if 40 <= d < 85 else 0.0) + (1.0 if d >= 85 else 0.0) for d in range(days + 1)}   # sudden changes on days 40 and 85
data = {d: day(d, 1500, shock=shocks[d]) for d in range(days + 1)}

def run(policy):
    m = sgd().fit(*data[0]); last, retrains, scores = 0, 0, []
    ref_pred = m.predict_proba(data[0][0])[:, 1]
    for d in range(1, days + 1):
        X, y = data[d]
        p = m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        scores.append(roc_auc_score(y, p))
        fire = {"every 30 days": d - last >= 30, "every 7 days": d - last >= 7,
                "when AUC drops": d > 1 and scores[-1] < 0.80,
                "when predictions drift": ks_2samp(ref_pred, p).statistic > 0.05}[policy]
        if fire:
            Xr = np.vstack([data[k][0] for k in range(max(0, d - 6), d + 1)])
            yr = np.hstack([data[k][1] for k in range(max(0, d - 6), d + 1)])
            m = sgd().fit(Xr, yr); last, retrains = d, retrains + 1
            ref_pred = m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    return np.mean(scores), retrains

for policy in ["every 30 days", "every 7 days", "when AUC drops", "when predictions drift"]:
    s, n = run(policy)
    print(f"{policy:<24} average AUC {s:.3f}   retrains {n:>3}")
Output
every 30 days            average AUC 0.833   retrains   4
every 7 days             average AUC 0.880   retrains  17
when AUC drops           average AUC 0.866   retrains  13
when predictions drift   average AUC 0.780   retrains   6
How to read it

Weekly retraining scores best here (0.880) with 17 retrains; the performance trigger comes close (0.866) with fewer retrains, but it needs labels. Monthly retraining lags (0.833). The drift trigger is a cautionary tale: these changes were concept drift, so inputs and predictions looked the same, and it fired 6 times on noise and missed the real changes (0.780). Choose triggers that can actually see the kind of change you expect.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1Continual LearningNEXT · SECTION 3How Often to Update
Book / Chapter 9 / Section 3
Section 3 of 4 · Summary

How Often to Update Your Models

The question every ML engineer asks. While updating is manual and slow, the answer is: as often as you can. Once it's automated, the answer depends on another question: how much better does fresh data make the model? Measure that, and weigh it against the other way to improve a model: changing the model itself.

3.1Value of data freshness3.2Model vs data iteration
3.1

The value of data freshness

Play · How stale is the training data?

To find out how much fresher data helps, train the same model on windows that end at different points in the past, and test them all on the most recent period. If a model trained on data from a quarter ago is much worse than one trained on last month's data, don't wait a quarter between updates.

In practice, run it in weeks, days or hours. In 2014, Facebook found that retraining ad click models daily instead of weekly cut loss by 1%, enough to switch. Some companies now retrain every few minutes.

Code lab · Python

Train on older or newer windows, test on the latest month

Step 9 trains on three months of orders ending 6, 3, 1 or 0 months before the test month, and scores each on the test month.

Python · step 9 · the value of data freshness
results = []
for months_old in [6, 3, 1, 0]:                          # train on 3 months of data ending this long before the test month
    end = 330 - months_old * 30
    X = np.vstack([day(d, 600)[0] for d in range(end - 90, end, 3)])
    y = np.hstack([day(d, 600)[1] for d in range(end - 90, end, 3)])
    m = sgd().fit(X, y)
    Xt = np.vstack([day(d, 600)[0] for d in range(330, 360, 3)]); yt = np.hstack([day(d, 600)[1] for d in range(330, 360, 3)])
    results.append((months_old, auc(m, Xt, yt)))
    print(f"training data ends {months_old} month(s) before the test month: AUC {results[-1][1]:.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
ax.plot([r[0] for r in results], [r[1] for r in results], "o-", color="#0E9466")
ax.set(xlabel="months between training data and test month", ylabel="AUC on the test month"); ax.invert_xaxis()
Output
training data ends 6 month(s) before the test month: AUC 0.924
training data ends 3 month(s) before the test month: AUC 0.988
training data ends 1 month(s) before the test month: AUC 0.991
training data ends 0 month(s) before the test month: AUC 0.992
How to read it

Data that ends six months back gives 0.924; three months back, 0.988; one month or none, about 0.99. Most of the value comes from not being months out of date; beyond that, extra freshness adds little on this task. So here, monthly updates would capture nearly all the gain, and daily ones would mostly add cost. Run the same experiment on your own data before choosing.

3.2

Model iteration vs data iteration

Play · Where to spend the next unit of effort?

Model iteration adds features or changes the architecture. Data iteration refreshes the same model with new data. You should do both from time to time, but resources spent on one can't go to the other.

If a new architecture needs 100 times the compute for a 1% gain, while refreshing on the last three hours of data needs 1 times the compute for the same 1%, iterate on data. If fresh data barely helps, look for a better model. No book can tell you which wins for your task: experiment.

Code lab · Python

A better model, fresher data, or both

Step 10 starts from a logistic regression trained on old orders, and compares: boosted trees on the same old data (model iteration), the same logistic regression on the last 30 days (data iteration), and both. It reports test AUC and training time.

Python · step 10 · model iteration vs data iteration
r = np.random.default_rng(10)
def orders(d, n):
    X, y = day(d, n)
    extra = (X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] > 0).astype(float)        # an interaction a better model could capture
    y = np.where(r.random(n) < 0.25, (extra > 0).astype(int), y)
    return X, y

X_old = np.vstack([orders(d, 400)[0] for d in range(0, 90)]); y_old = np.hstack([orders(d, 400)[1] for d in range(0, 90)])
X_new = np.vstack([orders(d, 400)[0] for d in range(150, 180)]); y_new = np.hstack([orders(d, 400)[1] for d in range(150, 180)])
X_test, y_test = orders(181, 6000)

def timed_fit(model, X, y):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); model.fit(X, y); return model, time.perf_counter() - t0

base, t_base = timed_fit(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X_old, y_old)
bigger, t_big = timed_fit(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=300, random_state=0), X_old, y_old)
fresh, t_fresh = timed_fit(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X_new, y_new)
both, t_both = timed_fit(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=300, random_state=0), X_new, y_new)
for name, m, t in [("current model, old data", base, t_base), ("model iteration: boosted trees, old data", bigger, t_big),
                   ("data iteration: same model, last 30 days", fresh, t_fresh), ("both", both, t_both)]:
    print(f"{name:<42} AUC {auc(m, X_test, y_test):.3f}   training time {t * 1000:6.0f} ms")
Output
current model, old data                    AUC 0.644   training time     16 ms
model iteration: boosted trees, old data   AUC 0.698   training time    755 ms
data iteration: same model, last 30 days   AUC 0.857   training time      4 ms
both                                       AUC 0.879   training time    867 ms
How to read it

Here, data iteration wins easily: refreshing the simple model jumps AUC from 0.644 to 0.857 and trains in milliseconds, while the bigger model on old data only reaches 0.698 at many times the cost. Combining both gives the best score (0.879), so the model upgrade isn't worthless; it just isn't the first thing to do on drifting data.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2Four StagesNEXT · SECTION 4Test in Production
Book / Chapter 9 / Section 4
Section 4 of 4 · Summary

Test in Production

Offline evaluation isn't enough when the data keeps changing. A fixed test set comes from the old distribution; a backtest on the latest data can be fooled by a pipeline bug. The only way to know how a model does in production is to try it there, carefully. Five techniques, roughly from safest to most data-efficient: shadow deployment, A/B testing, canary release, interleaving and bandits.

4.1Static tests and backtests4.2Shadow deployment4.3A/B testing4.4Canary release4.5Interleaving4.6Bandits
4.1

Static test sets and backtests

Play · Which test do you trust?

Static test splits must stay fixed so models can be compared fairly, but after a model adapts to new data, a test set from the old distribution says little.

A backtest evaluates on recent data the model hasn't seen, such as the last hour. That's closer to reality, but if the last hour is corrupted by a pipeline bug, the backtest is corrupted too. Use both: the static set as a trusted sanity check, the backtest for recency. And even a good backtest doesn't promise good performance tomorrow.

Code lab · Python

A challenger that only looks good on broken data

Step 11 has a pipeline bug that flips the sign of one feature. A challenger is trained on that broken data; the champion was trained before the bug. Both are scored on the (equally broken) last hour and on a trusted static test set.

Python · step 11 · static test sets and backtests
X_static, y_static = day(50, 5000, seed=777)            # a static, well-studied test set
X_hour, y_hour = day(60, 3000, seed=778)
X_hour_bad = X_hour.copy(); X_hour_bad[:, 2] *= -1       # last hour: a pipeline bug flipped a feature's sign
champ = sgd().fit(*day(58, 8000))
X_tr_bad, y_tr = day(59, 8000); X_tr_bad = X_tr_bad.copy(); X_tr_bad[:, 2] *= -1
chall = sgd().fit(X_tr_bad, y_tr)                        # challenger trained on the same broken pipeline
for name, m in [("champion", champ), ("challenger (trained on broken data)", chall)]:
    print(f"{name:<36} backtest on last hour {auc(m, X_hour_bad, y_hour):.3f}   static test set {auc(m, X_static, y_static):.3f}")
Output
champion                             backtest on last hour 0.688   static test set 0.815
challenger (trained on broken data)  backtest on last hour 0.809   static test set 0.699
How to read it

On the backtest, the challenger looks like a big win: 0.809 against the champion's 0.688. Promote it on that evidence and you'd ship a model trained on a bug. The static test set tells the truth: the champion scores 0.815, the challenger 0.699. Pair every backtest with a trusted static set.

4.2

Shadow deployment

Play · Requests flow to both models

Possibly the safest way to deploy. Run the candidate alongside the live model; send every request to both; serve only the live model's answer; log the candidate's. Replace the live model only once the candidate's logged predictions look good.

Users are never exposed to the candidate, so the risk is no higher than today. The cost: every request is predicted twice, roughly doubling inference compute.

Code lab · Python

Log a shadow model's decisions

Step 12 serves 4,000 requests from the champion while a candidate trained a day later runs in shadow. When labels arrive, both are scored.

Python · step 12 · shadow deployment
r = np.random.default_rng(12)
Xs, ys = day(61, 4000, seed=1201)
champ = sgd().fit(*day(59, 8000)); cand = sgd().fit(*day(60, 8000))
served = champ.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1]                   # users only ever see these
shadow = cand.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1]                    # logged, never served
log = pd.DataFrame({"served": served >= 0.5, "shadow": shadow >= 0.5, "label": ys})
print(f"requests: {len(log):,}; model calls: {2 * len(log):,} (inference cost doubled)")
print(f"decisions where the two models disagree: {(log.served != log.shadow).mean():.1%}")
print(f"once labels arrive: champion accuracy {(log.served == log.label).mean():.3f}, shadow candidate {(log.shadow == log.label).mean():.3f}")
print("users affected by the candidate's mistakes: 0")
Output
requests: 4,000; model calls: 8,000 (inference cost doubled)
decisions where the two models disagree: 7.0%
once labels arrive: champion accuracy 0.747, shadow candidate 0.750
users affected by the candidate's mistakes: 0
How to read it

The models disagree on 7% of decisions, which is exactly where to look closely. Once labels arrive, the shadow candidate is very slightly more accurate (0.750 vs 0.747). No user saw any of its mistakes, at the price of 8,000 model calls instead of 4,000. A difference this small would need a proper test before switching, which is where A/B tests come in.

4.3

A/B testing

Play · How many users do you need?

The most common online test: send a share of traffic to the candidate, the rest to the live model, and compare. Microsoft and Google each ran over 10,000 A/B tests a year by 2017. When the models affect each other (prices change driver supply, for example), alternate them by day instead of running them side by side.

Two essentials. Randomise: if phone users get A and desktop users get B, you're comparing devices, not models. And use enough samples to reach statistical significance. Even then, a significant result can occasionally point the wrong way, and a non-significant one may simply mean the models are about equally good. Tests can have more than two arms (A/B/C/D).

Code lab · Python

Biased routing, and how big a test needs to be

Step 13 routes two identical models by device, then at random. Then a candidate that truly converts 5% better (10.5% vs 10.0%) is tested 1,000 times at three sizes.

Python · step 13 · A/B testing: randomise, and get enough samples
r = np.random.default_rng(13)
n = 20_000
desktop = r.random(n) < 0.4
conv = r.random(n) < np.where(desktop, 0.12, 0.07)       # desktop users order more, whichever model they get
biased = np.where(desktop, "B", "A")                     # routing by device: not random
random_arm = np.where(r.random(n) < 0.5, "B", "A")
for name, arm in [("routed by device", biased), ("routed at random", random_arm)]:
    a, b = conv[arm == "A"].mean(), conv[arm == "B"].mean()
    print(f"{name:<17} A {a:.2%}  B {b:.2%}  -> B looks {b / a - 1:+.0%} better (the models are identical)")

def ab_once(n_per_arm, pa=0.100, pb=0.105):
    ca, cb = r.binomial(n_per_arm, pa), r.binomial(n_per_arm, pb)
    p1, p2 = ca / n_per_arm, cb / n_per_arm; pp = (ca + cb) / (2 * n_per_arm)
    z = (p2 - p1) / np.sqrt(pp * (1 - pp) * 2 / n_per_arm)
    return z
print("\nB truly converts 5% better (10.5% vs 10.0%). 1,000 repeated experiments:")
for n_arm in [2_000, 20_000, 120_000]:
    zs = np.array([ab_once(n_arm) for _ in range(1000)])
    print(f"  {n_arm:>7,} users per arm: significant win for B {np.mean(zs > 1.96):5.1%}   A looks better {np.mean(zs < 0):5.1%}")
Output
routed by device  A 6.85%  B 11.96%  -> B looks +75% better (the models are identical)
routed at random  A 8.73%  B 9.14%  -> B looks +5% better (the models are identical)

B truly converts 5% better (10.5% vs 10.0%). 1,000 repeated experiments:
    2,000 users per arm: significant win for B  6.8%   A looks better 28.9%
   20,000 users per arm: significant win for B 35.1%   A looks better  5.4%
  120,000 users per arm: significant win for B 97.8%   A looks better  0.0%
How to read it

Route by device and an identical model looks 75% better, because desktop users simply order more. Random routing removes that bias; the remaining +5% is noise, which is why significance tests exist. For a real 5% uplift, 2,000 users per arm almost never reaches significance and picks the worse model 29% of the time; 20,000 per arm finds it a third of the time; 120,000 per arm finds it 98% of the time. Small effects need big tests.

4.4

Canary release

Play · Roll out step by step

Named after the canaries miners carried to detect gas. Deploy the candidate (the canary) next to the live model, send it a small share of traffic, and if its key metrics hold up, increase the share; if they degrade, abort and send everyone back to the live model. Stop when the canary serves everyone, or when it's aborted.

A canary can be used to run an A/B test, but it doesn't have to be random: you might first roll out to a less critical market. Netflix and Google have described automating this canary analysis.

Code lab · Python

A canary with an automatic abort

Step 14 rolls a candidate out at 1%, 5%, 25%, 50% and 100% of traffic, comparing its error rate with the champion's at each stage and aborting if it's significantly worse. It tries a good candidate and a bad one.

Python · step 14 · canary release with automatic abort
def canary(cand_error, champ_error=0.050, stages=(0.01, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0), users=200_000, seed=14):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed); exposed = 0
    for share in stages:
        n_c = int(users * share * 0.1)                   # observe a tenth of a day's traffic at each stage
        e_c = r.binomial(n_c, cand_error) / n_c
        e_h = r.binomial(n_c * 5, champ_error) / (n_c * 5)
        exposed += n_c
        z = (e_c - e_h) / np.sqrt(e_h * (1 - e_h) * (1 / n_c + 1 / (5 * n_c)))
        status = "abort" if z > 2.5 else "continue"
        print(f"  {share:>5.0%} of traffic: canary error {e_c:.3f} vs champion {e_h:.3f} -> {status}")
        if status == "abort":
            return f"rolled back; {exposed:,} users saw the canary"
    return f"canary now serves everyone ({exposed:,} users observed on the way)"
print("good candidate (error 4.8%):"); print("  " + canary(0.048))
print("bad candidate (error 7.5%):");  print("  " + canary(0.075))
Output
good candidate (error 4.8%):
     1% of traffic: canary error 0.060 vs champion 0.051 -> continue
     5% of traffic: canary error 0.036 vs champion 0.050 -> continue
    25% of traffic: canary error 0.045 vs champion 0.050 -> continue
    50% of traffic: canary error 0.046 vs champion 0.051 -> continue
   100% of traffic: canary error 0.049 vs champion 0.050 -> continue
  canary now serves everyone (36,200 users observed on the way)
bad candidate (error 7.5%):
     1% of traffic: canary error 0.095 vs champion 0.051 -> abort
  rolled back; 200 users saw the canary
How to read it

The good candidate (true error 4.8%) wobbles at the tiny first stage (6.0% on 200 users) but isn't significantly worse, so it continues and ends up serving everyone. The bad candidate (7.5% error) is caught at the very first stage and rolled back after only 200 users saw it. The early stages trade a little speed for a small blast radius.

4.5

Interleaving experiments

Play · Team draft: build one list from two rankings

Each slot: a coin decides which model picks next; it takes its best dish not already chosen.

With an A/B test, each user sees one model's recommendations. With interleaving, each user sees a single list mixing both models' picks, and whichever model's picks get more clicks wins that user. Netflix found interleaving reliably identifies the better algorithm with far fewer users than A/B testing.

Position matters (top slots get more clicks), so each position must be equally likely to come from either model. Team-draft interleaving does this like picking sides for a game. One caveat: interleaving measures user preference, which doesn't guarantee better core business metrics.

Code lab · Python

Interleaving vs A/B: how often each finds the better model

Step 15 simulates users whose activity varies a lot (most click little, a few click a lot). Model B ranks dishes better than A. For several numbers of user sessions, it repeats each experiment 150 times and counts how often each method finds B significantly better.

Python · step 15 · interleaving with team draft
r = np.random.default_rng(15)
N_ITEMS, K = 40, 6
POS = 1 / np.log2(np.arange(2, K + 2))                   # people click higher positions more

def team_draft(rank_a, rank_b):
    shown, from_a, ia, ib = [], [], 0, 0
    while len(shown) < K:                                # for each slot a coin decides which model picks next
        pick_a = r.random() < 0.5
        src, i = (rank_a, ia) if pick_a else (rank_b, ib)
        while src[i] in shown:
            i += 1
        shown.append(src[i]); from_a.append(pick_a)
        ia, ib = (i + 1, ib) if pick_a else (ia, i + 1)
    return np.array(shown), np.array(from_a)

def experiment(sessions):
    ab_a, ab_b, prefs = [], [], []
    for s in range(sessions):
        activity = min(r.lognormal(-1.2, 1.0), 2.5)      # some users click a lot, most hardly at all
        rel = r.uniform(0, 0.4, N_ITEMS)                 # how much this user would like each dish
        rank_a = np.argsort(-(rel + r.normal(0, 0.25, N_ITEMS)))   # model A: noisier ranking
        rank_b = np.argsort(-(rel + r.normal(0, 0.05, N_ITEMS)))   # model B: better ranking
        click = lambda items: r.random(len(items)) < np.minimum(activity * rel[items] * POS[:len(items)], 1)
        # A/B: this user sees only one model's list
        (ab_a if s % 2 == 0 else ab_b).append(click((rank_a if s % 2 == 0 else rank_b)[:K]).sum())
        # interleaving: this user sees one merged list; whose picks got more clicks?
        items, from_a = team_draft(rank_a, rank_b)
        c = click(items)
        prefs.append(np.sign(c[~from_a].sum() - c[from_a].sum()))
    a, b = np.array(ab_a), np.array(ab_b)
    z_ab = (b.mean() - a.mean()) / np.sqrt(a.var() / len(a) + b.var() / len(b) + 1e-12)
    p = np.array(prefs); p = p[p != 0]
    z_il = p.sum() / np.sqrt(max(len(p), 1))
    return z_ab > 1.96, z_il > 1.96

for sessions in [200, 600, 2000]:
    res = np.array([experiment(sessions) for _ in range(150)])
    print(f"{sessions:>5} sessions: A/B test finds B better {res[:, 0].mean():5.0%} of the time; interleaving {res[:, 1].mean():5.0%}")
Output
  200 sessions: A/B test finds B better   17% of the time; interleaving   29%
  600 sessions: A/B test finds B better   39% of the time; interleaving   54%
 2000 sessions: A/B test finds B better   90% of the time; interleaving   99%
How to read it

With 200 sessions, interleaving finds the better model 29% of the time vs 17% for A/B; with 600, 54% vs 39%; with 2,000, 99% vs 90%. The gain comes from comparing both models within the same user: differences between heavy and light users cancel out, while an A/B test has to average them away with more traffic.

4.6

Bandits

Play · Thompson sampling, live

A one-armed bandit is a slot machine. With several machines of unknown payout, a multi-armed bandit balances exploiting the best so far with exploring the others. Treat each candidate model as an arm: route more traffic to the ones doing well while still learning. In one experiment, A/B testing needed over 630,000 samples for a confident answer while Thompson sampling found a 5% better model with under 12,000.

Methods: ε-greedy (mostly the best, sometimes random), Thompson sampling (pick each arm with the probability it's the best) and UCB (an optimism bonus for uncertain arms). Bandits need online predictions, short feedback loops and machinery to track payoffs, so they're mostly used at big tech firms. Contextual bandits apply the same idea to which items to show, the cure for the feedback loops of Chapter 8.

Who runs the tests?Evaluation shouldn't be ad hoc by whoever built the model. Define the tests, their order and pass thresholds as an automated pipeline, like CI/CD for software.
Code lab · Python

A/B/C split vs ε-greedy vs Thompson sampling

Step 16 has three candidate models converting at 10.0%, 10.5% and 11.0%, and 30,000 users to serve. It averages five runs of each policy and compares orders won and traffic sent to the best model.

Python · step 16 · bandits: test while serving
TRUE = np.array([0.100, 0.105, 0.110])                   # three candidate models' true conversion rates
def ab_split(n, r):
    arms = r.integers(0, 3, n); conv = r.random(n) < TRUE[arms]
    return conv.sum(), np.bincount(arms, minlength=3)
def eps_greedy(n, r, eps=0.1):
    s, c = np.ones(3), np.full(3, 2.0); total = 0; pulls = np.zeros(3)
    for _ in range(n):
        a = r.integers(3) if r.random() < eps else np.argmax(s / c)
        x = r.random() < TRUE[a]; s[a] += x; c[a] += 1; total += x; pulls[a] += 1
    return total, pulls
def thompson(n, r):
    alpha, beta = np.ones(3), np.ones(3); total = 0; pulls = np.zeros(3)
    for _ in range(n):
        a = np.argmax(r.beta(alpha, beta))               # pick by the chance each model is the best
        x = r.random() < TRUE[a]; alpha[a] += x; beta[a] += 1 - x; total += x; pulls[a] += 1
    return total, pulls

n = 30_000
for name, f in [("A/B/C split (equal thirds)", ab_split), ("epsilon-greedy (10% explore)", eps_greedy), ("Thompson sampling", thompson)]:
    tots, shares = [], []
    for seed in range(5):
        t, p = f(n, np.random.default_rng(seed)); tots.append(t); shares.append(p[2] / n)
    print(f"{name:<29} orders {np.mean(tots):7,.0f}   traffic to the best model {np.mean(shares):5.0%}")
print(f"{'always the best (hindsight)':<29} orders {n * TRUE.max():7,.0f}")
Output
A/B/C split (equal thirds)    orders   3,179   traffic to the best model   33%
epsilon-greedy (10% explore)  orders   3,260   traffic to the best model   52%
Thompson sampling             orders   3,223   traffic to the best model   74%
always the best (hindsight)   orders   3,300
How to read it

An equal split sends only a third of users to the best model and wins the fewest orders (3,179). Thompson sampling sends 74% of all its traffic to the best model, learning the answer with far less traffic spent on weaker models. ε-greedy happens to win slightly more orders here (3,260 vs 3,223) because it commits early, but it sends only half its traffic to the best model and, with less luck, can commit to the wrong one. Both beat an equal split, the hidden cost of a plain A/B test.

Book / Chapter 9 / Recap
Chapter 9 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Continual learning lets models keep up with a changing world, and it's mostly an infrastructure problem: fresh data, fast labels, safe evaluation. Training can run in batch, but online evaluation needs streaming, and streaming tools have matured fast. Decide how often to update by measuring the value of fresh data, and never ship an update without testing it, ideally on live traffic. Next: the infrastructure and tooling that make all of this possible.

Eight takeaways

In our words.

1. Update a copyThe challenger replaces the champion only if it proves better.
2. Fine-tune when you canStateful updates use far less data and compute than training from scratch.
3. Labels set the paceNatural labels with short feedback loops, computed by streaming.
4. Running statisticsScale features with statistics that don't jump between batches.
5. Automate, then triggerScript retraining, add lineage, then update on the signals that matter.
6. Measure freshnessTrain on older vs newer windows to decide how often to update.
7. Backtest and sanity-checkRecent data plus a trusted static test set.
8. Test live, safelyShadow, randomised A/B, canary, interleaving, bandits, as an automated pipeline.

Quick quiz

0 / 7

Book / Chapter 10
Chapter 10 · Broad summary

Infrastructure and Tooling for MLOps

Many data scientists know the right thing to do but can't, because their infrastructure won't let them. Good infrastructure automates work, cuts bugs and makes new use cases possible; bad infrastructure is painful and expensive to replace. Needs vary: a one-off analysis needs only a notebook, Google-scale search needs custom everything, and most companies sit in between, at "reasonable scale" (gigabytes to terabytes a day). This chapter walks up four layers: storage and compute, the development environment, resource management, and the ML platform, then asks what to build and what to buy.

The chapter in one minute

  1. Storage and compute. Storage is cheap and commoditised. A compute unit is defined by its memory and its speed; real utilisation is far below advertised FLOPS. The cloud suits bursty, early-stage work, but costs can push large companies back to their own data centres.
  2. Dev environment. Where engineers spend their days, so the best single place to invest. Notebooks are powerful but stateful. Standardise packages, Python versions and even machines (cloud dev environments). Containers carry the environment from dev to production.
  3. Resource management. ML jobs repeat and depend on each other. Cron runs jobs on a timer; schedulers handle dependencies (DAGs), retries and resources; orchestrators find the machines. Airflow, Argo, Prefect, Kubeflow and Metaflow manage whole workflows.
  4. ML platform. Shared tools across ML teams: model deployment, a model store that tracks every artifact, and a feature store for sharing, computing and serving features consistently. Whether to build or buy depends on your stage, your focus and how mature the tools are.

Sections

Each section has its own summary, sub-sections and code labs.

  • FLOPS and utilisation
  • Cloud vs data centre

Where the work actually happens.

Shared tools for every ML team.

Book / Chapter 10 / Section 1
Section 1 of 4 · Summary

Storage and Compute

The storage layer is where data lives: a disk, Amazon S3, Snowflake, on-premises or in the cloud. It's now so cheap that most companies keep everything (Chapter 3 covers it). The compute layer is the engine that runs jobs: a CPU core, a GPU, or slices of cloud machines, from short-lived serverless units to long-running instances. Engines like Spark and Ray think in "jobs"; Kubernetes thinks in "pods", wrappers around containers.

1.1Memory and speed1.2FLOPS and utilisation1.3Cloud vs data centre
1.1

A compute unit is memory plus speed

Play · Does the data fit?

To run a job, data must first be loaded into the compute unit's memory, then operated on. So a compute unit is mostly described by two things: how much memory it has (8 GB holds more than 2 GB, and costs more) and how fast it runs operations. Some providers also advertise how quickly data moves in and out of memory (I/O bandwidth).

If the data doesn't fit, the job is impossible, unless you use an out-of-core algorithm that processes it in pieces.

Code lab · Python

Process 1.6 GB of data with 8 MB of memory

Step 1 computes the mean and spread of 200 million order values by streaming them in 1-million-row chunks and keeping running totals, instead of loading everything at once.

Python · step 0 · setup
import time, json, hashlib, itertools, warnings
from collections import deque, defaultdict
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 110)
print("numpy", np.__version__, "| pandas", pd.__version__)
Output
numpy 1.26.4 | pandas 2.0.3
Python · step 1 · a compute unit is memory plus speed
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
rows, chunk = 200_000_000, 1_000_000
print(f"{rows:,} order values as float64 need {rows * 8 / 1e9:.2f} GB in memory at once")

# Out-of-core: stream the data in 1M-row chunks and keep running totals (never more than 8 MB loaded)
total, total_sq, n = 0.0, 0.0, 0
for i in range(rows // chunk):
    block = r.lognormal(5, 1, chunk)                       # stand-in for reading one file from storage
    total += block.sum(); total_sq += (block ** 2).sum(); n += len(block)
mean = total / n
std = np.sqrt(total_sq / n - mean ** 2)
print(f"streamed in {rows // chunk} chunks of {chunk * 8 / 1e6:.0f} MB: mean ₹{mean:.1f}, std ₹{std:.1f}")
print(f"peak memory for the data: {chunk * 8 / 1e6:.0f} MB instead of {rows * 8 / 1e6:,.0f} MB")
Output
200,000,000 order values as float64 need 1.60 GB in memory at once
streamed in 200 chunks of 8 MB: mean ₹244.7, std ₹320.8
peak memory for the data: 8 MB instead of 1,600 MB
How to read it

The full array would need 1.6 GB of memory. Streaming it needs only one 8 MB chunk at a time, and gives the same mean (₹244.7) and spread. This is how tools handle data bigger than memory, at the cost of reading through it in a single pass and being careful about which statistics can be combined chunk by chunk.

1.2

FLOPS and utilisation

Play · Advertised vs achieved

An illustrative accelerator advertised at 100 TFLOPS, running a 1-exaFLOP training job.

Speed is usually quoted in FLOPS, floating-point operations per second; vendors advertise teraFLOPS. The number is contentious: vendors count operations differently (does a fused operation count once or twice?), and a chip that can do a trillion FLOPS rarely does.

Utilisation is the share of that capacity a job actually uses. 100% is near impossible; whether 50% is good depends on hardware and workload, and on how fast data can be fed in. Benchmarks such as MLPerf (training ResNet-50 on ImageNet, for example) are more useful. Most people simply compare cores and memory, remembering that an AWS vCPU is roughly half a physical core.

Code lab · Python

Measure your own machine's FLOPS

Step 2 times matrix multiplications of growing size (about 2n³ operations each) and reports the GFLOPS achieved, compared with the best this machine managed.

Python · step 2 · FLOPS and utilisation
def gflops(n, reps=3):
    a, b = np.random.rand(n, n).astype(np.float32), np.random.rand(n, n).astype(np.float32)
    best = min((lambda t0: (a @ b, time.perf_counter() - t0)[1])(time.perf_counter()) for _ in range(reps))
    return 2 * n ** 3 / best / 1e9                         # a matrix multiply does about 2n³ operations

results = {n: gflops(n) for n in [32, 128, 512, 2048]}
peak = max(results.values())
for n, g in results.items():
    print(f"{n:>5} x {n:<5} matrix multiply: {g:7.1f} GFLOPS   ({g / peak:5.1%} of the best this machine reached)")
print("\nsame chip, same operation: small jobs can't keep the hardware busy")
Output
   32 x 32    matrix multiply:    35.0 GFLOPS   (12.3% of the best this machine reached)
  128 x 128   matrix multiply:   137.1 GFLOPS   (48.1% of the best this machine reached)
  512 x 512   matrix multiply:   149.1 GFLOPS   (52.3% of the best this machine reached)
 2048 x 2048  matrix multiply:   285.3 GFLOPS   (100.0% of the best this machine reached)

same chip, same operation: small jobs can't keep the hardware busy
How to read it

The same chip doing the same operation reaches very different speeds: small multiplications use only a small fraction of what the largest one achieves, because overheads and data movement dominate. Exact numbers vary by machine and run. The lesson: a FLOPS figure tells you the ceiling, not what your workload will get. Benchmark your own jobs.

1.3

Public cloud vs private data centres

Play · Steady workload size

Compute is commoditised: pay a cloud provider for exactly what you use. That's ideal for bursty ML work, such as weeks of experiments followed by steadier production. The cloud is elastic, not infinite: providers impose limits, and cheap spot instances can vanish. By 2020, enterprise cloud spending was growing about 35% a year while data-centre spending fell.

As companies grow, though, cloud bills can reach about half their cost of revenue. Some move workloads back to their own data centres (cloud repatriation): Dropbox saved about $75 million over two years before its IPO. Repatriation is hard, so many choose a hybrid. Others end up multicloud, usually by accident (acquisitions, separate teams, investors' clouds) rather than by design.

Code lab · Python

A rough cost model: bursty and steady workloads

Step 3 uses illustrative prices (a cloud core-hour vs owned cores with up-front and running costs, plus a small team to run a data centre) for a bursty team and for steady workloads of growing size.

Python · step 3 · public cloud vs your own data centre
# Illustrative prices: cloud core-hour $0.05; an owned core costs $350 up front + $120/year to run, lasting 3 years
cloud_rate, own_capex, own_opex, life = 0.05, 350, 120, 3
def cloud_cost(core_hours): return core_hours * cloud_rate
def own_cost(peak_cores): return peak_cores * (own_capex / life + own_opex)

bursty = 10 * 24 * 364 + 1000 * 24 * 1                     # 10 cores all year, 1,000 cores for one day
print(f"bursty team (10 cores, 1,000 for one day): cloud ${cloud_cost(bursty):>9,.0f}/yr vs own ${own_cost(1000):>9,.0f}/yr")
print()
for cores in [50, 200, 1000, 5000]:                        # steady workloads of growing size
    c, o = cloud_cost(cores * 24 * 365), own_cost(cores * 1.2) + 150_000   # 20% headroom + a small infra team
    print(f"steady {cores:>5} cores: cloud ${c:>11,.0f}/yr   own data centre ${o:>11,.0f}/yr   -> {'cloud' if c < o else 'own'} is cheaper")
Output
bursty team (10 cores, 1,000 for one day): cloud $    5,568/yr vs own $  236,667/yr

steady    50 cores: cloud $     21,900/yr   own data centre $    164,200/yr   -> cloud is cheaper
steady   200 cores: cloud $     87,600/yr   own data centre $    206,800/yr   -> cloud is cheaper
steady  1000 cores: cloud $    438,000/yr   own data centre $    434,000/yr   -> own is cheaper
steady  5000 cores: cloud $  2,190,000/yr   own data centre $  1,570,000/yr   -> own is cheaper
How to read it

For the bursty team (10 cores all year, 1,000 for one day), the cloud costs about $5,600 a year; owning enough machines for the peak would cost over $230,000. For steady workloads, the cloud wins while small, but somewhere around 1,000 cores running all year, owning becomes cheaper, and at 5,000 cores it saves over $600,000 a year. Your prices will differ; the shape of the trade-off won't.

Book / Chapter 10 / Section 2
Section 2 of 4 · Summary

The Development Environment

The dev environment is where engineers write code, run experiments, and reach the production environment where champion models run and challengers are tested. It includes the IDE, versioning (Git for code, DVC for data, experiment trackers, MLflow for model artifacts) and CI/CD. Outside a few tech companies it's badly under-invested. As one infrastructure author put it, if you can set up only one piece of infrastructure well, make it the dev environment: improvements there go straight into productivity.

2.1IDEs and notebooks2.2Standardise it2.3Containers
2.1

IDEs and notebooks

Play · Run the cells in any order

IDEs can be native apps (VS Code, Vim) or run in the browser. Data scientists also live in notebooks (Jupyter, Colab), which mix code with charts and tables, ideal for exploration.

Notebooks are stateful: data loaded once stays in memory, and if step 4 fails you rerun only step 4. That same statefulness lets cells run out of order, which makes notebooks hard to reproduce. Tools help: Netflix's Papermill runs one notebook with many parameter sets, Commuter shares notebooks across a company, and nbdev keeps docs and tests beside the code.

Code lab · Python

One notebook, three answers

Step 4 has three cells: set prices, add 18% GST, sum. It runs them in three different orders in a shared namespace, just as a notebook kernel would.

Python · step 4 · notebooks are stateful: order matters
cells = {
    1: "prices = [100, 250, 400]",
    2: "prices = [p * 1.18 for p in prices]      # add 18% GST",
    3: "total = sum(prices)",
}
for order in [(1, 2, 3), (1, 2, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2)]:
    ns = {}
    for c in order:
        exec(cells[c], ns)
    print(f"run cells {'-'.join(map(str, order)):<9} -> total = {ns['total']:.2f}")
print("\nsame notebook, three answers: the right one depends on an order nobody wrote down")
Output
run cells 1-2-3     -> total = 885.00
run cells 1-2-2-3   -> total = 1044.30
run cells 1-3-2     -> total = 750.00

same notebook, three answers: the right one depends on an order nobody wrote down
How to read it

In order, the total is ₹885. Run the GST cell twice and it's ₹1,044.30 (tax applied twice). Run the sum before the tax and it's ₹750. Nothing errors in any of these. That's why notebooks used for production work need a clear run order, or a "restart and run all" before results are trusted.

2.2

Standardise the dev environment

Play · Three steps to "works on my machine"

The book's own startup story: first, unpinned packages meant code ran on one laptop and not another, so they pinned versions. Then a bug appeared only on Python 3.8, so they standardised the Python version. Then a new laptop with a new chip couldn't run their tools, so they moved to a cloud dev environment: everyone on the same machine type.

Most people keep a local IDE (often VS Code) connected over SSH. Cloud dev environments make IT support easier, help remote work, help security (revoke a stolen laptop's access), and shrink the gap between dev and a cloud production environment. Costs are modest: a 4-vCPU, 8 GB instance was about $0.10 an hour, and tools auto-stop idle machines. Some companies can't, for security reasons.

Code lab · Python

Diff two laptops, then pin everything

Step 5 compares two engineers' environments, fingerprints each with a hash, and writes a pinned requirements list for the team.

Python · step 5 · standardise the dev environment
laptop_a = {"python": "3.8.10", "numpy": "1.21.6", "pandas": "1.3.5", "scikit-learn": "1.0.2", "torch": "1.10.0"}
laptop_b = {"python": "3.9.13", "numpy": "1.21.6", "pandas": "1.4.2", "scikit-learn": "1.0.2", "torch": "1.12.1"}
diff = pd.DataFrame({"engineer A": laptop_a, "engineer B": laptop_b})
diff["same?"] = np.where(diff["engineer A"] == diff["engineer B"], "yes", "NO")
print(diff.to_string())

def env_hash(spec):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(spec, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
print(f"\nenvironment fingerprint A {env_hash(laptop_a)}  B {env_hash(laptop_b)}")
print("pinned requirements.txt for everyone:")
print("\n".join(f"  {k}=={v}" for k, v in laptop_a.items() if k != "python"))
Output
             engineer A engineer B same?
python           3.8.10     3.9.13    NO
numpy            1.21.6     1.21.6   yes
pandas            1.3.5      1.4.2    NO
scikit-learn      1.0.2      1.0.2   yes
torch            1.10.0     1.12.1    NO

environment fingerprint A b645b58ecdca  B 9c3aeb25b45d
pinned requirements.txt for everyone:
  numpy==1.21.6
  pandas==1.3.5
  scikit-learn==1.0.2
  torch==1.10.0
How to read it

Three of five components differ, including the Python version, so the two fingerprints differ too: these machines can produce different results from the same code. A pinned requirements file (plus one Python version, and ideally one machine image) makes the fingerprints match. Comparing fingerprints is a cheap first check when a bug won't reproduce.

2.3

From dev to prod: containers

Play · Change one thing, see what rebuilds

Production runs on many instances that come and go with traffic (a celebrity mention can bring a 10-fold spike), and each new one needs the same environment. A Dockerfile lists the steps to recreate it. Building it gives an image (the mould); running an image gives a container. Images can build on others (say, an NVIDIA image with GPU libraries) and are shared through registries such as Docker Hub or AWS ECR.

Real apps need several containers: featurising on cheap CPU machines, training on GPUs, or steps with clashing dependencies. Managing many is container orchestration: Docker Compose on one host, Kubernetes (K8s) across many, which scales containers up and down and keeps services available, though it's not friendly to data scientists.

Code lab · Python

How Docker's layer cache decides what to rebuild

Step 6 models a five-line Dockerfile. Docker reuses cached layers until it meets the first one whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. It tries a code change, a requirements change, and a badly ordered Dockerfile.

Python · step 6 · containers: image layers and the build cache
dockerfile = [
    ("FROM python:3.10-slim", "base"),
    ("COPY requirements.txt .", "requirements"),
    ("RUN pip install -r requirements.txt", "requirements"),
    ("COPY model.joblib .", "model"),
    ("COPY app.py .", "code"),
]
def rebuild(changed, layers):
    """Docker reuses cached layers until the first changed one; everything after it is rebuilt."""
    out, dirty = [], False
    for cmd, depends in layers:
        dirty = dirty or depends in changed
        out.append((cmd, "rebuild" if dirty else "cached"))
    return out

for change in [{"code"}, {"requirements"}]:
    print(f"you changed: {', '.join(change)}")
    for cmd, status in rebuild(change, dockerfile):
        print(f"  {status:<8} {cmd}")
bad_order = [dockerfile[0], dockerfile[4], dockerfile[1], dockerfile[2], dockerfile[3]]
n_bad = sum(s == "rebuild" for _, s in rebuild({"code"}, bad_order))
print(f"\nsame Dockerfile with app.py copied first: a one-line code change rebuilds {n_bad} of 5 layers, including pip install")
Output
you changed: code
  cached   FROM python:3.10-slim
  cached   COPY requirements.txt .
  cached   RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
  cached   COPY model.joblib .
  rebuild  COPY app.py .
you changed: requirements
  cached   FROM python:3.10-slim
  rebuild  COPY requirements.txt .
  rebuild  RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
  rebuild  COPY model.joblib .
  rebuild  COPY app.py .

same Dockerfile with app.py copied first: a one-line code change rebuilds 4 of 5 layers, including pip install
How to read it

With dependencies installed before the code is copied, a code change rebuilds just one layer. Changing requirements rightly rebuilds from pip install onwards. But copy the app code first and every one-line code change rebuilds 4 of 5 layers, reinstalling every package each time. Put things that change rarely at the top of a Dockerfile.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 1Storage and ComputeNEXT · SECTION 3Resource Management
Book / Chapter 10 / Section 3
Section 3 of 4 · Summary

Resource Management

With finite data-centre resources, giving one job more meant giving another less. In the cloud, the question shifts from squeezing out utilisation to spending cost-effectively. Engineers' time usually costs more than compute, so automation that wastes a little compute but saves people's time is often worth it. ML workflows have two features that shape this: they are repetitive (retrain weekly, predict every four hours) and full of dependencies.

3.1Cron, schedulers, DAGs3.2Schedulers and orchestrators3.3Workflow management tools
3.1

Cron, schedulers and DAGs

Play · Run the workflow

Cron runs a script at a fixed time and reports success or failure. That's all: it can't say "run B if A succeeds, C if A fails".

Real workflows have dependencies: pull data, extract features, train models A and B, compare, then deploy the better one (a conditional dependency). Drawn out, that's a DAG, a directed acyclic graph: directed to express order, acyclic so it can't loop forever. A scheduler is cron that understands DAGs: it runs steps in order, starts jobs on events, retries failures, and queues jobs until the resources they need are free. Slurm, for example, takes a start time, memory and CPU count for each job.

Code lab · Python

A tiny scheduler: topological order, a condition, and retries

Step 7 defines the workflow above as a dict of dependencies and runs it in dependency order (a topological sort). The data pull times out once; the deploy steps run only if their condition holds.

Python · step 7 · from cron to a scheduler: a DAG with conditions and retries
flaky = {"pull_data": 1}                                   # this task fails once, then succeeds
def task(name, ctx):
    if flaky.get(name, 0) > 0:
        flaky[name] -= 1
        raise RuntimeError("warehouse timeout")
    if name == "train_A": ctx["auc_A"] = 0.81
    if name == "train_B": ctx["auc_B"] = 0.84

dag = {"pull_data": [], "features": ["pull_data"], "train_A": ["features"], "train_B": ["features"],
       "compare": ["train_A", "train_B"], "deploy_A": ["compare"], "deploy_B": ["compare"]}
when = {"deploy_A": lambda c: c["auc_A"] >= c["auc_B"], "deploy_B": lambda c: c["auc_B"] > c["auc_A"]}

def run(dag, retries=2):
    indeg = {t: len(d) for t, d in dag.items()}
    ready, ctx, log = deque(t for t, k in indeg.items() if k == 0), {}, []
    while ready:
        t = ready.popleft()
        if t in when and not when[t](ctx):
            log.append(f"skip     {t} (condition false)")
        else:
            for attempt in range(retries + 1):
                try:
                    task(t, ctx); log.append(f"ok       {t}" + (f" (after {attempt} retry)" if attempt else "")); break
                except RuntimeError as e:
                    log.append(f"retry    {t}: {e}")
        for nxt, deps in dag.items():
            if t in deps:
                indeg[nxt] -= 1
                if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                    ready.append(nxt)
    return log
print("\n".join(run(dag)))
Output
retry    pull_data: warehouse timeout
ok       pull_data (after 1 retry)
ok       features
ok       train_A
ok       train_B
ok       compare
skip     deploy_A (condition false)
ok       deploy_B
How to read it

The pull fails, is retried and succeeds, so the run carries on instead of dying at 2 a.m. Both models train after features are ready, the comparison waits for both, and since B scored higher, deploy_A is skipped and deploy_B runs. Cron alone could do none of that; real schedulers add queues, priorities and quotas on top.

3.2

Schedulers and orchestrators

Play · Pack jobs onto 64 GB machines

Schedulers decide when to run jobs and what resources they need; orchestrators decide where those resources come from: machines, instances, clusters, replication. If there are more jobs than machines, an orchestrator provisions more. Schedulers suit periodic jobs; orchestrators suit long-running services. The lines blur: Kubernetes, the best-known orchestrator (usually used as a managed service such as EKS or GKE), can schedule, and schedulers often run on top of orchestrators.

People's resource requests are often wrong: a job may ask for 4 GB and use 3, or peak at 4 and idle at 1–2. Google's Borg estimates real usage and reclaims the rest. A general-purpose scheduler is hard to build, and if it fails, every workflow it touches stops.

Code lab · Python

Requested memory vs real peaks

Step 8 has 40 jobs requesting 4, 8 or 16 GB but peaking at 30–90% of that. It packs them onto 64 GB machines by request, and by measured peak plus a 10% margin.

Python · step 8 · schedulers: requested vs actual resources
r = np.random.default_rng(8)
jobs = pd.DataFrame({"job": [f"job{i:02d}" for i in range(40)],
                     "requested_gb": r.choice([4, 8, 16], 40, p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15])})
jobs["actual_peak_gb"] = (jobs.requested_gb * r.uniform(0.3, 0.9, 40)).round(1)   # people over-ask for memory

def machines_needed(sizes, capacity=64):
    bins = []                                              # first-fit decreasing bin packing
    for s in sorted(sizes, reverse=True):
        for b in bins:
            if b[0] + s <= capacity:
                b[0] += s; break
        else:
            bins.append([s])
    return len(bins)

need_req, need_act = machines_needed(jobs.requested_gb), machines_needed(jobs.actual_peak_gb * 1.1)
print(f"40 jobs ask for {jobs.requested_gb.sum():.0f} GB in total but peak at {jobs.actual_peak_gb.sum():.0f} GB")
print(f"64 GB machines needed, packing by request: {need_req}")
print(f"packing by measured peak + 10% margin:   {need_act}   (what Borg-style schedulers reclaim)")
print(f"memory utilisation: {jobs.actual_peak_gb.sum() / (need_req * 64):.0%} -> {jobs.actual_peak_gb.sum() / (need_act * 64):.0%}")
Output
40 jobs ask for 240 GB in total but peak at 135 GB
64 GB machines needed, packing by request: 4
packing by measured peak + 10% margin:   3   (what Borg-style schedulers reclaim)
memory utilisation: 53% -> 70%
How to read it

The jobs ask for 240 GB but never use more than 135 GB. Packing by request needs 4 machines at 53% memory use; packing by measured peaks needs 3 at 70%. Across thousands of jobs, that's a quarter of the machines saved, which is why large schedulers measure rather than trust requests.

3.3

Data science workflow management

Play · Compare the tools

Workflow tools let you define a whole workflow as a DAG of tasks, in Python or YAML, then hand it to a scheduler and orchestrator to run.

Airflow (Airbnb, 2014) pioneered "configuration as code" and has huge integrations, but it's monolithic, its DAGs aren't parameterised, and they're static. Prefect added parameters and dynamic DAGs. Argo runs every step in its own container but uses YAML and needs Kubernetes, awkward for local testing. Kubeflow and Metaflow let the same code run in dev and prod; the book prefers Metaflow, where a decorator sets each step's libraries and resources, and adding @batch sends a step to the cloud.

Code lab · Python

Static vs parameterised, dynamic workflows

Step 9 builds a workflow two ways: a static list of steps with the learning rate baked in, and a function that creates one featurise step per clinic found in the database today and one training step per learning rate.

Python · step 9 · parameterised and dynamic workflows
def static_workflow():
    return ["load", "featurize", "train_lr_0.01", "evaluate"]       # learning rate baked in; fixed steps

def dynamic_workflow(learning_rates, clinics):
    steps = ["load"]
    steps += [f"featurize[{c}]" for c in clinics]                  # one step per clinic, known only at run time
    steps += [f"train[lr={lr}]" for lr in learning_rates]          # one step per parameter value
    steps += ["pick_best", "evaluate"]
    return steps

print("static DAG:", static_workflow())
todays_clinics = ["Andheri", "Bandra", "Thane", "Powai"]          # read from the database this morning
flow = dynamic_workflow([0.01, 0.03, 0.1], todays_clinics)
print(f"\nparameterised + dynamic DAG ({len(flow)} steps):")
print(" ", " -> ".join(flow[:3]), "...")
print(" ", " | ".join(flow[5:8]))
print(f"\ntomorrow there are 6 clinics: the dynamic DAG makes {len(dynamic_workflow([0.01, 0.03, 0.1], todays_clinics + ['Vashi', 'Borivali']))} steps; the static one still makes 4")
Output
static DAG: ['load', 'featurize', 'train_lr_0.01', 'evaluate']

parameterised + dynamic DAG (10 steps):
  load -> featurize[Andheri] -> featurize[Bandra] ...
  train[lr=0.01] | train[lr=0.03] | train[lr=0.1]

tomorrow there are 6 clinics: the dynamic DAG makes 12 steps; the static one still makes 4
How to read it

The static DAG always has the same 4 steps, so trying a new learning rate means writing a new workflow, and a new clinic gets no featurise step. The parameterised, dynamic DAG builds 10 steps today and 12 tomorrow when two clinics open, without any code change. That flexibility is the main reason newer tools replaced early Airflow-style DAGs for ML.

PREVIOUS · SECTION 2Development EnvironmentNEXT · SECTION 4ML Platform
Book / Chapter 10 / Section 4
Section 4 of 4 · Summary

The ML Platform

A common story: a recommender team builds tools for feature management, model management and monitoring; the company notices other ML teams need the same, and an ML platform team is born. Platforms are new and vary, but usually include model deployment, a model store and a feature store. When choosing tools, check that they work with your cloud (or data centre), and weigh open source (self-host, more control, more maintenance) against managed services (less work, but your data may leave your systems). Finally, decide what to build and what to buy.

4.1Model deployment4.2Model store4.3Feature store4.4Build vs buy
4.1

Model deployment

Play · What should a deployment service handle?
Pick a requirement.

A deployment service pushes a model and its dependencies to production and exposes it as an endpoint: for online prediction it computes the answer; for batch prediction it fetches a precomputed one. Deployment is the most mature part of the platform: SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML and many startups (MLflow Models, Seldon, Ray Serve and others).

Check how easily a tool does both online and batch prediction; batch is often harder, and many companies run separate pipelines for each. And check whether it supports the tests from Chapter 9: shadow, canary, A/B.

Code lab · Python

One artifact, two serving modes

Step 10 trains one pipeline and serves it two ways: an online function answering one request at a time, and a batch job scoring everyone in one call and storing the results. It checks the two agree.

Python · step 10 · one model, served online and in batch
r = np.random.default_rng(10)
X = r.normal(0, 1, (5000, 4)); y = (X @ [1.2, -0.8, 0.5, 0.3] + r.normal(0, 1, 5000) > 0).astype(int)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X, y)

def predict_online(features):                              # endpoint: one request, answered now
    return float(model.predict_proba(np.array(features).reshape(1, -1))[0, 1])

batch_table = dict(enumerate(model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]))  # batch job: everyone, stored for lookup
t0 = time.perf_counter(); online = [predict_online(X[i]) for i in range(1000)]; t_online = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); _ = model.predict_proba(X); t_batch = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"online:  1,000 requests one at a time in {t_online * 1000:.0f} ms")
print(f"batch:   5,000 rows in one call in {t_batch * 1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"same artifact, same answers: {np.allclose(online, [batch_table[i] for i in range(1000)])}")
Output
online:  1,000 requests one at a time in 69 ms
batch:   5,000 rows in one call in 1.0 ms
same artifact, same answers: True
How to read it

Serving 1,000 requests one by one takes tens of milliseconds; scoring 5,000 rows in one batch call takes a millisecond or two (exact times vary). Both use the same artifact and give identical answers. A good deployment setup makes both modes use one model and one feature definition, so they can't drift apart.

4.2

The model store

Play · Eight artifacts worth storing
Pick an artifact.

"Just put the model file in S3" falls apart the first time something goes wrong. A model misbehaves for some inputs: who owns it, among 20 data scientists? The owner reproduces it locally and gets different outputs. Is it the wrong model binary, the wrong feature list, outdated featurising code, or a pipeline bug? And what if the owner has left?

So store everything needed to explain and rebuild a model, much of which also belongs in its model card. In practice these artifacts end up scattered (S3, a container registry, Snowflake, an experiment tracker, serverless functions), tracked in a README that gets lost. MLflow is the most popular independent model store, yet artifact storage is its most-asked-about problem, so companies such as Stitch Fix built their own.

Code lab · Python

Answer "who owns it?" and "why is prod different?"

Step 11 stores two versions of a no-show model with their artifacts, then compares a data scientist's local notebook setup with what production is actually running.

Python · step 11 · a model store that can answer "why is prod different?"
def card(**kw):
    return kw
store = {
    "noshow:v7": card(owner="noshow-team@clinic-ml", task="no-show risk", framework="scikit-learn 1.4.2",
                      params_uri="s3://models/noshow/v7.joblib", features=["age", "missed_before", "distance_km"],
                      featurize_commit="a1c9e2f", data="appointments@dvc:4f2a", image="ecr/noshow:1.4",
                      test_auc=0.771, hyperparams={"C": 1.0}),
    "noshow:v8": card(owner="noshow-team@clinic-ml", task="no-show risk", framework="scikit-learn 1.4.2",
                      params_uri="s3://models/noshow/v8.joblib", features=["age", "missed_before", "distance_km", "sms_reminder"],
                      featurize_commit="d77b310", data="appointments@dvc:9e01", image="ecr/noshow:1.5",
                      test_auc=0.789, hyperparams={"C": 0.5}),
}
production = "noshow:v8"
local_notebook = {"features": ["age", "missed_before", "distance_km"], "featurize_commit": "a1c9e2f"}

print(f"who owns {production}? {store[production]['owner']}")
print("\nwhy does the local copy disagree with production?")
for k, v in local_notebook.items():
    if store[production][k] != v:
        print(f"  {k:<17} local {v}  vs  production {store[production][k]}")
print(f"\nartifacts tracked per version: {', '.join(store[production])}")
Output
who owns noshow:v8? noshow-team@clinic-ml

why does the local copy disagree with production?
  features          local ['age', 'missed_before', 'distance_km']  vs  production ['age', 'missed_before', 'distance_km', 'sms_reminder']
  featurize_commit  local a1c9e2f  vs  production d77b310

artifacts tracked per version: owner, task, framework, params_uri, features, featurize_commit, data, image, test_auc, hyperparams
How to read it

The owner is one lookup away. The difference is found in seconds: production runs v8, which uses an extra sms_reminder feature and newer featurising code (commit d77b310), while the notebook still matches v7. Without a store recording features, code commit, data version and image together, finding that could take days.

4.3

The feature store

Play · Three problems a feature store solves

"Feature store" means different things to different vendors, but it addresses three problems. Management: Uber had about 10,000 features by 2017, and one team's churn feature may help another's conversion model; a store acts as a searchable catalogue with access rules for sensitive features (Amundsen, DataHub). Computation: compute expensive features once and store them, like a warehouse. Consistency: one definition for training (batch) and serving (streaming), instead of rewriting Python features in Java for production.

Feast is the most popular open-source store (strongest on batch); Tecton is managed and covers streaming; SageMaker and Databricks have their own. In the book's 2022 survey of 95 companies, about 40% used a feature store, and half of those built their own.

Code lab · Python

A feature registry with ownership, caching and one definition

Step 12 registers features with a decorator that records owner and sensitivity, serves a slow feature to three models through a cache, and computes the same feature for training and for serving from the one definition.

Python · step 12 · a feature store: define once, compute once, serve consistently
calls = defaultdict(int)
REGISTRY = {}
def feature(name, owner, sensitive=False):
    def wrap(fn):
        REGISTRY[name] = {"fn": fn, "owner": owner, "sensitive": sensitive}
        return fn
    return wrap

@feature("avg_prep_time_yesterday", owner="kitchen-ops")
def avg_prep(orders):
    calls["avg_prep_time_yesterday"] += 1
    time.sleep(0.05)                                       # pretend this is an expensive warehouse query
    return orders.groupby("restaurant").prep_min.mean()

@feature("customer_income_band", owner="finance", sensitive=True)
def income(orders):
    return orders.groupby("restaurant").size() * 0

cache = {}
def get(name, orders):                                     # compute once, then reuse for every model
    if name not in cache:
        cache[name] = REGISTRY[name]["fn"](orders)
    return cache[name]

r = np.random.default_rng(12)
orders = pd.DataFrame({"restaurant": r.choice(list("ABCDE"), 2000), "prep_min": r.gamma(4, 5, 2000)})
for model_name in ["eta_model", "ranking_model", "staffing_model"]:
    get("avg_prep_time_yesterday", orders)
print(f"3 models used avg_prep_time_yesterday; it was computed {calls['avg_prep_time_yesterday']} time(s)")
print("catalogue:", {k: {"owner": v["owner"], "sensitive": v["sensitive"]} for k, v in REGISTRY.items()})

batch_value = get("avg_prep_time_yesterday", orders)["C"]                 # used for training
online_value = REGISTRY["avg_prep_time_yesterday"]["fn"](orders)["C"]     # computed at request time, same code
print(f"restaurant C: training value {batch_value:.2f} min, serving value {online_value:.2f} min -> consistent: {np.isclose(batch_value, online_value)}")
Output
3 models used avg_prep_time_yesterday; it was computed 1 time(s)
catalogue: {'avg_prep_time_yesterday': {'owner': 'kitchen-ops', 'sensitive': False}, 'customer_income_band': {'owner': 'finance', 'sensitive': True}}
restaurant C: training value 19.45 min, serving value 19.45 min -> consistent: True
How to read it

Three models asked for "average prep time yesterday", and the expensive query ran once. The catalogue shows who owns each feature and flags the finance one as sensitive. And because training and serving call the same function, restaurant C gets 19.45 minutes in both, with no train/serve skew of the kind Chapter 7 warned about.

4.4

Build vs buy

Play · Three questions

At one extreme, buy a complete ML application from a vendor and only move data in and out. At the other, with highly sensitive data, build everything, even your own data centre. Most companies mix: compute from AWS, a warehouse from Snowflake, their own feature store and dashboards. Managed Databricks might need one engineer; self-hosted Spark clusters, five more.

Three factors drive the choice: your stage (buy to move fast early; build when vendor costs balloon), your focus ("if we want to be really good at it, we build it", as Stitch Fix put it; non-tech companies usually buy), and tool maturity (if nothing fits, you build). Building isn't automatically cheaper: it needs engineers, and custom infrastructure makes adopting new tools harder later.

Code lab · Python

Three years of buy vs build for a growing product

Step 13 compares a vendor charging per prediction plus a platform fee with an in-house build (two engineers for six months, then one, plus infrastructure), as usage grows 12% a month. All prices are illustrative.

Python · step 13 · build vs buy over three years
months = np.arange(1, 37)
predictions_m = 2e6 * 1.12 ** (months - 1)                 # usage grows 12% a month
vendor = 0.0004 * predictions_m + 1500                      # per-prediction fee + platform fee ($)
build = np.where(months <= 6, 2 * 9000, 1 * 9000) + 0.00004 * predictions_m + 800   # engineers + infra
cum_v, cum_b = vendor.cumsum(), build.cumsum()
cross = int(np.argmax(vendor > build)) + 1
print(f"month 1:  vendor ${vendor[0]:>8,.0f}   build ${build[0]:>8,.0f}")
print(f"month {cross}: vendor's monthly bill passes the in-house cost")
print(f"month 36: vendor ${vendor[-1]:>8,.0f}   build ${build[-1]:>8,.0f}")
print(f"3-year total: vendor ${cum_v[-1]:,.0f}   build ${cum_b[-1]:,.0f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3))
ax.plot(months, vendor / 1000, label="buy (vendor)", color="#D97E06")
ax.plot(months, build / 1000, label="build (in-house)", color="#1C7FD0")
ax.set(xlabel="month", ylabel="monthly cost ($ thousand)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
Output
month 1:  vendor $   2,300   build $  18,880
month 23: vendor's monthly bill passes the in-house cost
month 36: vendor $  43,740   build $  14,024
3-year total: vendor $441,570   build $445,557
How to read it

Buying is far cheaper at first ($2,300 vs about $19,000 a month) and lets the team focus on the product. Usage growth eventually flips that: by month 23, the vendor bill passes the in-house cost, and by month 36 it's three times higher. Over the full three years the totals are almost equal. The real question is timing: buy now, and plan when (or whether) to build.

Book / Chapter 10 / Recap
Chapter 10 · Wrap-up

Recap, mind map & quiz

Bringing models to production is largely an infrastructure problem. Storage and compute are commoditised, though cloud costs grow with you. The dev environment is where productivity is won or lost. Resource management turns repetitive, interdependent ML work into reliable workflows. And an ML platform gives every team shared deployment, model and feature stores. What you build and what you buy is one of the most important decisions an infrastructure lead makes. Next, the final chapter: the people side of ML.

Eight takeaways

In our words.

1. Right-size itA notebook for one-off analysis; shared infrastructure at reasonable scale.
2. Benchmark, don't trust FLOPSUtilisation is what your job really gets.
3. Cloud for burstsRevisit the maths as steady usage grows.
4. Invest in the dev environmentPinned packages, one Python, ideally one machine type.
5. Containers carry the environmentOrder Dockerfile layers from rarely to often changed.
6. DAGs, not cronDependencies, conditions, retries; parameterised and dynamic.
7. Store every artifactOwner, features, code commit, data version, image, metrics.
8. One feature definitionShare, compute once, serve the same in training and production.

Book / Chapter 11
Chapter 11 · Broad summary

The Human Side of Machine Learning

ML systems aren't only technical: they're built by people, used by people, and leave marks on society. This last chapter looks at user experience (ML is probabilistic, mostly right and sometimes slow, so design for that), team structure (bringing in domain experts, and whether data scientists should own everything end to end), and responsible AI: two real failures, and a practical framework for fairness, privacy, transparency and accountability.

The chapter in one minute

  1. User experience. Keep the interface consistent even when predictions change; when predictions are only mostly right, show several options people can judge; and when a model is slow, fall back smoothly to a faster backup.
  2. Team structure. Involve subject-matter experts across the whole lifecycle, not only for labelling. Separate dev and ops teams create handoffs and finger-pointing; end-to-end data scientists work only with good tools underneath.
  3. When AI goes wrong. An exam-grading algorithm optimised the wrong objective, skipped fine-grained evaluation and lacked transparency. An "anonymised" fitness heatmap exposed military bases.
  4. Responsible AI. Find where bias enters; know the limits of data; understand trade-offs (privacy vs accuracy, compactness vs fairness); act early; write model cards; build processes; keep learning.
